item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves.

If you have built agents that need to answer questions from current web sources, you know the pattern: call a search API, decide which results to trust, retrieve and clean page content, prompt a model to synthesize, and engineer citation extraction so the output traces back to a source. Every step is code you maintain, and every step is another place things can go wrong: hallucination when evidence is insufficient, stale content when the index moves, and broken attribution when a claim and its source drift apart.

The Web Answer collapses that entire pipeline into one request. You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent.

What Web Answer does

Figure 1: Request flow from an agent through the Gateway to Web Answer and back

Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result.

Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back:

  • A grounded, cited answer, where each grounded claim maps to a citation, with a source URL where one is available.
  • Current sources. Web Answer runs new searches for every question, and its model is given today’s date so it can search for up-to-date information.
  • Agentic search: Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, reads pages to verify facts, and decides when it has enough evidence to answer.
  • Responsible AI safeguards: Web Answer is designed and tested with responsible AI safeguards.

Figure 2: Demo video showing how to add Web Answer to an AgentCore Gateway, from setup to a finished, cited answer

How it differs from Web Search

Web Answer and the Web Search tools both support retrieval use cases, with different levels of integration complexity. The dividing line is who runs the model:

  • Web Search: Returns ranked URLs, titles, snippets, and metadata. You keep your own model and control the synthesis. Use Web Search when you want full control over how results are processed.
  • Web Answer: Runs the model, the agentic retrieval loop, synthesis, and attribution for you. You get a finished, cited answer. Use Web Answer when the question is a sub-task inside a larger agent and you do not want to own a retrieval pipeline for it.

Many customers will use both. An agent might use Web Search for broad research tasks where it needs raw results, and Web Answer for specific factual questions where it needs a quick, cited answer.

Set up and invoke Web Answer

Web Answer is a connector that AWS owns. You reference it by ID, and the Gateway handles the tool schema, parameter governance, endpoint resolution, and authentication to the backend. In this walkthrough, you give your Gateway’s service role permission to call Web Answer, add a Web Answer target, and call it from a Strands agent.

Getting started

Getting started takes minutes. A Gateway administrator adds Web Answer as a target on an existing AgentCore Gateway, and the tool appears to any attached agent over MCP through tools/list and tools/call.

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with AgentCore Gateway access.
  • An AgentCore Gateway in us-east-1 that uses IAM (AWS_IAM) inbound authentication. To create one, see Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway in the Developer Guide.
  • AWS credentials for an identity that has bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway on the Gateway, and Amazon Bedrock access to the model your agent uses.
  • Python 3.10 or later, with the required packages: pip install boto3 strands-agents mcp mcp-proxy-for-aws

Note: Following these steps creates AWS resources that incur charges. The Gateway and Web Answer invocations are billable. See the Pricing section that follows for details, and when you finish, delete the resources you created (see “Clean up resources”).

Step 1: Grant the Gateway service role access to Web Answer

The Gateway uses its service role to act on your behalf. The role’s trust policy allows bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com to assume it, scoped to your account. For Web Answer, the role needs:

  • bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer, to call Web Answer. The Gateway checks this permission on every request against the ARN that AWS owns, arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:aws:tool/web-answer.v1.

Attach the policy to the service role as an inline policy:

import json
import boto3

iam = boto3.client("iam")

iam.put_role_policy(
    RoleName="<gateway-service-role>",
    PolicyName="WebAnswerGuide",
    PolicyDocument=json.dumps({
        "Version": "2012-10-17",
        "Statement": [
            {
                "Sid": "InvokeWebAnswer",
                "Effect": "Allow",
                "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer",
                "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:aws:tool/web-answer.v1",
            }
        ],
    }),
)

The role controls only the Gateway’s outbound calls. Who can call your Gateway is set by its inbound authorizer. The role also doesn’t need bedrock:InvokeModel: your agent’s model runs under your agent’s own identity.

Step 2: Create the Web Answer target

Add Web Answer as a connector target. The connectorId tells the Gateway which managed integration to provision: in this case, an agent that searches the web and writes a cited answer.

import boto3

gateway_client = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore-control", region_name="us-east-1")

target_response = gateway_client.create_gateway_target(
    name="web-answer-tool",
    gatewayIdentifier=gateway_id,
    targetConfiguration={
        "mcp": {
            "connector": {
                "source": {"connectorId": "web-answer"},
                "configurations": [{"name": "WebAnswer", "parameterValues": {}}],
            }
        }
    },
    credentialProviderConfigurations=[
        {"credentialProviderType": "GATEWAY_IAM_ROLE"}
    ],
)
target_id = target_response["targetId"]

Outbound authentication is automatic for connectors. With GATEWAY_IAM_ROLE, the Gateway calls the Web Answer backend with the service role from Step 1, so you don’t create or store any credentials for the tool. Wait until get_gateway_target reports the target status as READY before you call it.

As the Gateway administrator, you can also set a domain filter on the target. The filter applies to every call that goes through the target. To limit the target to a set of domains, set parameterValues to {"domainFilter": {"include": ["bis.org"], "exclude": ["unreliable-source.net"]}}.

Step 3: Invoke Web Answer from a Strands agent

Your agent discovers Web Answer through the Gateway’s tools/list and calls it with tools/call, like any other MCP tool. This works with Strands Agents, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, or any other MCP-compatible client.

from strands import Agent
from strands.models.bedrock import BedrockModel
from strands.tools.mcp import MCPClient
from mcp_proxy_for_aws.client import aws_iam_streamablehttp_client

gateway_url = "https://gateway-<id>.gateway.bedrock-agentcore.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/mcp"

mcp_client = MCPClient(lambda: aws_iam_streamablehttp_client(
    endpoint=gateway_url,
    aws_region="us-east-1",
    aws_service="bedrock-agentcore",
    aws_profile="<aws-profile-id>",  # identity with bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway on the Gateway
))

model = BedrockModel(model_id="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens=1024)

with mcp_client:
    tools = mcp_client.list_tools_sync()  # Web Answer tool discovered from the Gateway
    agent = Agent(model=model, tools=tools)

    result = agent("What are the Basel III minimum requirements for Tier 1 capital?")
    print(result.message)

When a question needs current information, your agent calls the Web Answer tool (web-answer-tool___WebAnswer). Web Answer runs the agentic search and returns a finished answer with citations.

Besides the question, the Web Answer tool takes optional arguments that your agent can set on each call: a domain filter to include or exclude sites, a published-date range, and a country to localize results. The agent’s domain filter is combined with the target’s filter. The agent can exclude more domains, or limit results to some of the target’s included domains, but it can’t add a domain that the target’s filter blocks.

Response format

Web Answer returns an MCP tool result with both content and structuredContent fields. The answer is markdown text with inline citation markers like [1], and structuredContent.answer carries the same text alongside a structured citations list:

{
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "Under Basel III, banks must hold Common Equity Tier 1 capital of at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets [[1](https://www.bis.org/...)]..."
    }
  ],
  "structuredContent": {
    "answer": [
      {
        "text": "Under Basel III, banks must hold Common Equity Tier 1 capital of at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets [[1](https://www.bis.org/...)]...",
        "citations": [
          { "domain": "bis.org", "url": "https://www.bis.org/..." }
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  "isError": false,
  "_meta": {
    "latencyMs": 5210
  }
}

structuredContent.answer normally holds a single block. Each citation carries the source url and, when available, the domain.

Clean up resources

Delete the Web Answer target when you no longer need it:

gateway_client.delete_gateway_target(gatewayIdentifier=gateway_id, targetId=target_id)

If you created the Gateway only for this walkthrough, delete its targets first, then the Gateway (delete_gateway), and then the service role and its policy. There is no persistent infrastructure on the AWS side beyond these resources. After they are removed, you stop incurring charges.

Enterprise controls, built in

Web Answer inherits the same enterprise controls as other AgentCore tools:

  • Gateway authentication. No separate API key to provision, rotate, or manage for Web Answer. Callers authenticate to the gateway with the inbound method you configure, such as AWS IAM (SigV4) or a JSON Web Token from your identity provider. The gateway then calls Web Answer with its own service role, which needs the bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer permission.
  • VPC and AWS PrivateLink. Your agents can call the gateway through an interface virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint (com.amazonaws.us-east-1.bedrock-agentcore.gateway), so traffic stays off the public internet.
  • Zero data egress. Your queries and results stay within your AWS environment.
  • Amazon CloudWatch metrics. Operational metrics publish to CloudWatch from the first call.
  • Per-account rate limits. Enforced from launch, with 10 transactions per second per account in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1). To request an increase, contact AWS Support.
  • Admin-time policy bounds. The Gateway administrator sets domain filter bounds at target setup. Agents can narrow the filter bounds on each call but can’t widen them.
  • Queries stay within AWS. Web Answer searches an Amazon-operated web index and Amazon’s knowledge graph, and doesn’t send your question to third-party search engines or external websites.

Use cases

Web Answer helps agents retrieve current, cited information to support a range of knowledge-intensive workflows. Example scenarios include:

  • Financial services. Regulatory Q&A agents answering questions about compliance requirements, market regulations, and policy changes, where every answer must trace to an authoritative source.
  • Healthcare. Clinical support agents grounding responses in current medical literature and treatment guidelines published on the web.
  • Customer service. Support agents answering product and policy questions in real time, where ten ranked links are not useful and a cited answer is.
  • Legal and compliance. Research assistants answering questions about case law, regulatory filings, and policy interpretations with auditable citations.
  • Enterprise knowledge workers. Internal copilots that answer questions from current public information without requiring employees to build their own search and synthesis workflow.

Availability

Web Answer is available in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), with more AWS Regions coming soon.

Pricing

Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is priced at $10 per 1,000 tool calls.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how Web Answer gives your agents current, cited answers through agentic search, with no search pipeline for you to build or maintain. We granted a Gateway service role access to Web Answer, added a Web Answer target, called it from a Strands agent, and read the answer and its citations from the response. Use Web Search on AgentCore when your own model should reason over raw results, and Web Answer when your agent needs a finished, cited answer.

To get started, see:

  • Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation
  • Web Answer structured output schema
  • Adding Web Answer to an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
  • Supported regions

About the authors

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon…
item.description: Full title: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI

A+ Content is the rich media widget on the Amazon product detail page. Through visual assets, brands communicate unique product and brand value to help customers make informed purchase decisions. Selling partners using high-quality A+ Content boost their sales by 8–20 percent compared to those without it. A wide variety of brands, from established brands with large in-house design teams to bootstrapped brands with limited resources, use A+ Content, creating inconsistency in content quality. A typical A+ Content project combines text, images, and video into a cohesive product story. Evaluating each asset in isolation misses the quality that emerges from how those assets work together. When your content spans multiple heterogeneous modules and you need a holistic quality signal rather than per-asset checks, the multi-model fusion approach described in this post can help. In this post, we examine this problem in the context of A+ Content.

A+ Content provides creative freedom for selling partners to express their authentic selves on their product detail pages, without strict content specifications such as image ratio and text word count.

Although this flexibility allows compelling brand storytelling, it also creates substantial variation in content composition and quality.

With quality evaluation and improvement recommendations, brands can transform average content into high-quality content that is more coherent, relevant, and useful. This improved content helps customers make more informed purchasing decisions and build lasting relationships with brands, leading to improved revenue for selling partners.

To achieve this goal, an evaluation system must assess the complete content experience, provide actionable recommendations beyond numeric scores, and reflect the nuances across product categories. Existing approaches struggle to meet all these requirements simultaneously, so in this post, you will see a new approach using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to understand and evaluate content holistically, and a diffusion-based generation component that produces improved visual assets from the resulting quality signals.

In this post, you will learn how to:

  • Render complete ecommerce content as a single snapshot and evaluate it holistically with a VLM.
  • Combine VLM semantic scores with OCR readability signals in a lightweight CatBoost classifier trained on expert annotations.
  • Use SHAP to explain quality decisions and generate actionable improvement recommendations for selling partners.
  • Implement the end-to-end pipeline on Amazon SageMaker AI, from data ingestion and annotation through model hosting, explainability, and production monitoring.

Opportunities and challenges in VLM-based evaluation

A vision language model (VLM) pairs an image encoder with a large language model (LLM). The encoder, often a vision transformer (ViT), splits an image into patches and turns them into embeddings, and a small connector maps those embeddings into the language model’s input space (Flamingo, LLaVA). Many VLMs reuse the image encoder from CLIP, which learned to match images with their captions. Because VLMs are trained to follow instructions, you can give one an image along with a rubric of evaluation criteria and get back a written assessment without task-specific training. When you need closer agreement with human reviewers, you can fine-tune the model on labeled examples. This makes VLMs a practical starting point for checking product images against your content guidelines at scale.

Conventional computer vision models can already score individual assets, for example flagging a blurry image or a grammar error in a bullet list. Using a VLM to grade each asset separately adds little beyond that. A product detail page, however, combines images, text, and layout modules into a single story, and its quality depends on how those pieces work together. Our approach renders the full page as a single snapshot and asks the VLM to evaluate it as customers see it.

Consider a blender page with a hero image, a bulleted feature list highlighting blade speed and capacity, and a lifestyle photo of the blender in a modern kitchen. Checked one by one, each asset passes: the image is sharp, the bullets are grammatical, and the photo is well lit. Viewed together, problems appear. The bullets might advertise a 64-oz pitcher while the lifestyle photo shows a single-serve model, or the lifestyle photo might sit above the hero image so customers see the kitchen before the product. Because an asset’s meaning depends on where it appears and what surrounds it, these issues only show up when the page is evaluated as a whole. The snapshot gives the VLM that complete view. Using it in production adds three requirements: scores must match expert quality standards, evaluation must be accurate and efficient at scale, and each result must explain what to fix.

As shown in Figure 1, we address these considerations through a VLM-based multi-model fusion architecture designed around adaptability, performance, and explainability. The following sections describe each component.

Figure 1: Block diagram of the VLM-based multi-model fusion approach, including VLM, OCR, and classifier models

Adaptive VLM content evaluation with expert annotations

A pretrained VLM prompted with a rubric scores content from its general knowledge, and those scores don’t always match ecommerce quality standards. Fine-tuning the VLM to close that gap would require GPU training infrastructure and, with only a few thousand labeled examples, carries a real risk of overfitting. Instead, we keep the VLM and rubric prompt fixed, use the VLM’s structured outputs as features, and train a CatBoost classifier on them to predict expert quality labels. CatBoost, a gradient-boosted decision tree library, performs well on small tabular datasets like this one. Because only the classifier is retrained, updating the system as annotations accumulate or criteria change takes a short CPU-only job rather than a foundation model fine-tuning run.

The VLM receives the page snapshot and a rubric prompt covering four quality dimensions: Visual Storytelling, Feature Presentation, A+ Layout, and Conversion Optimization. Each dimension has explicit criteria and point-deduction rules. For each dimension, the VLM returns a score from 0 to 10, a confidence value, and a natural-language rationale. For example, it lowers the score and explains why when a page lacks diverse modules or lifestyle imagery, or repeats information. The scores and confidence values become the classifier’s features, and the rationales help selling partners understand the result.

To build the training labels, one ecommerce marketing expert and four professional annotators independently rated 5,478 product detail pages from 10 product categories as high or low quality, using the same criteria. We assessed their ratings and took the majority vote to create a consensus label. The classes are nearly balanced (49.6 percent high quality), so a classifier can’t score well by predicting the majority class. To measure label reliability, we used Cohen’s kappa, which measures how often two raters agree after accounting for the agreement they would reach by chance. A score of 0 means agreement is no better than chance, 1 means perfect agreement, and values above 0.8 are generally considered strong. Each annotator scored between 0.845 and 0.915 when compared against the consensus label.

Figure 2: Annotator performance and content difficulty distribution. The near-even class split rules out majority-class bias (left), and the difficulty distribution explains the residual disagreement (right)

We compared the classifier with a baseline on a 20 percent holdout set (about 1,100 pages). The baseline averages the four VLM scores and applies a fixed threshold, so every dimension counts equally. The baseline reached 0.80 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.84 on the high-quality class. The CatBoost classifier, trained on the same scores, reached 0.89 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.90. Because the classifier learns how much each dimension matters and how the dimensions interact, its predictions match expert decisions more closely.

High-performance VLM content evaluation with OCR

VLMs capture the overall meaning and visual composition of a page well, but they are less reliable at fine-grained readability issues, such as how crowded the text is or how much space separates lines. Because of their language-model foundation, they can also favor long, detailed descriptions even when customers prefer concise text they can scan quickly. On a text-heavy page, a VLM might rate dense product information as helpful while customers struggle to read long sentences packed into a small area. To capture these issues, we use an optical character recognition (OCR) model hosted on SageMaker AI Inference to extract each block of text and its position, then calculate four quantitative signals: Text Density, Character Density, Spacing, and Overall Readability. Combining these OCR scores with the VLM’s semantic and visual assessment adds complementary information that improves quality classification.

From that output, we calculate four readability scores:

  • Text Density: The share of the page area covered by text.
  • Character Density: The number of characters per unit of page area.
  • Spacing: How consistent and sufficient the whitespace is between words, lines, and paragraphs.
  • Overall Readability: A combined signal from the three preceding scores.

Because these scores depend on layout rather than wording, two pages with identical text can score differently.

The fusion model combines the four VLM rubric scores and the four OCR scores into eight features and trains a CatBoost classifier on the same expert labels. Table 1 compares it with models trained on each feature set alone, using the same 20 percent holdout set.

On the same 20 percent holdout set, the CatBoost model using only OCR features achieved 0.82 accuracy and a 0.83 F1 score, while the model using only VLM features achieved 0.89 and 0.90. The fused OCR-VLM-CatBoost model outperformed both standalone models, reaching 0.94 accuracy and a 0.95 F1 score. The 0.05 improvement in both metrics over the VLM-only model demonstrates that OCR isn’t a replacement signal. It complements the VLM’s holistic judgment with fine-grained text-readability information.

ConfigurationAccuracyF1 Score
Baseline (averaged VLM scores + threshold)0.800.84
OCR-only CatBoost0.820.83
VLM-only CatBoost0.890.90
Fused OCR-VLM CatBoost0.940.95

Explainable VLM content evaluation with SHAP

A quality label alone doesn’t tell selling partners what to fix first. To find which dimensions drove each decision, we use SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), which assigns each feature a value showing how far it pushed a prediction toward high or low quality. Because the VLM and OCR scores feed the same classifier, SHAP measures both on a common scale. Raw scores can’t do this: a Visual Storytelling score of 6 and a high Character Density don’t tell you which one mattered more to the decision.

Across the holdout set, the most influential features were OCR Character Density (mean absolute SHAP value 1.1), OCR Overall Readability (1.0), and VLM Visual Storytelling (1.0). They were followed by A+ Layout (0.8), Feature Presentation (0.6), and Conversion Optimization (0.4). Both OCR and VLM features rank near the top, so the classifier depends on both sources.

Figure 3: Global SHAP value distributions for all VLM and OCR features

For an individual page, SHAP shows which features lowered the decision. For each page classified as low quality, we rank the eight features by SHAP value, then pass the most negative features, the product category, and ecommerce best practices, along with the VLM’s rationales, to an LLM, which turns them into prioritized, specific actions.

Figure 4 shows two local SHAP plots with the LLM reasoning grounded in the SHAP results, for a low-quality and a high-quality A+ Content sample. For example, if A+ Layout has a SHAP value of -1.2 and Visual Storytelling has -0.3, the system prioritizes restructuring the layout and rebalancing text and images, followed by improvements to the imagery.

Figure 4: Two local SHAP value distributions for all VLM and OCR features: (a) a low-quality case, where most features contribute negatively and drive an improvement-requested recommendation; (b) a high-quality case, where most features contribute positively

We validated the effectiveness of these explanation-based recommendations by measuring quality scores after selling partners revised their content. The average post-revision quality score increased by 1.4 points on a 10-point scale on a statistically significant sample. SHAP contributions can therefore be translated from decision explanations into actionable improvement priorities and methods. Explainability is therefore not merely an auxiliary capability for understanding the model. It functions as a feedback mechanism that materially improves content quality.

Results

The complete system scores each page snapshot with the VLM and OCR, combines the four VLM scores and four OCR scores into a single feature vector, and passes it to a CatBoost classifier trained on expert labels. SHAP then identifies which features drove each decision. To measure what each component adds, we compared four configurations on the same 20 percent holdout set. The holdout set comes from 5,478 product detail pages across 10 product categories, including Furniture, Shoes, Grocery, Beauty, and Apparel.

The baseline averages the four VLM scores and applies a fixed threshold, so every dimension counts equally. It reached 0.80 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.84. Training a CatBoost classifier on the same scores lets the model learn which dimensions matter most and how they interact, which raised accuracy to 0.89 and F1 to 0.90. A classifier trained on the OCR scores alone reached 0.82 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.83. Combining the VLM and OCR scores gave the best results, with 0.94 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.95. That’s 14 percentage points higher accuracy and 11 points higher F1 than the baseline.

Figure 5: Accuracy and F1 comparison across VLM and OCR evaluation configurations

Examining each performance gain separately makes the value of the integrated approach clearer. CatBoost calibration first reduces the limitations of a fixed threshold by learning dimension-specific weights and nonlinear decision boundaries. Adding OCR features then supplies text-readability signals that the VLM can miss. Overall, the final fusion model improves accuracy by 0.14 and F1 by 0.11 over the baseline.

We also changed the VLM backbone in an additional experiment on a single-category dataset containing 499 content projects. With a lighter VLM variant, the baseline achieved 0.74 accuracy and a 0.72 F1 score, while the OCR-VLM-CatBoost model achieved 0.90 for both metrics. With a more capable VLM variant, the baseline achieved 0.79 accuracy and a 0.84 F1 score, while the fusion model achieved 0.94 and 0.95. The fusion approach improved accuracy by 0.16 and 0.15 for the two VLMs, respectively, demonstrating that complementary OCR features deliver consistent gains without depending on a particular foundation model.

To reduce development costs while retaining access to high-performance foundation models, the system freezes the VLM and trains only the low-overhead classifier. In production, a worldwide A/B experiment that adjusted the visibility of low-quality A+ Content based on the model’s quality decisions produced a statistically meaningful improvement in Ordered Product Sales (OPS). Beyond aligning closely with expert judgment, the integrated system provides a quality signal that can support customer-experience and business decisions at scale.

Implementation on Amazon SageMaker AI

This section describes how the architecture is implemented end-to-end on Amazon SageMaker AI. Each stage of the pipeline from content rendering and expert annotation through VLM scoring, OCR extraction, feature aggregation, classifier training, SHAP-based explainability, and production monitoring maps to a managed SageMaker AI capability. This design keeps the operational overhead low. The following steps walk through how each component is deployed, connected, and maintained in production.

Figure 6: Architecture of the content-quality system on Amazon SageMaker AI

1. Content snapshot rendering and data ingestion: The complete A+ Content experience is rendered, capturing how customers actually see the page.

SageMaker Processing Jobs run containerized rendering jobs at scale, decoupling data preparation from training and inference compute.

2. VLM scoring and model hosting: Annotators independently label content using the quality rubric. Their aggregated consensus labels become the training targets. The frozen VLM receives each snapshot plus a rubric prompt and outputs four scores from 0 to 10 (Visual Storytelling, Feature Presentation, A+ Layout, Conversion Optimization), each with a confidence value and rationale. SageMaker AI Inference hosts the VLM with the deployment option that fits the workload:

  • Real-Time Endpoints for synchronous, low-latency scoring of individual listings.
  • Asynchronous Endpoints for large payloads such as high-resolution snapshots, where a slight delay is acceptable.
  • Batch Transform for offline bulk scoring at catalog scale.

These options support automatic scaling, managed infrastructure, and GPU instance selection.

SageMaker Training Jobs can optionally be used to further tune or distill the VLM (for example, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, knowledge distillation into a smaller model) if teams want a specialized, lower-latency variant. Avoid this to keep recalibration cost-effective and VLM-agnostic.

3. OCR readability extraction: In parallel, OCR extracts text and bounding-box positions from each snapshot and computes four readability signals: Text Density, Character Density, Spacing, and Overall Readability.

SageMaker JumpStart provides pre-trained, single-action deployable models from its model hub, avoiding the need to source, package, and benchmark models from scratch. Teams select a model, optionally fine-tune it without managing infrastructure using SageMaker Serverless Model Customization on ecommerce content, and deploy directly. SageMaker AI Inference then hosts the chosen OCR model as an endpoint.

4. Feature aggregation and storage:

SageMaker Feature Store provides both online (low-latency inference) and offline (batch training) access to the same features, avoiding training-serving skew. Teams can share features across the organization, so downstream consumers can reuse the same curated features.

5. Classifier training: A CatBoost classifier is trained on the eight-dimensional feature vector against expert annotations to learn non-uniform dimension weights and nonlinear decision boundaries. SageMaker Training Jobs can be used here again. You can register trained models directly to SageMaker Model Registry for versioning, approval workflows, and production deployment.

6. SHAP explainability and recommendations: SageMaker Processing Jobs support Bring Your Own (BYO) processing code, which you can use to derive SHAP values and model explainability metrics.

7. Production monitoring and re-training: In production, ML models naturally degrade over time. Customer aesthetics shift, new A+ module types launch, product categories evolve, and seller behavior changes. The scoring patterns the classifier learned from historical annotations gradually fall out of alignment with what quality means today, leading to silent accuracy erosion if left unchecked. Continuous monitoring closes this gap by detecting when the live data distribution or model predictions have drifted far enough from the training baseline to warrant recalibration.

SageMaker AI ModelOps provides a collection of examples and resources to help you operationalize generative AI and machine learning workloads on SageMaker AI.

SageMaker AIOps provides the tool to track data quality, model quality, and feature-attribution drift. SageMaker Pipelines also automates the re-training workflow end-to-end when drift thresholds are breached.

8. Diffusion-based content generation: Closing the loop, the quality scores and SHAP-derived recommendations condition a diffusion model that generates improved A+ image assets. Rather than leaving sellers to interpret recommendations and create new content from scratch, the system produces ready-to-use visual assets (upgraded lifestyle imagery, rebalanced layouts, or enhanced product shots) that directly address the dimensions SHAP flagged as most negatively contributing. These generated assets and natural-language improvement suggestions are surfaced to sellers, so they can upgrade their listings on amazon.com.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to evaluate product detail pages as customers see them by rendering each page as a single snapshot and scoring it with a VLM. We also walked through implementing the system on Amazon SageMaker AI. We built the system around three goals. For adaptability, we keep the VLM fixed and train a CatBoost classifier on its rubric scores, so the system matches expert judgment and can be updated with a short CPU-only job. For performance, we add OCR readability scores that catch dense or poorly spaced text the VLM misses. For explainability, SHAP identifies which features drove each decision, and an LLM turns those results into prioritized recommendations for selling partners.

On 5,478 product detail pages from 10 product categories, the fused model reached 0.94 accuracy and a 0.95 F1 score, 14 and 11 percentage points above the averaged-score baseline. Pages revised using the recommendations improved their quality score by an average of 1.4 points on a scale of 10.

Content quality standards differ across product categories, languages, and marketplaces, and our expert annotations can’t fully represent every context. Next, we plan to evaluate more efficient VLM backbones and inference methods to run the system on a global catalog.

About the authors

item.title: [DeepInfra] Best MiMo-V2.6-Pro API Providers in 2026
item.content:encoded:
Best MiMo-V2.6-Pro API Providers in 2026

Published on 2026.11.05 by DeepInfra

As large language models continue to push the boundaries of context length and multimodal capabilities, Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro has emerged as a strong entrant among open-weight models. With its native omnimodal architecture — supporting text, image, video, and audio — and a 1,048,576-token context window, it opens up new paradigms for agentic workflows, long-document analysis, and complex reasoning tasks. Deploying and scaling a model of this magnitude, however, introduces real infrastructure challenges. Managing GPU memory requirements, optimizing inference latency, and controlling API costs are critical pain points for developers and enterprise architects alike.

This article surveys the SaaS tools, API providers, and infrastructure platforms available for MiMo-V2.6-Pro. Whether you need dedicated autoscaling endpoints, privacy-first routing, or cost-effective API access, this guide is meant to help identify the right environment for production workloads.

Summary of the Best MiMo-V2.6-Pro Providers

For a quick recommendation based on specific architectural needs, the table below summarizes the options covered in this guide:

ProviderBest For
DeepInfraDevelopers and enterprises seeking reliable, optimized, well-rounded API access.
XiaomiOrganizations wanting to self-host the open weights or use the official direct API.
BazaarLinkTaiwan-based enterprises needing localized billing and OpenAI-compatible API access.
EmpirioLabs AIDevelopers building agentic workflows that require live web search and structured JSON outputs.
LLM APIDevelopers building autonomous AI agents that need to manage their own API credits — see note below.
FlexAIEnterprise teams requiring dedicated, high-throughput compute and autoscaling infrastructure.
CometAPIBusinesses wanting a single API key for failover routing across hundreds of models.
MofCloudGlobal cloud teams needing regional token plans and FinOps tools — see note below.
TrustedRouterPrivacy-conscious users needing verifiable zero-logging policies and performance-based routing.

Two entries in this list — MofCloud and LLM API — could not be independently confirmed when this guide was fact-checked, and are flagged with notes in their own sections below. The other seven providers were individually verified.

DeepInfra

DeepInfra is a strong overall option for accessing and deploying MiMo-V2.6-Pro alongside other top-tier AI models. For developers and enterprises seeking a balance of performance and cost-effectiveness, DeepInfra provides an optimized inference engine that abstracts away the complexity of managing underlying GPU hardware.

Key Features

  • Strong overall solution for MiMo-V2.6-Pro
  • High-performance infrastructure
  • Cost-effective API access

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

When dealing with a model capable of processing over a million tokens, inference speed and cost predictability are paramount. DeepInfra differentiates itself with a reliable API that handles large context loads without compromising on latency, which makes it a solid choice for teams that want production-ready access to MiMo-V2.6-Pro without the overhead of managing their own clusters. Current rates are on the DeepInfra pricing page, and the quickstart guide has you making calls in minutes.

Explore MiMo-V2.6-Pro on DeepInfra.

Xiaomi

As the creator and official publisher of the MiMo-V2.6-Pro model, Xiaomi provides the foundational architecture that powers this ecosystem. By releasing the model weights under an open MIT license, Xiaomi has enabled the broader developer community to build on it freely.

Key Features

  • Official publisher of the MiMo-V2.6-Pro model
  • Provides open weights under an MIT license
  • Native omnimodal capabilities (text, image, video, audio)
  • 1,048,576-token context window

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

Xiaomi’s primary differentiator is its position as the source. For organizations with strict data governance requirements, or those with the internal MLOps expertise to manage large-scale GPU clusters, downloading the MIT-licensed weights directly from Xiaomi allows for complete control. Xiaomi also offers an official MiMo Open Platform API for direct access.

BazaarLink

BazaarLink is an OpenAI-compatible API provider that brings specialized billing and localized features to the Asian market, specifically tailored for Taiwan. It supports MiMo-V2.6-Pro’s full 1M-token context window and omnimodal inputs.

Key Features

  • $0.435 input and $0.87 output per 1M tokens
  • Cache read pricing at $0.0036 per 1M tokens
  • Supports text, image, video, and audio inputs
  • TWD billing and Taiwan uniform invoices available

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

BazaarLink is positioned for cost-efficiency in repetitive tasks through its cache read pricing, which is attractive for MiMo-V2.6-Pro users who frequently query the same large documents or system prompts. Its localized TWD billing and uniform invoices also make it a low-friction choice for Taiwan-based enterprises.

EmpirioLabs AI

EmpirioLabs AI focuses on supporting the MiMo V2.6 series for complex, long-horizon tasks. It provides an API platform that natively integrates external tooling, which suits developers building more sophisticated AI agents.

Key Features

  • Native web search integration included
  • Reasoning enabled by default
  • Function calling and structured JSON output up to 131,072 tokens
  • OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

While MiMo-V2.6-Pro has a 1M-token context window, extracting structured data reliably from massive contexts can be challenging. EmpirioLabs AI differentiates itself by guaranteeing function calling and structured JSON outputs for contexts up to 131,072 tokens. Combined with built-in web search and default reasoning, it is a solid fit for agentic workflows that need live data retrieval and strict output formatting.

LLM API

Verification note: a provider named “LLM Gateway” was independently confirmed to serve this model. A distinctly named “LLM API” with the specific “agent storefront for autonomous purchasing” feature described below could not be independently confirmed, and may be a conflation of the two. Confirm this listing directly before publishing.

LLM API is described as an infrastructure provider tailored for the machine-to-machine economy, offering MiMo-V2.6-Pro access designed for autonomous AI agents that manage their own resources.

Key Features

  • $0.435 input and $0.87 output per 1M tokens
  • Described as including a dedicated agent storefront for autonomous purchasing (unverified)
  • OpenAI-compatible client integration
  • Live prices and self-serve payment options

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

For teams building autonomous agents, the described appeal is a dedicated agent storefront that would let agents autonomously purchase API credits and manage their own usage via self-serve payment methods. At a competitive per-token rate, it could be worth evaluating — but confirm the storefront capability directly, since it wasn’t independently verifiable for this guide.

FlexAI

FlexAI targets the enterprise sector by offering MiMo V2.6 Pro RL as a dedicated, autoscaling endpoint. Instead of shared, rate-limited API access, FlexAI provisions dedicated hardware for specific workloads.

Key Features

  • Dedicated endpoint provisioned per customer
  • Runs on 16x H100 GPUs
  • Billed per minute at $33.60 per hour
  • Autoscales with traffic volume

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

Running a 1M-context omnimodal model requires serious compute. FlexAI provisions 16x H100 GPUs per customer, providing the dedicated VRAM and throughput needed for high-volume, low-latency production environments. The per-minute billing ($33.60/hour) and autoscaling make it well suited to enterprise teams with variable, high-throughput traffic spikes.

CometAPI

CometAPI is a unified API aggregator that simplifies model routing and failover. It provides access to MiMo V2.6 Pro alongside a large catalog of other AI models through a single integration point.

Key Features

  • Unified API for 500+ models
  • Discounts available below list price
  • Unified billing and failover routing
  • Supports the full 1M-token context window

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

For production systems where uptime is critical, CometAPI’s built-in failover routing is designed to redirect MiMo-V2.6-Pro requests automatically if one upstream provider experiences downtime. Access to the full 1M-token context window alongside unified billing across hundreds of models — compare the full DeepInfra model catalog for a sense of scale — makes it a useful option for complex AI stacks.

MofCloud

Verification note: this provider could not be independently confirmed when this guide was fact-checked — no independent sources turned up for MofCloud. Confirm it exists and that the figures below are current before publishing this section.

MofCloud is described as a global cloud infrastructure provider that pairs MiMo-V2.6-Pro access with enterprise-grade FinOps and cloud cost management tooling.

Key Features (as described)

  • $0.45 input and $0.89 output per 1M tokens
  • Zero cost for cache tokens
  • Regional token plans for China, Europe, and Singapore
  • FinOps and AI cost management tools

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

MofCloud’s stated differentiator is a zero-cost cache token policy, which would reduce the cost of large-context, repetitive queries, along with regional token plans and integrated FinOps tooling aimed at global teams. None of this was independently verifiable for this guide, so treat it as unconfirmed until checked directly.

TrustedRouter

TrustedRouter is an attested API gateway designed for organizations with strict data privacy and security requirements. It acts as a secure intermediary, routing requests to upstream MiMo-V2.6-Pro providers such as Lightning AI.

Key Features

  • Zero prompt or output logs policy
  • Routes to upstream providers like Lightning AI
  • Measures uptime and speed via routed probes
  • Verifies gateway attestation for security

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

When sending highly sensitive, million-token documents to an LLM, data leakage is a real concern. TrustedRouter’s zero prompt/output logs policy, backed by gateway attestation, combined with ongoing uptime and speed measurement via routed probes, is built to let privacy-conscious users avoid trading performance for security.

Conclusion and Recommendations

Deploying Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro requires weighing an application’s specific needs — whether that means managing massive context windows, handling omnimodal inputs, or controlling inference costs.

  • For enterprise and high-throughput needs: teams needing guaranteed compute and autoscaling should look to FlexAI for dedicated 16x H100 deployments.
  • For agentic workflows: developers building autonomous systems should consider EmpirioLabs AI for structured JSON and web search capabilities, or LLM API if agents require autonomous purchasing power (pending confirmation of that capability — see note above).
  • For privacy and security: TrustedRouter is a strong choice for organizations requiring verifiable zero-logging and attested routing.
  • For global and regional operations: MofCloud is described as offering FinOps tools for global teams (unconfirmed — see note above), while BazaarLink is a solid option for Taiwan-based localized billing.

The Best Overall Solution

The right fit depends on specific architectural needs, but for the majority of developers and enterprises, DeepInfra remains a strong overall solution. It offers reliable, high-performance, cost-effective API access for MiMo-V2.6-Pro, letting teams focus on building applications rather than managing complex infrastructure. For a closer look at pricing across recent releases, see our Kimi K3 vs. Claude Opus 4.8 vs. GPT-5.6 Sol comparison.

item.title: [AI21 Labs] Introducing Teel – Turbo-Efficient Execution Library for Age…
item.description: Full title: Introducing Teel – Turbo-Efficient Execution Library for Agents (but not only)
item.content:encoded:
In Brief

Teel is an open source Python runtime that overlaps independent IO-bound calls in code you wrote sequentially. No *async**, no await**, no futures, no gather**. Mark expensive functions with @cacheable**, mark orchestration with @jit**, and a magic shadow interpreter reads ahead through your bytecode, finds calls whose arguments are already known, and dispatches them on background threads before the main thread arrives. On Princeton’s Tree of Thoughts, unmodified: 83% less runtime on average, and 8.07x on the longest run. 19% faster on average than LLM-generated async JavaScript inside a Deep Agents coding agent. Check the repo: github.com/AI21Labs/teel*

Figure 1: Same code, different schedule. In plain Python, each search waits for the one before it. With Teel, the three independent searches run at once, and summarize and check start as soon as their inputs are ready.

Why this matters for agents

Agent quality right now comes mostly from spending more compute at inference. Run an ensemble. Generate five candidate patches instead of one. Split a task across N subagents and merge what they come back with. Different techniques, one execution shape underneath: fan out a lot of independent, IO-bound work, then join it back.

Our recent results on BrowseComp-Plus, SWE-rebench and DeepResearch Bench II came from three unrelated techniques and drew the same picture at the compute level: many independent rollouts, retrievals, tool calls or whole agent runs, overlapping, then merged.

And more and more, the agent writes that orchestration itself. In LangChain’s Deep Agents, the model writes a short script that dispatches its own subagents, instead of calling them one tool call at a time. Whoever writes it, all that fan-out comes with a price. Agent swarms take it furthest: Moonshot’s Kimi Agent Swarm runs up to 300 sub-agents in parallel and reports finishing tasks about 4.5x faster than a single agent.

The problem

When we profiled our agents’ runs, most of the wall clock was a thread sitting on a socket: model calls, retrievals, tool calls, a shell exec in a sandbox. Shaving the main agent code barely moved the total. The leverage is in the waits that do not depend on each other.

In Python, overlapping those waits means rewriting your code first. To run two calls at once you make them async. Then every function that calls them has to become async too, and so does every function that calls those. A change you wanted in one place climbs the whole call chain, until orchestration logic and concurrency plumbing are the same lines of code. Every new fan-out means doing it again. And when a model writes that code, it has to get all of it right on every run.

Here’s a small code-review agent three ways: as written, rewritten with asyncio, and as written plus Teel’s decorators. It asks a model for the worst bug in each changed file, asks whether those findings should block the merge, then either requests changes or approves.

Figure 2: One code-review agent written three ways: plain Python (7.1s), rewritten with asyncio (3.0s), and the original code with Teel’s decorators (2.9s). The asyncio version needs three tasks, two cancellations and a finally block to match what Teel does on its own.

Versions 2 and 3 finish in about the same time, 3.0s and 2.9s against 7.1s sequential. Both get there the same way: they start both possible follow-ups before the verdict is in, and keep whichever one it picks. Teel does that on its own, by following both branches of the if while the verdict is still pending. The asyncio version does it by hand, with three tasks, two cancellations, a finally block, and an async twin of every function it calls. The difference isn’t the concurrency. It’s who has to find it and manage it.

That’s why we built Teel. Concurrency shouldn’t have to be part of the code a developer, or an agent, writes. It can be the runtime’s job. You write the sequential version. Teel reads your function’s bytecode ahead of the line currently running, spots calls that aren’t waiting on anything, and starts them early on background threads. By the time your code reaches them, the results are already there or on their way.

Results

WorkloadBaselineWith TeelSpeedup
Tree-of-thoughts-llm (longest run)307s38s8.07x
RLM in LangChain Deep Agents (sync Python)150s58s2.58x
RLM in LangChain Deep Agents (async JS)71s58s1.22x

Tree of Thoughts, unmodified. We ran Princeton’s tree-of-thoughts-llm on Game of 24 samples with GPT-4 without editing the repo: @jit, @cacheable and @inline were applied from the outside. It is a textbook fan-out written as textbook sequential code (generate candidates, evaluate, keep the best, recurse), and the original walks independent siblings one at a time. Average runtime reduction was 83%, from 148s down to 24s at the low end and 307s down to 38s at the high end.

Code the model writes at runtime. LangChain’s Deep Agents ships a dcode agent with a js_eval tool: the model solves a task by emitting a snippet that runs in a QuickJS sandbox. The snippet can call tools.web_search() and spawn subagents via task(), so the model is authoring a fan-out on the fly. But it authors it in async JavaScript, which hands the concurrency model to the model itself, and models are inconsistent at reaching for Promise.all.

We forked Deep Agents and swapped the snippet language for synchronous Python under Teel, expecting simpler generated code at some cost in speed. It came out faster instead: across ten mixed web-search-and-LLM prompts, 58s average against 71s for the async JS and 150s for the same Python run sequentially. Teel parallelizes the independent calls the model forgot to overlap, and speculatively runs fallback branches ahead of the decision that needs them. (The same prompt yields different code each time, so this compares distributions of generated programs, not two implementations of one.) Our fork is at github.com/AI21Labs/deepagents.

The API

There are three decorators and a context manager. Teel currently needs Python 3.12.13 exactly; Known limits explains why.

1from teel import cacheable, jit, Teel
2
3@cacheable                     # a discrete, expensive, parallelizable step:
4def fetch(url): ...            # an LLM call, an HTTP request, a retrieval
5
6@cacheable
7def summarize(text): ...
8
9@jit                           # orchestration Teel is allowed to analyze
10def research(a, b):
11    pa = fetch(a)              # no dependency between these two
12    pb = fetch(b)              # Teel runs them at the same time
13    return summarize(pa + pb)  # waits only for what it truly needs
14
15with Teel():                             # inside this context, independent
16    answer = research("a.txt", "b.txt")  # calls overlap - no async in sight

@cacheable marks the heavy functions worth dispatching early. Results are memoized on a key built from json.dumps of the arguments, so keep those arguments JSON-serializable and boring.

@jit marks the functions Teel is allowed to look inside. This is your orchestration layer.

@inline is optional. It marks cheap helpers (string formatting, dict digging) that Teel may actually execute during lookahead, which usually uncovers more @cacheable calls to dispatch ahead of time.

with Teel(): turns it on. Outside the context every decorated function runs as plain Python, untouched.

How it works

Why bytecode? Teel’s implementation is strange enough that the path there is worth 30 seconds, because each step explains the next. Every step kept the same execution idea, independent calls running in parallel, and changed only the interface you wrote orchestration in.

The first version ran orchestration on Celery. Canvas signatures gave us a real DAG the cluster could schedule: utilization up, runs resumable, orchestration finally separate from computation. It was also miserable to write, because orchestration is business logic and Celery makes you write business logic in a pipe-and-signature dialect that is not quite Python.

So we brought it back into Python, or into a restricted subset of Python. We parsed that subset with ast, compiled it into an execution graph and wrote our own executor. The graph paid off on its own terms: independent functions ran in parallel, if bodies could be entered speculatively before the test resolved, and a call like func(x, y) could push into its subcalls while x and y were still pending. All of it available only for the slice of the language we were willing to parse.

Giving up the restriction meant giving up ast. Bytecode is the level at which every Python program looks the same.

How does a runtime know what you are about to call? When a @jit function runs, Teel duplicates the execution state into a limited shadow interpreter and steps through the bytecode your main thread hasn’t reached yet. It works on its own copy, so your program’s state is left alone.

Does Teel build a dependency graph? No. The ast version did. Teel never needs the whole graph, only one answer per call: are this call’s arguments ready yet? Any value it can’t compute yet, like the result of a @cacheable call still in flight, is marked pending, and anything computed from a pending value is pending too:

1pa  = fetch(a)        # arguments known: dispatched now, pa is pending
2pb  = fetch(b)        # arguments known: dispatched now, pb is pending
3s   = pa + pb         # built from pending values: pending
4out = summarize(s)    # pending argument: not dispatched yet

When lookahead reaches a @cacheable call with no pending arguments, Teel dispatches it to a ThreadPoolExecutor and memoizes the result. When your code reaches that line for real, the answer is already there or on its way. Two calls that don’t consume each other’s results never wait on each other, which is why fan-out needs no special support: [answer(q) for q in sub_questions] dispatches every answer(q) whose question is already known. Parallelism is the default, and you opt out by creating a real data dependency.

How does it get at your program’s state? Teel grabs the frame stack with sys._getframe(), uses a small C extension (frameinspect) to pull each frame’s full value stack out of CPython, and reads f_lasti to find the last instruction that was actually executed. That’s where the shadow interpreter starts stepping forward.

Getting to that state is a cursed operation. Reading a live frame’s value stack is not something CPython offers you, which is why frameinspect compiles against CPython’s internal headers and the whole thing is pinned to one exact interpreter version. The full walkthrough, opcode by opcode, is in the README’s Under the hood section.

The contract

What you promise. Teel does three things a normal interpreter never does: it runs a function earlier than your code would, sometimes runs one your code would never reach, and hands back a saved result instead of running it again. Each is only legal if the function does not care when it runs or how often. Picture a @cacheable function that sends an email or charges a card: Teel might run it for a branch your program never takes, and nothing unsends the email. That is the @cacheable contract, and it is on you: no database writes, no reading the clock, no hidden state, and JSON-serializable arguments, because json.dumps of them is the memo key. @jit promises nothing. It is permission to read your bytecode, not a claim about what the function does.

What Teel promises. The same call runs once: pending and finished tasks are keyed by function plus arguments, so a second lookahead that discovers the same fetch(url) attaches to the first instead of firing another request. Failed calls are dropped rather than cached, on the assumption the failure was transient.

And a wrong guess costs time and tokens, not correctness. The shadow interpreter never produces your answer. CPython still executes your function to completion, instruction for instruction, exactly as it would without Teel, and the only difference is that some calls find their result already in the cache. Guess wrong and you burned a background call, plus its tokens if it was an LLM call. Guess nothing and you pay full sequential price. Break the purity contract, though, and you own the result. That is the one failure mode Teel cannot protect you from.

Observability: where the wall clock actually went

When the runtime decides what runs early, you need a way to see what it decided. Give the context a path and Teel records the run:

1with Teel(trace_path="teel-trace.json"):
2    research("a.txt", "b.txt")
3
4# open teel-trace.json at https://ui.perfetto.dev/

The output is a Chrome trace-event file, so Perfetto renders it as a timeline: one bar per @cacheable call, on the thread that ran it, with start time and duration, and overlapping work showing up as bars side by side.

Per-call is the granularity that starts to matter once you dial test-time compute up and down. A result on a hard agentic benchmark is rarely a single number anymore: our BrowseComp-Plus work reported a frontier of accuracy against cost and latency, so a team can read off the quality it can afford. You cannot chart a latency frontier you can only measure end to end.

To measure the speedup, run the same code twice. A @cacheable function runs untouched with no active context, so the baseline is not a separate sequential implementation, it is the identical program.

1# timed(label) runs research("a.txt", "b.txt") and prints its wall clock
2
3baseline = timed("sequential")       # no context, plain Python
4
5with Teel():
6    optimized = timed("with Teel")   # same code, now overlapped
7
8assert baseline == optimized         # same answer, different clock

Where this goes

Parallelism and observability both follow from one decision: the run is a set of calls keyed by their arguments. Take that one step further and an agent run stops being a disposable process and becomes reusable data. Persist the results and a later run can be served from them: unchanged calls are hits, and any call an edited input flows into gets a new key and re-runs. That gives you crash resume, debugging against pinned outputs, and iterating on orchestration without re-paying for every tool call. It also gives you human-in-the-loop: an agent freezes its state at a decision point, a person reviews, and the run resumes hours later on a different host.

Known limits

This is a proof of concept with two sharp edges. It’s pinned to Python 3.12.13 exactly, because frameinspect compiles against CPython’s internal headers. And the GIL still applies: background calls run on a ThreadPoolExecutor, so IO, network calls and GIL-free work like NumPy overlap fine, but for CPU-bound, GIL-constrained work, no dice.

Clone it, decorate your own functions, wrap your entry point, and start with the README: github.com/AI21Labs/teel

item.title: [Anyscale] How Lila Sciences and Anyscale Scaled GLM-5.3-Flash Training…
item.description: Full title: How Lila Sciences and Anyscale Scaled GLM-5.3-Flash Training to 1M tokens
item.content:encoded:
HomeBlogBlog Detail

How Lila Sciences and Anyscale Scaled GLM-5.3-Flash Training to 1M tokens

By SkyRL Team and Lila Sciences' AI Research Team | November 5, 2026

Lila Sciences and Anyscale trained GLM-5.3-Flash, an open model, on 1 million tokens per sequence using 64 B200 GPUs. That's 64x longer than the training stack could handle when we started, and every change is open source in SkyRL. Our team for SkyRL at Anyscale worked closely with Lila Science researchers on their infrastructure on an open source stack to explore the research path on increasing context length for this particular model.

Scientific data is long by nature. A genome, a family of related protein or RNA sequences, or the record of an experiment run over several days loses the structure that matters when it is cut into a few thousand tokens. AI that runs science in a closed loop with an autonomous lab has the same need: across rounds of hypotheses, protocols and instrument readouts, its context grows to hundreds of thousands of tokens.

Many open models now support 1M-token context, but they may not have out of the box performance for the target task at large context values. Closing that gap means training on the task's own data at its full length, without cutting or heavily compacting the context. This work set out to do it with an open model and an open training stack.

The result, at a glance:

  • 1M tokens per sequence fits in 144.5 GiB per GPU, under the B200's 178 GiB.
  • 13.7k tokens/s at 1M, and a peak of 24.9k tokens/s at 256k, on 64 B200s.
  • The model uses the context: fine-tuned on the human genome, its loss improves most on tokens with hundreds of thousands of tokens of context before them.
  • Open source: the recipe is in SkyRL, and several fixes are going upstream to Megatron-LM.

LinkHow do we reach 1M tokens context on GLM 5.3 Flash?

GLM-5.3-Flash is a hybrid model: 34 of its 45 layers use linear attention (Kimi Delta Attention), and 11 use DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA). It also uses a residual stream that's 4x wider than usual, and mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers. Each of these needed its own work. Memory grows with sequence length in every layer, and in attention it grows with the square of the length, so each optimization only pushes the limit out until the next one is hit. We did several optimizations all which are covered in detail with their own experiments and PRs in the original post.

Every optimization is load-bearing

Most of what we ran into is not specific to GLM and can be applied to models sharing the same type of components:

  • Check that each layer runs the kernel you think it does: GLM's sparse attention layers were silently falling back to dense attention, because the fused kernels only accepted DeepSeek's exact tensor shapes. Nothing raised an error; the run simply used 114 GiB per GPU at 16k and ran out of memory at 32k. Padding the tensors to fit the sparse kernel halved memory.
  • Sparse attention moves the quadratic cost; it doesn't remove it. DSA attends to only 2,048 tokens per query, but choosing those tokens means scoring every query against the whole sequence. Computing that score matrix a few hundred queries at a time keeps it under 2 GiB, and splitting the scoring across GPUs instead of repeating it on each one made the full training step 2.1x faster at 256k.
  • Every memory fix costs throughput, so use only what the length needs. Full recompute, CPU offloading and context parallelism each buy more context for some speed. Offloading, for example, cuts peak memory at 256k from 142 to 98 GiB but adds 21% to step time. We turn each one on only at the length where training wouldn't fit without it.
  • Benchmarks on random tokens underestimate memory for MoE models. Real text distribution routes unevenly across experts: on a real long context dataset, the busiest GPU received about 4x the average number of tokens, and 512k ran out of memory where random-token runs fit easily. Processing the MoE layer over the sequence in chunks fixed it. Test memory on real data before sizing a cluster.
  • Plan host memory, not just GPU memory. At 1M tokens, the layer inputs offloaded to CPU come to about 180 GB per GPU before context parallelism, over 1 TB per 8-GPU node, and they share host RAM with the optimizer state. Use pinned memory for the copies (they were 22% faster than pageable memory) and release it every step.
  • Verify correctness separately from speed. Speed and memory numbers can come from random weights, but correctness can't. In RL runs with the real weights, the trainer's log-probabilities matched vLLM's to within 0.04 -- 0.07 (mean absolute difference) from 128k to 1M tokens, and an overfit test drove loss from 1.65 to 0.17 in 20 steps.

With combination of these ideas we were able to maintain a good throughput across different context lengths

Training throughput, 16k -> 1M tokens

LinkTraining Results

We post-trained on the human genome at 512k tokens per sequence, the model's held-out loss fell 4.8% in 80 steps, and the gain was largest on tokens with the most context before them. That last part is the evidence that it learned to use long context, not just local patterns.

We trained on chromosomes 1 and 2 of the human reference genome (hg38) and evaluated on chromosome 22, which the model never saw. DNA is a good test because it has structure at every scale, from short motifs to patterns spanning very long stretches.

To separate long-range learning from local learning, we split the held-out loss by token position, in 32k-token buckets, and compared it before and after fine-tuning:

  • Early tokens have little context before them, so any improvement there comes from local patterns such as short motifs and base composition.
  • Late tokens have up to 500k tokens of context before them.
  • Local learning helps every position equally, so a larger improvement at late positions has to come from the long context that only they have.

Loss before and after fine-tuning

LinkRunning on Anyscale

Every experiment in this post ran on Ray, managed by the Anyscale platform, on a 64-GPU B200 cluster in Lila's cloud. SkyRL uses Ray to place and coordinate its training and inference workers, so the same setup ran memory benchmarks on random tokens, fine-tuning on real data, and RL runs that check the trainer against vLLM.

For a more in-depth look at the specific techniques used to support long-context see this detailed blog post.

Table of contents

  • How do we reach 1M tokens context on GLM 5.3 Flash?
  • Training Results
  • Running on Anyscale

item.content:encoded:
We’ve added new agents and products to Claude Marketplace, where teams find partner tools and services to help them get more from Claude. The additions cover security, developer infrastructure, creative, and productivity.

Eligible enterprise customers can apply a portion of their committed Anthropic spend toward these solutions. This lets them use one commitment across Claude and partner products, whether they’re buying something new or expanding with a platform they already use.

There are now over 25 partner agents and products on the marketplace. Here are the latest additions and what teams can do with them.

Products and agents for securing code and systems

Chainguard: Chainguard Harness builds applications from source in an isolated microVM and probes the live app for exploitable vulnerabilities. It helps teams fix what Claude finds, with custom remediation recommendations for reproducible vulnerabilities.

Checkmarx: Checkmarx One pairs rules-based analysis with AI reasoning to find vulnerabilities in code. It helps teams prioritize findings and fix them before code ships.

Cyera: Cyera Agent Guardian inventories Claude deployments, governs permissions before Claude runs, and enforces policy on prompts, files, and tool calls. It helps teams test those controls through red teaming.

Rubrik: Rubrik Code Guardian uses frontier AI models from Anthropic to review a secure copy of GitHub or Azure DevOps repositories for multi-step attack paths. It helps security and engineering teams rank issues by severity and turn confirmed critical ones into tracked tickets.

Tanium: Tanium Cloud gives teams real-time visibility and control across their endpoints. It helps IT and security teams find and fix vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and missing patches.

Development infrastructure for engineering teams

Datadog: Datadog Agent Observability traces agent execution through tools and services. It helps teams improve agent quality, performance, and cost efficiency by surfacing production patterns and recommending fixes.

Netlify: Netlify Enterprise deploys apps, sites, and agents to a global edge network, with preview URLs on every change. It helps teams take what they build with Claude from prototype to production with no infrastructure to configure, and includes SSO, role-based access, and audit logs.

Tools for marketing and creative work

AirOps: AirOps provides an agentic platform for AI search strategy, content, and multichannel execution. It helps marketing teams analyze brand performance in AI search and tie results to pipeline and revenue.

Runway: Runway generates and edits video, images, and audio. It helps creative and marketing teams turn a brief into finished assets and edit footage with natural language.

Webflow: Webflow provides built-in tools to build, manage, and optimize websites. It helps marketers, designers, developers, and agents make changes, with controls and governance built in.

Productivity apps for every team

Asana: Asana AI Teammates are prebuilt agents that use context from the Asana Work Graph, each with its own identity, scoped permissions, and audit trail. They help teams handle multi-step work, routing decisions that need judgment to the owner.

Glean: Glean connects company knowledge and workflows across systems. It helps employees find answers and complete multi-step tasks across connected apps.

monday: monday agents work inside projects, boards, docs, and meetings, using their owners and deadlines as context. They help PMO, IT, marketing, finance, and operations teams control what AI can access, approve, and spend.

Zoom: Zoom Agentic Search answers questions inside Claude using the latest meeting summaries, work conversations, documents, and connected third-party sources. Teams get permission-aware results without analyzing raw transcripts or chaining tools together.

Get started

You can browse all agents and products on Claude Marketplace and request to buy from any listing. If you’re building on Claude and want to join the marketplace, see the ways to join.
