item.title: [DeepInfra] MiMo-V2.6-Pro: Model Documentation & Integration Guide
item.content:encoded:
MiMo-V2.6-Pro: Model Documentation & Integration Guide

Published on 2026.11.04 by DeepInfra

MiMo-V2.6-Pro is a flagship sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model built for omnimodal intelligence and autonomous agentic workflows. It has 1.02 trillion total parameters, with 42 billion activated during inference, and is natively built to process text, image, video, and audio within a single, unified architecture.

With a 1,048,576-token (1M) context window and optimization via large-scale mixed reinforcement learning, MiMo-V2.6-Pro is designed for demanding technical tasks, including long-horizon coding, complex multi-tool interactions, and enterprise-grade cybersecurity analysis.

Key Innovations and Recent Updates

Xiaomi has positioned MiMo-V2.6-Pro as the flagship of the V2.6 series, introducing several methodologies aimed at AI self-improvement and multimodal reasoning.

Mixed Reinforcement Learning: “You Only RL Once”

At the heart of MiMo-V2.6-Pro is a training approach Xiaomi calls “You Only RL Once.” Rather than running separate reinforcement learning (RL) passes for different domains, the model is trained with a single, mixed RL run across coding, general agent tasks, visual processing, and cybersecurity. This lets capabilities reinforce one another, with the goal of transferring strategies to scenarios not directly covered during training.

This is paired with a self-improvement loop Xiaomi calls Groupwise Agentic Grading, which uses fully asynchronous Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). The system evaluates and ranks the model’s own trajectories, steering it toward more efficient problem-solving paths while applying adversarial screening for alignment.

Omnimodal Capabilities

MiMo-V2.6-Pro includes a dedicated 681-million-parameter MiMo Vision Transformer (ViT) and separate audio encoders, allowing simultaneous analysis of multiple data types. Combined with the 1M-token context window, the model can take in entire code repositories, long tool traces, and multi-session agent runs without losing context.

Ecosystem Integration

Weights are available on Hugging Face and ModelScope. The model is integrated into Xiaomi’s own AI Studio and MiMo Code, and supports deployment via the SGLang and vLLM serving frameworks.

Performance Benchmarks

The table below reflects Xiaomi’s own published benchmark comparisons against Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol; these are vendor-reported figures rather than independently reproduced third-party results, and should be read accordingly.

Benchmark (Category)MiMo-V2.6-ProClaude Opus 5GPT-5.6 Sol
DeepSWE v1.1 (Coding)71.974.073.0
AutomationBench v1.0.6 (General Agent)53.150.345.8
OSWorld-Verified (General Agent)82.083.483.0
GDPVal 2.1 — AA (Reasoning, Elo)167317081588
Terminal Bench 2.1 (Terminal/OS)89.989.188.8
MiMo Visual Coding (Visual Agent)72.370.073.4

Specialized Strengths

The following are also Xiaomi-reported figures:

  • Cybersecurity: 94.0 on CyberGym and 80.2 on the MiMo Cyber Bench, aimed at exploit verification and autonomous threat mitigation.
  • Scientific research: In “co-scientist” use cases, Xiaomi reports the model has been used to help design metal-organic frameworks for environmental adsorption, including literature review and hypothesis generation.
  • Creative engineering: Native support for MIDI generation, orchestral composition, and end-to-end video creation, including beat-synced editing.

Technical Architecture

To keep inference fast despite its scale, MiMo-V2.6-Pro uses several architectural optimizations:

  • Sparse MoE: 70 total layers (60 sliding-window attention / 10 global attention), balancing efficiency against long-range dependency modeling.
  • Multi-Token Prediction (MTP): A 5-layer speculative decoder predicts up to 7 tokens per forward pass, improving throughput.
  • Speculative decoding: An EAGLE-style algorithm verifies multiple tokens in parallel to reduce latency.

Getting Started with the API

The MiMo-V2.6-Pro API uses standard OpenAI-compatible HTTP POST endpoints, so it integrates easily into existing workflows.

Authentication

Requests require an API key passed via the standard HTTP Authorization header.

Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_API_KEY>Content-Type: application/json

API Endpoints

  • Hosted (DeepInfra): https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai/chat/completions
  • Self-hosted (SGLang/vLLM): http://<host>:<port>/v1/chat/completions
  • Model identifiers: XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.6-Pro or XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL, listed alongside every other hosted model in the DeepInfra model catalog

Implementation Example (Python)

import os
import requests
 
api_key = os.environ.get("DEEPINFRA_API_KEY")
url = "https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai/chat/completions"
 
payload = {
    "model": "XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.6-Pro",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain the role of sparse MoE in LLMs."}],
    "temperature": 1.0,
    "top_p": 0.95
}
 
response = requests.post(url, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}, json=payload)
print(response.json())copy

Common Parameters

ParameterTypeDescription
messagesarrayRequired. Supports text, image, video, and audio inputs.
temperaturefloatRecommended: 1.0.
toolsarrayList of callable functions for agentic workflows — see DeepInfra’s function calling guide.
max_tokensintegerMaximum tokens within the 1M context window.

Pricing and Usage

Pricing scales with consumption and is billed per 1 million tokens, with a substantial discount on cached input tokens. Full current rates for MiMo-V2.6-Pro and every other hosted model are on the DeepInfra pricing page.

Model VariantInput (cache miss)Input (cache hit)Output
MiMo-V2.6-Pro$0.435 / 1M tokens$0.0036 / 1M tokens$0.87 / 1M tokens
Pro-UltraSpeed$4.35 / 1M tokens$0.036 / 1M tokens$8.70 / 1M tokens
  • Usage-based billing: Pricing scales directly with consumption, billed per 1 million tokens.
  • UltraSpeed mode: Available via MiMo Desktop and API, offering substantially faster output speed for real-time interactions. Confirm current throughput figures for your workload, as serving-mode performance can vary by provider.

Conclusion

MiMo-V2.6-Pro combines a trillion-parameter MoE architecture with native omnimodal support and a 1M-token context window, giving developers the building blocks for long-horizon agentic applications and security tooling. Whether the workload is complex software engineering or advanced scientific research, MiMo-V2.6-Pro is built for reasoning depth and throughput at production scale.

For a deeper look at how it compares to other recent releases on cost and benchmarks, see our coverage of DeepSeek V4 Pro’s pricing and providers. For further technical detail, refer to the MiMo-V2.6 technical report or the developer community on Discord and Telegram.

Supporting the Next Wave of AI Startups with the NVIDIA Inception Program

Published on 2026.11.04 by Aray Sultanbekova

DeepInfra is proud to be a member of the NVIDIA Inception program. We started as a startup in 2022, and we know how much the right support matters early on: compute you can afford, tools that just work, and people in your corner.

NVIDIA Inception is a free program designed to help startups accelerate innovation and growth. Members get access to the latest developer resources and training, exclusive pricing on NVIDIA hardware and software, and exposure to the venture capital community. It's been a great community to be part of.

Now we want to pay that support forward. DeepInfra's serverless inference platform, accelerated by NVIDIA, is now available to NVIDIA Inception members through an exclusive offer that helps startups build and scale faster: 10 billion free tokens for NVIDIA Nemotron models, about $1,000 of inference.

What fellow NVIDIA Inception members get

  • 10 Billion free tokens for NVIDIA Nemotron models
  • Serverless inference. Call an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and pay per token. There's no cluster to manage.
  • Production-grade throughput on the latest NVIDIA AI infrastructure, on the same platform you'll scale on
  • Credits valid for one year from redemption

Claim the offer at deepinfra.com/nvidia-inception. You can also find it in the NVIDIA Inception member portal's benefits catalog.

More support for startups: DeepStart now offers 50B free tokens

Supporting startups is core to who we are. That's why we built DeepStart, our program for early-stage AI companies, and why we're expanding it today. Approved startups now get roughly 50 billion free tokens (about $1,000 at DeepSeek V4 Flash prices). That's 50x the 1 billion tokens the program offered before. You can use them on any of the 200+ models DeepInfra hosts, and they're valid for one year after approval.

Stack both benefits

NVIDIA Inception members get both benefits with a single application. When you claim the NVIDIA Inception offer at deepinfra.com/nvidia-inception, we verify your membership automatically and add your DeepStart credits too. There's no separate DeepStart application. NVIDIA Inception credits go to NVIDIA Nemotron models, and DeepStart credits cover everything else.

Who's eligible

  • Current NVIDIA Inception members
  • Startups less than 5 years old
  • Raised between $250K and $10M USD
  • One grant per company

Why we're doing this

"AI startups are moving from prototype to production faster than ever, and infrastructure can quickly become the constraint. We want teams to be able to focus on building products instead of managing infrastructure. By expanding DeepStart and working with NVIDIA Inception, we're giving more companies the capacity to test, build and scale on the same infrastructure they can use in production." — Nikola Borisov, co-founder and CEO, DeepInfra

We're grateful to NVIDIA for the support we've received along the way, from early access to new NVIDIA Nemotron models, which we've served on DeepInfra from day zero of their release, to direct help from NVIDIA engineers as we built our inference stack on TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, SGLang and NVIDIA Dynamo. Supporting fellow NVIDIA Inception members is our way of giving back, and we can't wait to see what they build.

Get started

  • NVIDIA Inception members: claim the offer to get both benefits
  • Other early-stage startups: apply to DeepStart
  • Not a member yet: learn more about NVIDIA Inception

Questions? Reach us at feedback@deepinfra.com.

item.title: [AI21 Labs] Post-training case study: Reaching frontier-level intelligen…
item.description: Full title: Post-training case study: Reaching frontier-level intelligence on global payroll with Deel
item.content:encoded:
This post is authored by Eran Goldstein, Asaf Karnieli, Shaked Meirom and Joanna Kramer, in collaboration with Deel’s Abhijit Mehta and Anthony Li.

Building a global payroll model that is available to reliably and truthfully answer employee questions across the world, each navigating highly individualized employment terms and local regulatory landscapes, is not a simple task.

Yet, over the course of a three-week engagement, AI21’s Forward-Deployed Researchers (FDRs) worked with the team at Emet, Deel’s AI lab for model evaluation and training, to post-train recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, delivering a model that surpasses the frontier at a fraction of the cost:

  • 20.7-point quality improvement over the base model
  • 8-point quality improvement over Claude Opus 5.5
  • 50x cheaper model than Opus 5.5 (as measured in cost per 1M tokens)

Figure 1: Our training recipe lifted Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 8 points above Claude Opus 5.5 on quality for a global payroll use case, while costing 50x less per 1M tokens.

Achieving those results was possible due to the expert criteria and benchmark built by Emet by Deel, whose in-country payroll specialists defined what a complete answer contains, as well as the AI21 FDR team’s sequentially training the model with SFT and then SDPO (self distillation policy optimization). This post details the methodology behind these results.

Why global payroll questions are challenging for models

The domain

Deel, the global HR and payroll platform, supports more than 45,000 companies across 150+ countries, answering payroll questions that span multiple countries and jurisdictions. What constitutes the right answer depends on local tax rules, employment contracts and company policies – and all three change regularly. A typical question, usually about 20 words long, might be: “As an EOR employee in France: We have an employee in France who started maternity leave on 14 August. My understanding was that CPAM would fund this. How does the funding and the employer’s part work?”

In addition to getting the answer right, the model also needs to phrase it according to Deel’s terminology, policies and style.

To grade the model’s answers, we relied on EmBench Payroll, Emet’s public payroll benchmark. Each question has 3–6 rubric assertions. Some are factual (“states the daily cap for the CPAM allowance is 101.94 euros”), while others check what the answer covers or how it frames the situation. Answers are graded on two metrics, with GPT-6 Sol as the LLM Judge:

  • Criteria met: the average share of a question’s assertions that the answer satisfies
  • All criteria met: the share of questions where every assertion is satisfied

While frontier models handle the domain well – for example, Opus 5.5 meets 64.0% of the criteria and fully answers 26.3% of the dev questions – they are also expensive. In contrast, open models are significantly cheaper, but generally start with lower quality – the base version of Nemotron 3.5 Super scores at just 51.3%.

Deel was looking for an open model that gives the complete answer unprompted, at a fraction of frontier cost. Post-training makes it possible to reach that desired cost-quality operating point.

Methodology

Where the base model falls short

We started by evaluating base Nemotron 3.5 Super and conducting error analysis on its rollouts. Most failed rollouts were incomplete rather than wrong. For example, they hedged where the law is definite, gave no concrete figures, or skipped framing facts and mixed up related concepts. Those patterns suggested the model mostly had the requisite knowledge – but needed to be steered towards a complete answer.

The figure below (Figure 2) shows a typical example. When a U.S. employee asked how much sick time they would have by the end of April, the base model recognized that the answer depends on state law, yet hedged and referred the user to HR instead of stating the rule and the relevant figures. As a result, the answer met none of the three rubric criteria, and none of eight sampled answers to this question was fully correct.

Figure 2: An example of how the base Nemotron 3.5 Super model handles atypical global payroll question, as measured by Deel’s rubric criteria.

Training the behavior into the weights

Step 1: Near-policy SFT

To improve the model while avoiding catastrophic forgetting, we kept training as on-policy as possible. That meant learning from the model’s own rollouts rather than from answers written by another model, since data close to the policy’s own distribution is easier to learn and causes less forgetting [3]. However, the base model rarely produced rollouts good enough to learn from. It fully answered only 10% of the dev questions.

To raise the quality of its rollouts without leaving its distribution (training ‘near-policy’), we provided the model with hints during generation. We refined the hints iteratively through error analysis. They covered the model’s role and what the task expects of it, the level of detail a payroll answer needs, Deel’s terminology and answer structure, and the distinctions users tend to blur. The hints added no new domain knowledge. They only steered the model toward using what it already knew.

We then sampled hint-guided rollouts from Nemotron 3.5 Super with reasoning turned on. We kept only the rollouts that met every rubric assertion, including their reasoning traces, and these formed our curated training set: just 412 examples, small by post-training standards. Finally, we trained the model with SFT on this set, with the hints withheld.

Near-policy SFT lifted performance on the dev set from 0.513 / 0.100 to 0.657 / 0.229 (criteria met / all criteria met).

Revisiting the sick-leave question shows the effect of this step. As can be seen in the figure below, the trained model states the federal rule, gives the figures for the states most likely to apply, and asks for the details it needs, raising criteria met on this question from 0.13 to 0.79.

Figure 3: An example of how the same question from Figure 2 is answered by the Nemotron 3.5 Super base model, and then the Nemotron 3.5 Super model post-trained with SFT.

Step 2: SDPO with a privileged teacher

Once we had established a stronger checkpoint with SFT, we turned to SDPO (self-distillation policy optimization) [1,2], a recent on-policy method that trains the model using self-distillation. The student (trained model) answers the plain question, and a teacher – the same model with access to privileged information for each question – then scores the student’s own tokens.

The information we gave the teacher remained the same as the injected hints above.

However, SDPO has advantages beyond training with SFT. First, SDPO is an on-policy training method, i.e., rollouts are generated by the most recent policy model. In addition, this method is a fine-grained approach to steer the student’s behavior by rewarding desired response characteristics (and penalizing undesired ones), instead of relying on the model to infer those characteristics from demonstrations alone.

As a result of training with SDPO, the model’s performance highly improved:

  • When training the base model using SDPO directly: dev-set results rose from 0.513 / 0.100 to 0.638 / 0.183, close to the SFT-trained scores (0.657 / 0.229) without any curated data.
  • When starting SDPO from the SFT checkpoint (SFT → SDPO): produced our best Nemotron 3.5 Super results: 0.720 / 0.339.

Notably, we reached these results with a small training set: 412 questions for SFT and 698 for SDPO, a superset of the SFT questions. This was possible because we kept both steps as close to on-policy as we could. In SFT, we trained on the model’s own hint-guided completions, so the curated training set stayed close to the model’s own distribution. In SDPO, training is fully on-policy: each pass over a question produces fresh rollouts from the current policy, and with them new training signal, rather than a fixed target the model could memorize. SDPO also needs no gold answer, so it could learn from the questions the model still got wrong. This shows that post-training a model for a specific task can be done effectively with a small dataset.

This case study offers an excellent example of a self-distillation pipeline. Similar to GRPO, where we rely on the student’s capabilities to bootstrap the performance and create a flywheel, SDPO does the same. The flip side is that on-policy training can only amplify what the student already produces: when the base model rarely produces good answers on its own, there is little signal to learn from. It is therefore standard practice to first distill from a teacher, or otherwise improve the base model, before on-policy training begins. Our work with Deel illustrates a situation where off-policy distillation from a self-teacher, the model itself guided by hints, works well as a precursor to SDPO, such that the combination of both methods improves over each of them separately.

Results

Figure 4: Final results on the two core metrics – criteria met and all criteria met – at each stage of the post-training process.

The sequential usage of SFT, followed by SDPO, produced our strongest model on both metrics, surpassing Claude-Opus-5.5 by ~8 points.

Reaching frontier-level quality with SFT and SDPO

By implementing a sequential training process that utilized both SFT and SDPO, AI21’s FDR team improved Nemotron 3.5 Super’s performance on Deel’s global payroll task by 20.7 points compared to the base model, and by 8 points compared to Claude Opus 5.5.

Working in a domain as complex as global payroll, where a right answer is defined both factually and stylistically, AI21’s FDR team utilized near-policy SFT followed by SDPO to steer the model’s behavior and highly improved the quality.

Together, AI21 and Deel demonstrated that, equipped with the right data and training recipe, companies don’t need to choose between a frontier models’ quality and an open models’ price. By post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Deel can now power its global payroll with a model that surpasses Claude Opus 5.5 on quality, while costing 50x less.

Read more about the project on Deel’s blog.

References

  • Siyan Zhao, Zhihui Xie, Mengchen Liu, Jing Huang, Guan Pang, Feiyu Chen, Aditya Grover. Self-Distilled Reasoner: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Language Models. arXiv:2601.18734, 2026.
  • Jonas Hübotter, Frederike Lübeck, Lejs Behric, Anton Baumann, Marco Bagatella, Daniel Marta, Ido Hakimi, Idan Shenfeld, Thomas Kleine Buening, Carlos Guestrin, Andreas Krause. Reinforcement Learning via Self-Distillation. arXiv:2601.20802, 2026.
  • Zhaorui Yang, Tianyu Pang, Haozhe Feng, Han Wang, Wei Chen, Minfeng Zhu, Qian Liu. Self-Distillation Bridges Distribution Gap in Language Model Fine-Tuning. ACL 2024, arXiv:2402.13669.

item.title: [Modular] Modular: LLVM Dev Meeting 2026: Durable Infrastructure in th…
item.description: Full title: Modular: LLVM Dev Meeting 2026: Durable Infrastructure in the Agentic Era
item.content:encoded:
November 4, 2026

LLVM Dev Meeting 2026: Durable Infrastructure in the Agentic Era

Michael Dunn-OConnor

Community

I attended this year’s LLVM Dev Meeting, and the talks kept returning to the same problem: accelerator code is multiplying faster than the shared tooling around it. Agentic development was, as Tuesday’s keynote put it, the elephant in the room. Teams can rapidly generate code to optimize for specific devices, and that speed can make architecture feel disposable. While the current pace pulls teams toward one-off solutions, durable software infrastructure still depends on shared standards, tools, and abstractions. Communities like LLVM will need to work through this tension in the coming years to continue building infrastructure that lasts. The recent proliferation of Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs) is a symptom of this tension, and one that presents a significant opportunity for MAX and Mojo.

Weiwei Chen presenting at the 2026 LLVM Dev Meeting MAX and Mojo Workshop

Maintaining open source software projects in the agentic era

Kristof Beyls’s keynote asked what agentic engineering means for the future of compilers. Drawing on the System 1 and System 2 distinction from Daniel Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow, Kristof compared agents to System 1 thinking: fast, intuitive, and prolific. Compilers, in his comparison, are System 2: slow, deliberate, and rule-bound. From that view, agents don’t make compilers less relevant. They make the deliberate, verifiable layer more important, because fast code generation is only useful if something dependable stands behind it.

Kristof’s exploration of the question also revealed a lot about the future of open source software projects. Kristof argued that durable open source projects depend on three things: communicating intent, maintaining cognition, and supporting contributors. If contributions are to maintain the architectural vision and standard of quality that the core maintainers expect, projects need to document and share that intent more deliberately.

Traditionally, contributors internalized a project’s architecture and standards organically by submitting and revising issues, proposals, and pull requests. Kristof emphasized the ongoing importance of “contributor poker”: betting that a new contributor will be a valuable addition to the project even if their first PR requires maintainer effort to land. If agents are taking the productive friction out of this process, it must be reinforced with communication (and better validation of submissions). The audience was more skeptical that contributor cognition is compatible with agentic contributions, citing “drive-by” PRs and a lack of communication from new contributors (Zig has banned AI contributions for this very reason). One key step to investing in contributors in the agentic era is keeping a project comprehensible to humans even as it scales, to discourage eager contributors from surrendering their thinking to the agent.

Reducing duplicative work

Wednesday’s keynote (from Google’s Nick Desaulniers, Anshul Nigham, and Jordan Rupprecht) focused on the opportunities and challenges of maintaining a tip-of-tree fork of LLVM. One finding stood out: delaying an update causes more delays as breaking changes compound. The maintainers found that teams were applying LLVM and MLIR updates independently across the same monorepo, duplicating maintenance work. The speakers’ solution was better shared tooling to allow for more efficient and coordinated efforts. These conclusions echoed the key points of the previous day’s keynote. One-off band-aid solutions are easier than ever, but drifting from shared architecture and tooling across teams duplicates effort and leaves code that is harder to understand and maintain.

Velocity through DSLs

New accelerator generations keep arriving while earlier ones stay in service, so the working assumption is that new hardware must run alongside existing hardware instead of replacing it. NVIDIA’s Rajat Bajpai presented on updating interfaces so developers can use new hardware features while preserving backwards compatibility. In hallway conversations, engineers described the same tension from the other side: how to write readable, accelerator-specific code while supporting multiple architectures. The most common answer seems to be creating more and more Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs).

Maksim Levental, Guray Ozen, and Amir Mohammad Tavakkoli’s talk on NVIDIA’s BaseDSL project demonstrated that teams are looking to create new DSLs more efficiently. BaseDSL is a platform for building custom Python DSLs on top of MLIR through a series of plugins, which reduces duplicated effort as teams spin up their own. Even with a shared framework, teams still end up with incompatible DSLs and no shared tooling, and every one of them has to be maintained. BaseDSL is internal to NVIDIA for now, but audience questions about open-sourcing suggest the wider community wants an easier way to create DSLs.

Yet the spread of DSLs conflicts with the principles established by the keynotes. Kristof argued that durable projects need shared intent and human-readable abstractions. Google’s keynote showed the costs of duplicative maintenance. A growing set of DSLs pulls teams in the other direction. Each DSL provides essential optimization, but together they multiply what has to be understood, documented, and maintained. The alternative path forward is a language like Mojo that enables shared abstractions and tooling across accelerators without compromising on performance.

The (not actually) unique opportunity Mojo presents

This year, Modular led a day-long pre-conference workshop on Mojo and MAX. At the end of the workshop, I was thinking that Mojo’s opportunity to create a shared ecosystem across diverse teams and hardware was unique. Chris Lattner pointed out to me that Mojo is in the same situation MLIR was in eight years ago.

At that point Chris was at Google, supporting AI compiler development for five different chips, each with its own stack. Each team was building its own SSA-based optimizers, with no way to share architecture or tooling. MLIR solved this by unifying the implementation details of these compilers in a single standard. Teams could work at a higher level of abstraction and interoperate much more efficiently.

Mojo provides a unifying layer the same way MLIR does, one level up the stack. It is a full language that lowers through MLIR, so it builds on the infrastructure LLVM contributors already know. The problems DSLs are solving call for a high degree of developer control and performance across diverse accelerators, and Mojo is designed around those requirements, with readable syntax and powerful metaprogramming. For more context on how Mojo compares to DSLs like Triton, see Fabio’s series on [Structured Mojo Kernels.]

MAX layers on Mojo to complete the unification. MAX provides accelerator support with Mojo as the programming interface. Hardware support is built once in MAX and optimized through a single language, instead of being rebuilt with each team’s DSL and stack. A unified MAX and Mojo ecosystem also enables the collaboration that keeps large projects aligned to an architectural vision. The Modular hardware alliance is advancing this effort by coordinating patterns for hardware bring-up. The alliance applies the LLVM model to AI compute: a software layer built in common across hardware vendors, with conformance testing to keep the ecosystem compatible.

Building a community

After Kristof’s keynote, an audience member (and LLVM maintainer) lined up for the Q&A and described feeling frustrated and discouraged by fielding a massive volume of drive-by AI-generated PRs, with no human developer willing to take feedback and see them through. Agreement and empathy were visible across the room. The problem isn’t limited to external contributions to open source. Maintaining critical software in the agentic era will take shared tooling, standards, and abstractions. It will also take a community willing to invest human time in collaborating, developing a shared vision, and mentoring new contributors. I see these practices emerging in the Mojo community, supported by resources like the Mojo contributor guide and the Modular AI Tool Use Policy (inspired by the LLVM AI Tool Use Policy). I left this year’s LLVM Dev Meeting convinced that this kind of community is still possible.

item.description: Full title: The world's leading open models, fully under your controlThe right model for the right job, all under your jurisdiction.
item.content:encoded:
Nov 03, 2026

4 minute read

The world's leading open models, fully under your control

The right model for the right job, all under your jurisdiction.

Key takeaways

  • Open models are now available on Model Vault: Enterprises can run both Cohere's models and leading open models (such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Gemma 4, GPT-OSS, and Phi) on a fully managed, encrypted inference platform.
  • Zero data retention by default: Neither prompts nor outputs are retained in Model Vault, providing a strong baseline of security.
  • Sovereign inference: You retain control over four key elements: where your data lives (data residency and regulatory compliance), who can access it (isolated tenant with full privacy in Encrypted), which models you can use (the right model for each task rather than just one provider's offerings), and how your AI runs (not dictated by the provider).
  • Regional availability: Model Vault is live in the United States, European Union, and Canada; Model Vault Encrypted is live in the US with EU and Canada support coming soon.

Sovereignty in AI means customers can choose, inspect, and deploy the models that best serve their needs without surrendering control to a single vendor, but that freedom should never come at the expense of security or privacy. Adding leading open models from Cohere and other providers across the globe inside of Model Vault gives our customers the flexibility they need to use the right tool for the job without sacrificing the standards that govern their business.

Every organization wants to use the best AI models available for the task at hand but many cannot. For a bank, a hospital or a government department, sending sensitive data to a shared API is often off the table. At the same time, managing inference for open or on-premise models may also not be possible due to capability or capacity constraints. Teams end up choosing between the model they want, the control they need, and the capacity they have to manage them.

They shouldn't have to. Today we're launching third party models inside Model Vault and Model Vault Encrypted, allowing Enterprises to run both Cohere’s models and leading open models on a fully managed and encrypted inference platform. Zero data retention of prompts and outputs is implemented by default in Model Vault.

Two levels of protection

Model Vault provides the full inference stack managed through an isolated instance dedicated to your organization alone. Model Vault Encrypted goes further, keeping your data encrypted even while the model processes it.

Model Vault: Your models and workloads run on single tenant infrastructure. You choose the region, and your prompts and outputs stay there. Cohere manages the infrastructure so you get production-grade serving without building and running your own cluster.

Model Vault Encrypted: For your most sensitive work, Model Vault Encrypted protects data in use, not just at rest and in transit. Prompts and outputs are processed inside isolated environments and stay encrypted throughout using confidential computing. Not even Cohere can see what you send to a model or what it sends back. Neither can any cloud provider.

What sovereign inference means

Sovereign inference means you decide how your AI runs, not your provider. It comes down to four things:

  • Where your data lives. Run inference workloads in your preferred supported region to help meet your organization’s data residency and regulatory requirements.
  • Who can access it. Model Vault keeps your workloads in a separate, isolated tenant. With Model Vault Encrypted, no one but you can see your prompts or outputs, including Cohere.
  • Which models you can use. The model that best fits the task, not just the one that happens to be available through a single provider.

What customers are saying

“Security is at the heart of what Language Weaver offers to our customers, whether that pertains to zero data retention, data residency requirements, or simply having more control over their AI model. Our customers around the globe trust us with some of their most sensitive content. Cohere Model Vault lets Language Weaver run models - including the LW Pro model - securely and efficiently, while ensuring our customers are in control over where their data goes. It’s fast and reliable, and because Cohere handles the hosting and scaling, our teams can stay focused on what we do best: delivering for our customers.”Dragos Munteanu, VP Research and Product Development, RWS

The right model for every job

No single model is best at everything. Model Vault lets you pick the right one for each task, and run every one of them with the same protections.

Cohere's models. Command for generative and agentic work, Embed and Rerank for search and retrieval, Parse for documents, Transcribe for speech and Translate for multilingual workflows.

High performing open models. Alongside our own models, Model Vault runs the most-used open models, including DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (the most-used open model on OpenRouter), GLM 5.3 Flash, MiMo V2.6 Pro, Gemma 4, and NVIDIA Nemotron. GPT-OSS and Phi models are available too.

With Model Vault you can choose the best model for each task and run it within a unified, production inference stack.

Explore Model Vault

Where it's available

Model Vault is live today with regional serving available in the United States, the European Union and Canada. Model Vault Encrypted is live in the US, with regional EU and Canada serving coming soon.

This is the start. Over the coming months we'll bring sovereign inference to more places and more workloads:

  • New regions, so more organizations can run models in their preferred region.
  • Model Vault Encrypted with regional supported for Canada and the EU.
  • Larger models in Model Vault Encrypted, extending confidential compute to more demanding workloads.
  • More models in every region, as new open models are released and adopted.

FAQ

Which option is right for me? Model Vault suits most regulated workloads that need an isolated tenant and in-region processing with a wide model catalogue. Choose Model Vault Encrypted for data sensitive workloads, when no one outside your organization, including Cohere, should be able to see your data.

Can I run open models in Model Vault Encrypted? Yes. Models like Gemma, GPT-OSS and Phi models run in Model Vault Encrypted today, alongside Cohere's Embed, Rerank, Transcribe and Translate. See the table above for the full list.

How is Model Vault priced? Pricing is by GPU type. Please visit cohere.com/pricing for details including on-demand (hourly) pricing and promotions. Reach out to sales for reserved capacity; monthly and annual commit pricing is available.

Get started

Model Vault and Model Vault Encrypted are available today. Sign up, or talk to our team about the right setup for your organization.

item.title: [Hugging Face] StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes…
item.description: Full title: StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents

Enterprise Article

Published November 3, 2026

17

Kyle Wiggers

Ai2Comms

allenai

📄 Tech Report | 🤗 Data | 💻 Code

We’re introducing StateBench, a benchmark for long-context state tracking—how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve.

State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack.

Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds.

To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer.

Four levels of state tracking

StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations:

  • R-trivial problems use immutable assignment. A variable’s value never changes, so the model only needs to recover what it was first set to. In code, this looks like let x = 4; in everyday life, it’s like a birth date—it stays fixed.
  • Aperiodic problems allow reassignment by value. The model needs to find the most recent value and can ignore earlier ones. In code, this looks like x = 4 followed later by x = 2; in everyday life, it’s like a thermostat, where the latest setting determines the current temperature.
  • Soluble problems add self-referential updates. Each update builds on the current value, so the model has to carry changes forward rather than simply find the latest assignment. In code, this looks like x = x + 5; in everyday life, it’s like a game score, where each point adds to the running total.
  • General finite problems add assignment by reference. One variable can take on another variable’s current value, creating dependencies across updates. In code, this looks like x = y or swapping two variables. Imagine a magician hiding a ball under one of five cups, then repeatedly swapping their positions. Finding the ball means keeping track of how those swaps change its location. This illustrates the S₅ state-tracking problem: following how successive swaps rearrange five objects. It belongs to the hardest of our four levels and is discussed in previous work on the limits of state tracking.

These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems – which can be viewed as word problems over finite monoids – can be decomposed into atomic primitives. Each level in our hierarchy corresponds to a class of state-tracking problems that can be built out of a different set of primitives.

To compare the four levels fairly, we start with a general finite sequence of variable assignments and derive three easier versions from it, producing four comparable StateBench problems—one at each difficulty level. All four use the same number of variables and distinct values, with assignments appearing at the same points in the sequence; only the type of assignment changes.

What we found

Pretrained models

We tested a range of open pretrained models on the r-trivial, aperiodic, and general finite levels of StateBench to see where their state tracking breaks down, and whether different architectures fail where theory predicts. Under standard theoretical assumptions, transformers can handle r-trivial robustly (and soluble and aperiodic to some degree) but are predicted to fail on general problems. In contrast, Gated DeltaNet with a more flexible memory update can, in principle, handle all four levels.

We started with open pretrained models, where the training data and context lengths are fully documented. These included two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), along with smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters. All of these models were pretrained on the same data; none had seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens during training, and we tested most of them on inputs well beyond that length.

When we scored each model, almost all performed well on r-trivial problems, lost accuracy on aperiodic ones as inputs grew, and stayed at chance on general finite problems. Problem format mattered here—the 275-million-parameter hybrid and Gated DeltaNet models scored near the ceiling on RULER-style r-trivial problems but were near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits. That gap is one reason StateBench tests the same underlying problem in several formats.

Frontier models

We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable.

All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong.

Models trained directly on the task

Next, we investigated whether models’ difficulty with the harder levels reflects limits of the architectures themselves, or whether pretraining simply doesn’t teach models to solve them. Targeted direct training is a more favorable setting that reveals to what degree state-tracking issues come from the underlying architecture and optimizer rather than the data used to pretrain a model.

We trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on StateBench: two transformer variants, two hybrids, and two Gated DeltaNet variants with different memory-update constraints. The models trained on sequences of up to 256 assignments and were tested on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, or 250 times the maximum training length.

The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments. Transformers learned the easier levels but degraded on longer sequences, and they never learned general finite problems. On the hardest level, the Gated DeltaNet variant with a more flexible memory update generalized the farthest, staying near perfect out to roughly 10 times the length of the longest sequences it saw during training.

For Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models, the gap points to training rather than architecture; trained directly, they learned to handle state-tracking levels their pretrained counterparts couldn’t. Transformers were different—even trained directly, they could never learn the hardest level.

Open questions and the release

Some questions remain open. Our new proof shows that Gated DeltaNet with a more limited memory update (non-negative eigenvalues) can solve all aperiodic tasks and certain periodic tasks, such as tracking whether a repeated input has occurred an even or odd number of times, under the paper’s fixed-precision arithmetic with rounding. Its exact placement in the hierarchy remains open, including whether it can solve all soluble tasks and how numerical precision or combining it with attention layers affects its capabilities. StateBench also assumes a fixed number of variables, while real tasks often introduce new entities over time. In a long conversation, for example, new people and objects can appear as it unfolds, and the model has to begin tracking them too. The current framework doesn’t yet cover that setting.

As new flavors of recurrent and hybrid architectures emerge, understanding which kinds of state tracking each can handle could help guide how future systems are developed and trained. We hope StateBench gives researchers a finer-grained way to find where models break down—and to build training and evaluation data for the capabilities that still fall short. More fundamentally, we hope it serves as a North Star for researchers to develop new architectures with more robust state-tracking abilities compared to current models.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your desig…
item.description: Full title: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Enterprise Article

Published November 3, 2026

11

Praveen Venkateswaran

praveenv

ibm-research

Anupama Murthi

anupamamurthi

ibm-research

Hamid Adebayo

harmedox

ibm-research

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

Why decks are hard for small models

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Build it like a human: a designer and a coder

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

  • The designer reads the plan and writes a structured JSON brief: the palette, the type system, and for each slide its layout, its exact content and a short design rationale.
  • The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the pptxgenjs JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning.

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

Synthesizing decks and their reasoning

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

The coder reasons about geometry:

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Steering a deck in plain English

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

## Rollout plan
- March: pilot with two teams
- May: security review complete
- July: rollout to all of engineering
- September: company-wide launch
- November: first adoption review
[[make this a timeline]]

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

CategoryExample directive
Layout[[make this a timeline]]
Tone[[be candid, no spin]]
Audience[[this is for the board]]
Order[[lead with the ask]]
Leaving out[[no pricing]]
Emphasis[[highlight the headline number]]

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Building a check-and-repair harness

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

Evaluation

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

What's next

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

What we learned

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

  • Put the reasoning in the data. Training on why a choice was made, including what was rejected, teaches more than the choice alone.
  • Fix the examples before adding a rule. When the teacher got something wrong, our first instinct was to add a rule to its prompt, and that rarely helped. The teacher copied its reference decks far more than it followed instructions, so fixing the reference was what actually changed its output.
  • Make repairs safe by default. A fix that's kept only when it measurably helps can run on every output.
  • Build the checker first. It's what makes the data trustworthy and the outputs safe to ship.

item.title: [Hugging Face] CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

Published November 3, 2026

Update on GitHub

9

Gonzalo Gonzalez

chalo2000

collinear-ai

Ajay Jagannath

ajayjagan2511

collinear-ai

Nazneen Rajani

nazneen

collinear-ai

Nathan Habib

SaylorTwift

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

  • Does the instruction read like a realistic instruction and not an evaluation setting?
  • Can every graded behaviour be inferred from the instruction?
  • Does the verifier check for correct behaviour and not for specific structure of one fix?
  • Does the starter code fail and the reference fix pass?
  • Does the original functionality still work with the new fix?
  • Do the verifiers fail memorized solutions like the known upstream patch?

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Run it from the Hub

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

harbor run --repo "https://huggingface.co/datasets/collinear-ai/cwe-bench" -d cwe-bench@2.0 -k 4 \
  --agent <agent> --model <model> --env docker \
  --allow-agent-host <model API host>

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

hf auth login --token $HF_TOKEN --add-to-git-credential

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Transformers Model Integration Contracts
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Transformers Model Integration Contracts

Published November 3, 2026

Update on GitHub

13

Tarek Ziadé

tarekziade

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Why bugs reach main

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

Introducing Model Integration Contracts

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

  • a fixture: the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned
  • a usage path: a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step
  • baselines: the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

inputs = tokenizer("The capital of France is", return_tensors="pt")
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=4, do_sample=False)
new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:]
print(tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens=True))

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

The UMT5 regression

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

How models are shrunk

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

The recipe now has four steps:

  • Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds, including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers. Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible. We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name.
  • Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte. Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test.
  • Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds.
  • Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Building MICs with agents

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git"
hf auth login
tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to ''

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

Random vs Overfit

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

  • Start with random weights and a fixed seed.
  • Overfit on a few examples, like "The capital of France is" => "Paris".

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

Open questions

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

  • How many real bugs does it catch on PRs, not just in replays?
  • How often does it send us chasing false alarms?
  • How much work do baseline reviews take?

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon…
item.description: Full title: Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon Quick
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon Quick

Organizations collect data in many forms. Structured data lives in databases and spreadsheets, whereas unstructured data sits in documents, reports, and files stored across file systems. Analyzing both together typically requires switching between multiple tools, running separate queries, and manually correlating results.

Amazon Quick addresses this with a unified experience. You can connect structured data through enriched datasets and unstructured data through S3-backed knowledge bases. You can then query both through a single conversational AI agent.

In this post, you learn how to:

  • Connect Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) as a data source and create a knowledge base.
  • Build a Space that combines structured and unstructured data.
  • Create and configure a custom chat agent that queries across both data types.
  • Ask questions that span structured and unstructured sources in a single conversation.

Solution architecture

The following diagram illustrates how each component connects to deliver a unified data experience through Amazon Quick.

Figure 1: Solution architecture for combining structured and unstructured data in Amazon Quick

The architecture has three layers:

  • Data layer: Your data exists in two forms. Unstructured content (documents, PDFs, reports) is stored in Amazon S3 and indexed through a knowledge base. Structured data (metrics, sales figures, and operational key performance indicators) is loaded as enriched datasets with semantic descriptions that the agent uses to translate questions into SQL.
  • Workspace layer: A Space brings both data types together into a single workspace. The Space references your knowledge base for unstructured queries and your datasets for structured queries. It can also include dashboards, file uploads, and action connectors. This is the layer where data from different sources converges into a unified context.
  • Agent layer: The custom chat agent links to the Space and uses it as its knowledge source. When a user asks a question, the agent determines whether to query the knowledge base, the dataset, or both, and returns a combined response with citations. Amazon Quick also applies built-in AI guardrails, such as content safety screening, to chat interactions.

With this layered approach, you can expand the solution over time. When you add a new data source to the Space, the agent linked to that Space can use it, and responses respect the permissions of the user who asks.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this walkthrough, you need:

  • An Amazon Quick account with an Enterprise subscription for the user who follows this walkthrough (creating datasets requires Enterprise). For details, see Amazon Quick pricing.
  • An Amazon S3 bucket for your business documents. To create one, see the Amazon S3 User Guide.
  • Amazon Quick access to your S3 bucket, granted by an Amazon Quick administrator. In the admin console, the administrator chooses Permissions, then AWS resources, selects Amazon S3, and chooses Select S3 buckets. Selected buckets have read-only permissions by default.
  • Permissions to create integrations, knowledge bases, datasets, spaces, and chat agents in Amazon Quick.

Prepare your sample data

This walkthrough uses two types of data:

Unstructured documents: Upload these to your Amazon S3 bucket for the knowledge base:

  • AnyCompany_Business_Review.pdf
  • AnyCompany_Market_Analysis_Report.pdf
  • AnyCompany_Product_Strategy_Memo.pdf

Structured data: Download this file to your computer. You upload it directly to Amazon Quick in Step 3:

  • Product_Sales.csv

Step 1: Create an Amazon S3 integration

Start by connecting Amazon Quick to your S3 bucket. From the Amazon Quick console, select Knowledge in the left navigation panel.

The knowledge page shows available connector types, including Amazon Q Business, Web Crawler, Amazon S3, and third-party options like Google Drive, OneDrive, and Microsoft SharePoint.

Under Amazon S3, choose Add. In the Create S3 knowledge base dialog, on the Connect S3 bucket page, provide the following details:

  • Name: A descriptive name for your integration (for example, “My Data Access Integration”).
  • S3 bucket location: Choose Quick Suite instance account to use a bucket in the same AWS account as Amazon Quick, or Other AWS account for a bucket in a different account.
  • S3 bucket URL: The S3 URI of the bucket containing your data. The bucket must be in the same Region as Amazon Quick.

Choose Next.

Figure 2: Create integration dialog showing the S3 connection fields

Step 2: Create a knowledge base

After the S3 integration is created, Amazon Quick prompts you to create a knowledge base. The knowledge base indexes your S3 content for AI-powered search.

Configure the knowledge base:

  • Name: “Business Knowledge Base”.
  • Description (optional): Notes about how the knowledge base will be used.
  • Content: Select “Add all content” to index everything in the connected S3 bucket, or “Add specific content” to specify the S3 prefixes for the folders and files to include (prefix filters are case-sensitive).

Next: Additional settings opens optional settings for document-level access control lists (ACLs) and a metadata files folder. Decide whether to use ACLs before you create the knowledge base, because you can’t change that choice later. This walkthrough uses sample data, so the default settings are sufficient. For details, see Set up and manage Amazon S3 integration.

Choose Create. A success banner confirms the S3 integration, and the knowledge base begins indexing in the background.

Figure 3: Create knowledge base dialog with the Business Knowledge Base name and content options

Step 3: Create and enrich a dataset
