export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="$OPENROUTER_API_KEY"
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL="anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5"
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL="anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5"
export CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL="anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5"

The first three lines connect Claude Code to OpenRouter; the last three set the models. Our Claude Code integration guide and setup tutorial cover the rest of the setup.

Keep sessions short

A 10-to-49-turn session costs about four to five times as much as a 2-to-9-turn one. When you move on to an unrelated task, start a fresh session or run /compact instead of carrying the old context with you.

Try a cheaper model for routine work

Through OpenRouter, Claude Code can call models from other labs, and the dataset shows people doing it. GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 sessions cost less than Opus sessions at every length, and our guide to the lowest-cost LLM inference on OpenRouter covers how to find cheaper options. To try one, pass it to Ori Harness:

ori claude --model z-ai/glm-5.3

Claude Code is built for Anthropic models, though, so test any other model on your own tasks before you switch. Ori Eval does this for you: your coding agent finds test material in your project, runs the models you want to compare on it, and recommends one with the scores and costs behind it.

Set a spending cap

You can set a credit limit on an API key, so a runaway session stops at a number you chose. In an organization, a guardrail with a budget limit caps each member or key per day, week or month, and OpenRouter applies it to sessions started with Ori Harness too. On Enterprise plans, workspace budgets cap a whole team’s spend per day, week, month or lifetime.

Frequently asked questions

How much does Claude Code cost per token?

Claude Code costs whatever the model it calls charges per token. Claude Opus 5.5 costs $4 per million input tokens, $20 per million output tokens, $5 per million tokens written to the prompt cache and $0.20 per million tokens read from it. Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs half those rates. Claude Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with cache reads at $0.01 per million. Most of a Claude Code session’s tokens are cache reads.

Is Claude Code cheaper with Sonnet or Opus?

Sonnet is cheaper. In our session-cost data, Claude Code sessions on Claude Sonnet 5.5 cost about half as much as sessions on Claude Opus 5.5 at every session length. In our own bug-fixing test, Sonnet fixed the same bugs as Opus.

Can I use Claude Code with other models?

Yes. When you point Claude Code at OpenRouter, it can call models from other labs. Our session-cost data includes Claude Code sessions on GLM, Kimi, DeepSeek, Qwen and GPT models. Claude Code is built for Anthropic models, so test another model on your own tasks before you switch to it.

Why is my first Claude Code request so expensive?

The first request writes Claude Code’s system prompt, tool definitions and project context to the prompt cache. In our test with Claude Opus 5.5 in an empty folder, that was about 17,000 tokens, which cost about $0.085, and a real project adds more. Later requests read the same context from the cache at a much lower price, 25 times lower on Opus 5.5.

Next steps

  • Ori Harness runs Claude Code, and other agent CLIs, on OpenRouter with one command.
  • Our session-cost dataset has the current medians for every model and session length.
  • Ori Eval tests models on your own tasks before you change your default.
  • The Claude Code integration guide covers the manual setup and the cost-tracking statusline.
  • Guardrails and workspace budgets cap what a person or team can spend.

item.title: [OpenRouter] Claude Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku: Which Should You Use?
item.content:encoded:
Claude Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku: Which Should You Use?

OpenRouter ·10/30/2026

Use Claude Sonnet 5.5 as your default, Claude Haiku 5.5 for high-volume and sub-agent work, and Claude Opus 5.5 when a task is long, ambiguous, or expensive to get wrong.

For most teams, the choice is between Opus and Sonnet, and the question is whether Opus is worth twice Sonnet’s price per token. On the coding tasks we tested, it wasn’t. We gave each model the same 11 coding tasks with hidden tests and the same bug-fix task in Claude Code. Every model passed everything, so what separated them was cost. Haiku was 19 to 30 times cheaper than Opus per task, and Sonnet cost between half and two-thirds as much as Opus.

Those results tell you how the three did on our tasks. The only way to know which one is best for your workflow is to test them on your own work. Ori Eval does this for you. You ask your coding agent which model is best for your project, and it finds test material in your code, writes the eval, runs the models you want to compare, and recommends one with the scores, times, and costs behind it. The section on switching between them shows how to point it at all three tiers.

Tl;dr

  • Use Claude Sonnet 5.5 as your default. It scored as well as or better than Opus 5.5 on our GPQA Diamond and τ-bench runs and passed every coding test, at half the per-token price.
  • Use Haiku 5.5 for high-volume and sub-agent work. It passed every coding test too, at a 12th to a 16th of Sonnet’s cost.
  • Keep Opus 5.5 for long, ambiguous tasks where a mistake costs more than the tokens. Our short tasks can’t rule out an advantage there.
  • Our tasks aren’t yours. Test the three on your own work with Ori Eval before you settle on one.
  • All three are one model string apart on OpenRouter, and Claude Code can use a different one for each role.

How do Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku differ?

Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 are three tiers of the same model generation. Anthropic released Opus 5.5 on September 22, 2026, Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, and Haiku 5.5 on October 7. All three have a 1-million-token context window and accept text, images, and PDFs. They differ mostly in price and, for Haiku, in lower benchmark scores.

Model Property / MetricOpus 5.5Sonnet 5.5Haiku 5.5
Input, per million tokens$4.00$2.00$0.10
Output, per million tokens$20.00$10.00$0.50
Cache read, per million tokens$0.20$0.10$0.01
Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index57.656.043.4
GPQA Diamond (our run)90.4%92.4%86.6%
τ-bench airline (our run)75.5%78.7%76.0%
Tokens on OpenRouter, Oct 12 to 186.18T2.45T2.07T

Prices are our list prices on October 21, 2026, from the model pages for Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5. The benchmark rows come from our benchmarks endpoint, pulled on October 21 (our runs of October 17). The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is a composite score across 10 evaluations from the independent benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis. T means trillions of tokens, from our daily rankings dataset.

Is Opus better than Sonnet?

On the benchmarks we run, Claude Opus 5.5 does not beat Claude Sonnet 5.5. Sonnet scored higher on our run of GPQA Diamond, a set of 198 graduate-level science questions (92.4% vs 90.4%). It also scored higher on τ-bench airline, a multi-turn customer-service agent benchmark (78.7% vs 75.5%). Opus leads by 1.6 points on the Artificial Analysis index. On both of our runs, Sonnet costs less than half as much per task, at $0.025 per GPQA question against $0.054 and $0.16 per τ-bench task against $0.34.

In the week of October 12, Opus 5.5 carried about two and a half times Sonnet’s token volume on OpenRouter. Opus is also Claude Code’s default model on most plans, and in our test Claude Code used Opus 5.5 through OpenRouter when no model was set. If you haven’t changed your model, Opus is what you’re running.

Is Haiku good enough to replace Sonnet?

Haiku 5.5 can replace Sonnet for well-specified, routine work. It scored 76.0% on τ-bench airline, half a point above Opus and 2.7 points behind Sonnet, at $0.011 per task. That is about a fourteenth of Sonnet’s cost. Our runs had 100 to 200 tasks per model, so gaps of a few points on this benchmark may be noise. Haiku trails Sonnet by 5.8 points on GPQA Diamond and by 12.6 points on the Artificial Analysis index, which weights agentic tasks and general knowledge at 30% each and coding and scientific reasoning at 20% each. On routine coding, our tests below found no gap.

What did our coding tests show?

We tested two things, writing a function to a spec and fixing a repo with Claude Code. All three models passed every test in both.

Functions with hidden tests

We wrote 11 Python tasks, each with a hidden test file. The eight everyday tasks were parsing durations, merging intervals, an LRU cache, an arithmetic evaluator without eval, the next run time of a cron expression, word wrapping, Semantic Versioning sort order, and a JSON path reader. The three hard tasks were a regex engine without the re module, a SQL WHERE filter with three-valued NULL logic, and free calendar slots across time zones on daylight-saving transition days. Each model answered each everyday task twice and each hard task three times, with the models’ default settings, for 25 attempts per model.

MetricOpus 5.5Sonnet 5.5Haiku 5.5
Attempts passed25 of 2525 of 2525 of 25
Cost per everyday task$0.0211$0.0112$0.0007
Cost per hard task$0.0739$0.0380$0.0027
Seconds per hard task32.125.722.6

Haiku used the most reasoning and still finished the hard tasks fastest. On the hard tasks it used 3,202 reasoning tokens on average, against 1,252 for Opus. Reasoning tokens are the tokens a model spends working through a problem before it writes its answer. Even with the extra reasoning, Haiku cost a 27th as much as Opus per hard task.

A bug-fix in Claude Code

We gave Claude Code a small invoicing library with three bugs and five tests. The bugs were rounding that used banker’s rounding (round half to even), a CSV parser that split on commas inside quotes, and a summary that overwrote quantities instead of adding them. We ran it three times per model through OpenRouter, choosing the model with the ANTHROPIC_MODEL environment variable.

MetricOpus 5.5Sonnet 5.5Haiku 5.5
Runs that fixed all three bugs3 of 33 of 33 of 3
Median cost per session$0.098$0.062$0.0052
Turns556 to 8
Wall-clock time24 to 30 s18 to 25 s22 to 31 s

A turn is one model response in the session. We computed session cost from each session’s token counts at our prices, because Claude Code’s own figure was wrong for Haiku.

Claude Code’s own total_cost_usd field didn’t recognize our Haiku slug and reported $0.16 to $0.31 per session, 30 to 60 times our computed median of $0.0052. In print mode (claude -p), Claude Code logs a warning when it doesn’t recognize a model slug. We saw it again on a one-word reply through Haiku, where Claude Code reported $0.107 and the request cost about $0.002 at our prices.

[claude-code:unrecognized_model] {"model":"anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5","query_source":"sdk"}

If you run Claude Code through OpenRouter, check spend on your Activity page instead, and use our spend controls if you need a cap.

These are small, well-specified tasks. On these tasks, the three tiers were equally reliable, and their costs differed widely. They don’t cover the work Anthropic built Opus for, which is long-running agentic coding and knowledge work where a mistake costs more than the tokens.

Which one should you use?

  • If you want one default, use Claude Sonnet 5.5. It scored as well as or better than Opus on both of our benchmark runs and matched it on all of our tests, at half the per-token price.
  • If you run a lot of requests, such as classification, extraction, sub-agents, or bulk code edits, use Haiku 5.5. It passed every test we gave it at a 12th to a 16th of Sonnet’s cost and a 19th to a 30th of Opus’s. Keep prompts under 100,000 tokens to stay on its lower price. Outside Claude Code, our Subagent server tool lets a larger model hand self-contained tasks to a smaller one.
  • Use Opus 5.5 for long tasks where a mistake is costly. That is the work it is built for, and our short tasks can’t rule out an advantage there.
  • If you can’t tell which group your workload is in, test your own tasks rather than ours, as described in the next section.

How do you switch between them?

We serve all three models through one API, one key, and one request format, so switching means changing the model string. This loop sends the same prompt to each tier and prints the output tokens and the cost we return on every response.

import os
import requests
for model in ["anthropic/claude-opus-5.5", "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5", "anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5"]:
    r = requests.post(
        "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"},
        json={"model": model, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a Python function that merges overlapping intervals."}]},
        timeout=300,
    )
    usage = r.json()["usage"]
    print(f"{model}: {usage['completion_tokens']} output tokens, ${usage['cost']:.4f}")

This is the output from our run on October 13, 2026.

anthropic/claude-opus-5.5: 1190 output tokens, $0.0239
anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5: 876 output tokens, $0.0088
anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5: 852 output tokens, $0.0004

Run your own tasks through each tier with Ori Eval. Ori Eval tests are TypeScript *.eval.ts files. Pass each of the three slugs to setupAgent({ model }) in one file, and the same tests run on every tier.

In Claude Code, you can keep Opus for planning and send routine work to cheaper models. Point Claude Code at OpenRouter with our setup guide, then set the model for each role.

export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL="anthropic/claude-opus-5.5"
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL="anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5"
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL="anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5"
export CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL="anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5"

Claude Code 2.1.307 recognizes the Opus and Sonnet slugs and gives them their 1-million-token context window. It doesn’t recognize the Haiku slug yet and assumes 200,000 tokens. To give Haiku its full window, add [1m] to its slug. We strip the suffix before routing. Leaving it off keeps Haiku sessions under about 200,000 tokens.

These variables set which model each name points to. They don’t change which one you use. To make Sonnet your main model, run /model sonnet in a session or set ANTHROPIC_MODEL=sonnet before you start Claude Code. To plan with Opus and write code with Sonnet, run /model opusplan instead. Because CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL is set, sub-agents that don’t name their own model run on Haiku.

If you’d rather have us pick per request, the Auto Router (openrouter/auto) chooses a model for each prompt. For coding, the Pareto Router picks a model that meets a minimum coding score you set.

Frequently asked questions

Is Claude Haiku cheaper than Sonnet?

Yes. On OpenRouter, Haiku 5.5 costs 20 times less per input and output token than Claude Sonnet 5.5 for prompts under 100,000 tokens, at $0.10 per million input tokens against $2.00. In our Claude Code runs the gap per session was smaller, about 12 times, partly because Haiku took more turns to reach the same result.

Is Sonnet 5.5 better than Opus 5.5 for coding?

In our Claude Sonnet vs Opus coding tests, the two were equal. Both passed all 25 hidden-test attempts and all three Claude Code runs through OpenRouter, and Sonnet was faster and cost half to two-thirds as much. Opus leads by 1.6 points on the Artificial Analysis index, and Anthropic positions it for long-running agentic coding, so it’s the safer choice for long, ambiguous sessions.

What is Claude Haiku good for?

Haiku 5.5 is good for high-volume, well-specified work such as classification, extraction, routing, sub-agent tasks, and routine code changes. In our tests through OpenRouter it passed every coding task, including a regex engine and SQL three-valued NULL logic, and scored half a point above Opus on τ-bench airline.

Which Claude model does Claude Code use?

Claude Code uses Opus 5.5 by default on Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise, and Anthropic API accounts, according to Anthropic’s model configuration docs. When you run Claude Code through OpenRouter, you can change the main model with ANTHROPIC_MODEL and set each role with the environment variables above.

Next steps

  • Ori Eval runs Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku on your own tasks and recommends one. To start, give your coding agent this instruction: run curl -fsSL https://openrouter.ai/skills/spawn-ori-eval and follow the instructions in its output to get started.
  • Our setup guide covers per-role model settings, and our tutorial Claude Code with OpenRouter: Setup, Models, and Costs covers model choice and costs.
  • The model pages for Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 show current prices, providers, and uptime. Our Opus 5.5 vs Sonnet 5.5 comparison page puts two of them side by side.
  • Prompt caching explains the cache-read prices in the table above.
  • The Claude 5.5 migration guide covers the API changes if you’re moving from an older Claude model.
  • Cost vs. Quality Tradeoff Framework for Agent Models and Confidence Thresholds for Model Escalation Routing cover when to move a request up a tier.

item.title: [OpenRouter] Guardrails Now Separate Organization Limits from Workspace D…
item.description: Full title: Guardrails Now Separate Organization Limits from Workspace Defaults
item.content:encoded:
Guardrails Now Separate Organization Limits from Workspace Defaults

Sasha Blumenfeld ·10/30/2026

A year ago, most companies on OpenRouter used AI in a few teams. Now it’s reaching across departments. People using OpenRouter on teams of 10 or more have grown 70x, and the average organization runs three times as many active API keys as more of that work moves to agents.

The admins managing all of this keep asking for the same thing: one set of rules for the whole organization, and room to make exceptions for the people who need more.

We’ve rebuilt how Guardrails is configured so admins can now set organization-wide restrictions, give people different budgets and model access within them, and change each policy on its own.

To get started, open your workspace’s Guardrails page to set up policies, or read the Guardrail Policies docs.

Why we changed Guardrails

We built the first version of Guardrails for that earlier pattern: a few teams, a handful of API keys. Today we see hundreds or thousands of employees signing in through SSO, coding agents running on every engineer’s laptop, and platform teams accountable for what all of it costs.

That shift showed up in what customers asked us for:

  • Budgets per person, with exceptions. Teams wanted a default monthly or weekly budget for everyone, plus a higher one for the people who need it. With one guardrail per budget level, one customer was on track to create a separate guardrail for each of its roughly 1,200 employees.
  • Defaults that start conservative. Customers wanted new members to start with the most conservative settings and be granted more over time. The old model worked the other way: the workspace default was the most anyone could get, and every other guardrail could only tighten it.
  • One rule across many workspaces. Companies with several business units wanted to set ZDR, provider, and region rules once, instead of copying the same guardrail into every workspace.
  • A way to handle requests. Admins kept getting asked for a bigger budget or access to a new model for a project, and wanted approving that to be a quick change, not a rebuild.

Some customers have now built their own internal workflows on top of Guardrails. An employee asks for a higher budget or access to a specific model for a project, explains why, and an admin approves it. With separate policy types and limits set by the organization, approving that request is a single change. They just assign the person a different budget or model access policy and it stays inside the organization’s limits automatically.

Organization limits are separate from workspace defaults

Organization admins can now set limits for whole workspaces, such as a maximum budget, Zero Data Retention requirements, or which models and providers can be used. These limits apply to every member and API key in the workspace, including people with their own budget or model policy.

Inside those limits, workspace admins set the defaults. New members get a default budget and model list as soon as they join, and the admin can give specific people a higher budget or access to more models. None of that can go past the organization’s limits.

In practice, that looks like an organization admin limits the Engineering workspace to $2,000 a month per person, ZDR-only providers, and no access to a particular high-cost model. The workspace admin sets the default for new members at $200 a month with the team’s standard models. A new engineer who joins gets that $200 default automatically. A senior engineer leading an agent project can get $1,500 a month and access to more models. No one in the workspace can go past $2,000 a month or use a non-ZDR provider.

Budget, model access, and moderation are separate policies

A guardrail used to bundle a budget, model and provider access, and content moderation into one named object. They’re now three separate policy types:

  • Budget sets a spending cap in USD that resets daily, weekly, or monthly.
  • Model and provider access controls which models and providers can be used, ZDR, and data regions.
  • Content moderation covers prompt injection protection, sensitive info detection, and custom content filters.

We split them up because they don’t change together. A person’s budget might change with every new project, while the team’s model list and moderation rules can stay the same for months.

Now the team shares one model access policy and one moderation policy, and you can change one person’s budget without touching anything else.

Backwards Compatible

You don’t need to change anything to keep your current setup. Existing guardrails keep their IDs and enforce the same rules, and the guardrails API and Terraform resources work as before. Each guardrail now also shows up as separate budget, model access, and moderation policies, so you can move over one workspace at a time when you’re ready.

If you manage guardrails through the API or Terraform, read Migrating to Guardrail Policies first, because changes made in the dashboard don’t sync back to your config.

Getting started

To try it, open the Guardrails page in any workspace you manage. Your existing guardrails will already be there as separate policies. A good first step is raising one person’s budget without touching anything else. Organization admins can set org-wide limits from Workspace-wide guardrails. For the full setup, see the Guardrail Policies docs.

FAQ

What are OpenRouter Guardrails?

Guardrails let organizations control spending, model and provider access, and content moderation for their members and API keys.

Can I set different AI budgets for different people?

Yes. Assign a budget policy to a member or API key. It resets daily, weekly, or monthly and can’t exceed the limits your organization admin sets.

Are budgets shared across a workspace?

No. Each budget applies per member or per API key, not as a shared pool. A $100/month limit means each person can spend up to $100.

What happens to my existing guardrails?

They keep enforcing the same rules and keep their IDs. Each one now also appears as up to three separate policies.

Do I need to migrate to a new API?

No. The existing guardrails API and Terraform resources keep working. New policy endpoints live alongside them under /api/v1/guardrails/policies.

Who can manage guardrail policies?

Organization admins can manage every policy, including org-wide limits. Workspace admins manage policies in the workspace.

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for Fin…
item.description: Full title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams

Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget?

Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume.

The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence.

In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults.

The operating model in one view

Five stages, run as a loop. Attribute: every Amazon Bedrock dollar lands on an identity, team, and application in the billing pipeline. Observe: every request is logged with enough metadata to explain what generated the spend. Enforce: budgets have teeth, with alerts at minimum and hard blocks where the risk demands them. Optimize: the platform defaults (model routing, caching, token limits) remove waste centrally instead of asking every team to be careful. Operate: a small scorecard and a review cadence turn the data into decisions. FinOps leads stages one and five. Platform engineering leads two through four. The review is joint. The stages are sequenced deliberately. Each one depends on the ones before it, and teams that jump straight to optimization without attribution and observability are guessing.

Figure 1: The five-stage operating model, run as a continuous loop

Stage 1: Attribute every dollar

You can’t manage what you can’t attribute, and everything downstream (chargeback, budgets, enforcement, anomaly detection) depends on this stage. The foundation is the granular cost attribution of Amazon Bedrock (see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock): Amazon Bedrock automatically attributes inference costs to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal that made the call, across all models, with no resources to manage. The caller’s ARN lands in the line_item_iam_principal column of the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0, and coverage spans IAM users, roles, federated identities, and API keys.

Setup is four steps:

  • Turn on IAM principal data in your CUR 2.0 data export.
  • Tag your IAM principals with business dimensions such as team, application, and cost center. For federated access, configure your identity provider to pass session names and tags through OIDC or SAML claims.
  • Activate those tags as cost allocation tags in AWS Billing (console or the UpdateCostAllocationTagsStatus API).
  • Analyze the tags: they surface in CUR 2.0 with an iamPrincipal/ prefix (for example, iamPrincipal/team) and appear in AWS Cost Explorer under the IAM category within 24–48 hours of activation, ready for filtering and grouping by team, application, or cost center.

This is invoice-grade, per-identity attribution with no custom infrastructure.

The shared-role problem

The pattern that deserves the most attention is the shared-role problem, because it is where most platforms silently lose attribution. A large language model (LLM) gateway that calls Amazon Bedrock through a single IAM role attributes every dollar to that one role, eliminating per-user visibility entirely. The fix is per-user session management. The gateway assumes the Amazon Bedrock invocation role once per user, passing the user’s identity as the role session name and their attributes as session tags, then caches those credentials for up to an hour (one AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) call per user per hour, not per request).

This needs two roles: a gateway execution role holding sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession permissions, and the Amazon Bedrock invocation role it assumes. The result is line_item_iam_principal entries like assumed-role/BedrockRuntimeRole/gw-alex, each carrying its user’s tags: per-user and per-tenant attribution restored behind a shared gateway.

import boto3

sts = boto3.client("sts")

# One call per user; cache the returned credentials up to 1 hour
response = sts.assume_role(
    RoleArn="arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/BedrockRuntimeRole",
    RoleSessionName="gw-alex", # the user, not the gateway
    Tags=[
        {"Key": "team", "Value": "sales-ai"},
        {"Key": "application", "Value": "renewal-agent"},
        {"Key": "costCenter", "Value": "CC-2041"}
    ]
)

A note on application inference profiles and Projects

Amazon Bedrock offers two more attribution mechanisms, each suited to a different pattern. Application inference profiles are pre-created, per-application resources on the bedrock-runtime endpoint that carry cost allocation tags. You create one profile per application per model per AWS Region, and callers reference the profile ARN, which fits teams with a small and stable set of applications and models. Projects and workspaces serve the bedrock-mantle endpoint (Responses API, Chat Completions API). A project isn’t tied to a specific model, so a single project ID spans many models, which fits teams whose model usage changes frequently. You pass the project ID at client initialization, and its tags flow to CUR 2.0 and Cost Explorer (see Manage AI costs with Amazon Bedrock Projects). Projects are the attribution path for OpenAI-compatible workloads on Amazon Bedrock.

For bedrock-runtime workloads, we recommend IAM principal attribution through session tags as the primary mechanism. It scales with your identity system, requires no pre-created resources, and covers every model and API operation. Application inference profiles work well when a small, stable set of business units needs invoice-grade billing separation without changes to identity design. Use projects for bedrock-mantle workloads that use the Responses API or Chat Completions API.

Stage 2: Make every request observable

CUR tells you who spent. Invocation logs tell you what happened. Amazon Bedrock supports model invocation logging of request data, response data, and metadata to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), or both. Use Amazon CloudWatch for fast operational queries and S3 plus Amazon Athena for long-term business intelligence (BI) access. Treat logging as infrastructure, not a manual toggle: provision the log group or bucket through code, define retention and encryption policies, and validate delivery during environment setup. If logging exists only in development or only in one Region, your cost program becomes fragmentary the moment usage grows.

Logging also closes the latency gap: CUR attribution lags roughly 24 hours, but CloudWatch plus OpenTelemetry can power near-real-time dashboards showing per-developer spend within minutes (Analyzing Claude Code usage with CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry demonstrates this end to end).

Request metadata for workload-level attribution

Raw logs answer identity-level questions. To answer workload-level questions (which feature, workflow, or tenant generated the tokens), stamp request metadata on every call. Amazon Bedrock captures this metadata in the invocation logs for later analysis:

The following example uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock through the US cross-Region inference profile. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. For availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

response = client.converse(
    modelId="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5",
    messages=[...],
    requestMetadata={
        "application": "renewal-copilot",
        "workflow": "renewal-risk-summary",
        "tenant": "enterprise-sales",
        "agent": "renewal-agent"
    }
)

Amazon Bedrock doesn’t enforce request metadata, and teams drift into inconsistent schemas quickly when every application does its own thing. The platform team should inject mandatory metadata centrally in a shared SDK wrapper or gateway, normalize the key set, and treat metadata coverage as a platform health metric.

Diagnostic queries

With logs and metadata in place, CloudWatch Logs Insights answers the standing questions. Who consumes the most tokens:

fields @timestamp, identity.arn as caller, modelId,
input.inputTokenCount as inTokens,
output.outputTokenCount as outTokens
| stats sum(inTokens + outTokens) as totalTokens,
count(*) as calls
by caller, modelId
| sort totalTokens desc
| limit 25

The same query grouped by requestMetadata.application and requestMetadata.workflow instead of caller produces the workload-level leaderboard: the view product and engineering teams will ask FinOps for the moment chargeback conversations start.

Note: Field paths shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema, which may vary by model, API operation, and logging configuration.

Stage 3: Enforce budgets

With attribution and observability in place, enforcement becomes an architecture choice rather than a wish. There are three viable tiers. The right one depends on your spend velocity, your risk tolerance for overspend, and how your tools connect to Amazon Bedrock.

Tier 1: Monitor and alert (no blocking)

Amazon Bedrock writes principal identity into the billing pipeline automatically. You put AWS Budgets on top for threshold alerts, with the OpenTelemetry dashboards from Stage 2 closing the 24-hour CUR gap for day-to-day visibility. Nothing to deploy, native AWS billing, and no added latency on inference calls. It works with tools that call Amazon Bedrock directly. Nothing can hard-stop spend, so you see the problem after it happens. Right for early adoption, where alerting plus human intervention is sufficient. Two builder guides walk through it: Limiting Bedrock usage and controlling costs, and Deep dive on managing Bedrock in Claude Code with AWS Budgets and Tags.

Tier 2: IAM tag enforcement (deny on breach)

An aggregator AWS Lambda function tallies per-user token and dollar counters in Amazon DynamoDB from invocation log data. When a user breaches their threshold, the function adds their identity to a shared IAM deny policy (denying bedrock:*) until a monthly reset or admin override. This enforcement runs entirely on IAM and Amazon Bedrock logging, with no third-party component in the inference path, and it works with tools that call Amazon Bedrock directly. The Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock in the AWS Solutions Library provides a deployable variant. It checks each user’s usage against per-user and per-team limits when it issues credentials, and withholds credentials once a user exceeds their limit. Because that check uses usage telemetry emitted by the client, its figures can differ from CUR. In either form, enforcement is asynchronous. A block takes effect seconds to minutes after the breaching call for an IAM policy update, or at the next credential refresh for the credential check. Your platform team owns the pipeline. This tier is right for teams that need real enforcement, can tolerate that lag, and want to keep third-party software out of the data path.

Tier 3: Gateway enforcement (synchronous block)

A gateway sits in the inference data path and enforces budgets synchronously, returning HTTP 429 the moment a user or team exceeds their limit. You get sub-second blocking, per-user model allowlists, token rate limits, and centrally enforced routing rules. The trade-off: a component in the data path that must be deployed, scaled, and security-reviewed. Clients must be configured to send their requests through the gateway.

For Claude Code and Claude Desktop fleets, the Claude apps gateway for AWS is the official recommendation. It ships inside the CLI binary and runs as a single stateless container backed by PostgreSQL. It provides OIDC identity, centrally managed policy, OpenTelemetry telemetry, multi-Region Amazon Bedrock routing, and per-user/group/org spend caps out of the box. For mixed-model workloads spanning multiple providers, general-purpose gateways remain the right choice: LiteLLM through the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate reference architecture, or a serverless alternative described in Build a proactive AI cost management system for Amazon Bedrock, Part 2.

Choosing a tier

Two factors dominate.

Connectivity: If developers call Amazon Bedrock directly with no proxy, only Tiers 1 and 2 are viable.

Spend velocity: If spend is already in the millions per month, build enforcement now. If alerts can hold the line for another quarter, invest in Stages 1 and 2 first and add enforcement when the data demands it.

Most organizations should phase it: observe at Tier 1, then step up. Treat all three as bridges, not destinations: the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens already codifies agent cost governance as a first-class architectural concern, and the attribution foundation from Stage 1 is what any managed enforcement will sit on.

Stage 4: Optimize the defaults

Most Amazon Bedrock waste is not individual carelessness. It is platform defaults nobody set. The two highest-impact levers are both platform-controlled.

Model routing

Not every task needs a frontier model. Routine completions (boilerplate, linting suggestions, small refactors) can run on smaller, cheaper models with quality reserved for complex reasoning, through intelligent prompt routing within a model family or routing rules at the gateway (see Reduce costs and latency with Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing and prompt caching for the full walkthrough). Which workflows can downshift is an empirical question: pull the workload leaderboard from Stage 2, run a quality evaluation on the cheaper model for the top entries, and route what passes. For agentic coding fleets, where boilerplate dominates call volume, more than half of calls landing on cheaper models is an achievable target.

Prompt caching

Prompt caching rewards stable repeated prefixes. As of October 2026, the published Amazon Bedrock pricing for Anthropic Claude models in US East (N. Virginia) bills a cache write at 1.25x the base input rate with the 5-minute time-to-live (TTL) (2x with the 1-hour TTL). A cache read is billed at 0.1x the base input rate on Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and at 0.05x on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5. Check the pricing page for your model and Region, because these multipliers vary by model and can change. The break-even math is friendlier than teams assume. With the 5-minute TTL, a single reuse already pays for the write, and ten calls against a stable prefix cost roughly a fifth of the uncached price (about 22 percent at a 0.1x read rate, 17 percent at 0.05x). The only losing case is writes that are never re-read, which cost 25 percent extra with the 5-minute TTL and double with the 1-hour TTL. So the platform dashboard should track cache-read volume against cache-write volume per workflow. A low read ratio means the prefix is not actually stable (usually a timestamp or session ID embedded before the cache point).

Candidates surface directly from the invocation logs:

fields requestMetadata.workflow as workflow, modelId,
input.inputTokenCount as inTokens
| stats count(*) as calls,
avg(inTokens) as avgInputTokens,
sum(inTokens) as totalInputTokens
by workflow, modelId
| filter calls > 50 and avgInputTokens > 2000
| sort totalInputTokens desc
| limit 25

Note: Field paths shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema, which may vary by model, API operation, and logging configuration.

Application-level optimization

A third class of savings (just-in-time retrieval instead of stuffed context, compaction of long conversations, distilling stable high-volume workflows onto smaller models) belongs to application teams rather than the platform. The platform’s job is to make those savings visible: publish the per-workflow token leaderboard, set token limits per model and workflow, and let the teams that own expensive workflows see exactly where they stand.

Stage 5: Operate the loop

The first four stages produce data. This one turns it into decisions. The platform team runs a standing health dashboard with four signals:

  • Model mix: Which models are called and how often, the direct measure of routing discipline.
  • Failed request rates: Errors, throttles, and timeouts. Each retry adds latency, and a client-side timeout on a request that still completes on the service side can be billed twice, once for the abandoned call and once for the retry.
  • Cache effectiveness: The read-versus-write ratio from Stage 4.
  • Metadata coverage: The percentage of production calls with complete metadata. Every uncovered call is an attribution blind spot that quietly degrades every other number.

When a signal drifts, the remediation is a policy change (routing rules, token limits, metadata enforcement), not an email asking teams to be careful.

The money loop

FinOps runs the money loop on the same data. When attribution is clean, anomaly detection becomes an investigation stream rather than a panicked all-hands: a spike in a tagged team or application triggers a lookup in the Stage 2 leaderboard, not a war room. Chargeback runs from CUR groupings by team and application.

Scorecard

The following thresholds are starting points, not prescriptions. Calibrate them against your own fleet data and pricing tier before adopting them as policy.

DimensionMetricGreenYellowRed
Unit economicsCost per successful outcome≤ budget1–1.5x budget>1.5x budget
Per-dev costDaily spend per developer<$100$100–$300>$300
Model routing% of calls to cost-efficient-models>50%30–50%<30%
Cache efficiencyCache-read hit ratio>60%30–60%<30%

Green means the workload operates inside its economic envelope. Yellow means routing or caching discipline is slipping. Red means spend is concentrating in premium models or uncached context, and the Stage 3 and 4 controls are the remediation path. Review this scorecard on a regular cadence (weekly for high-velocity fleets, biweekly otherwise) and treat it as the joint FinOps-plus-platform decision surface.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to build a five-stage operating model that takes Amazon Bedrock spend from uncontrolled to fully governed:

  • Attribute every dollar to an owner using IAM principal tags, session tags, and CUR 2.0.
  • Observe every request through model invocation logging and stamped request metadata.
  • Enforce budgets at the tier that matches your risk: monitor-only, IAM deny on breach, or synchronous gateway blocking.
  • Optimize platform defaults with intelligent prompt routing and prompt caching to remove waste centrally.
  • Operate a scorecard and review cadence that turns telemetry into policy decisions.

Notice the first row of that scorecard: cost per successful outcome, not cost per call. That distinction is where this playbook hands off. Everything here makes Amazon Bedrock spend visible, attributable, capped, and efficient, but a workflow can be perfectly efficient and still not be worth running. Deciding that requires measuring the agent against the human process it replaced, which is a product and analytics discipline rather than a FinOps one. What the cost platform contributes is the foundation: clean attribution and per-workflow cost data are exactly the inputs that outcome measurement joins against.

Build the five stages and you can answer, end to end: who spent it, why, and whether it was controlled. That is what it means to manage Amazon Bedrock cost, and it is the difference between a monthly bill review and an operating model.

To get started, deploy the Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock reference architecture for Stages 1–3, then use the cost attribution best practices documentation to configure your tagging strategy.

About the authors

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with…
item.description: Full title: Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime

Coding agents now build working web apps: a dashboard, a product page, a prototype that a product team wants to try. The fastest way to review that work is to open the app, use it, ask for a change, and check the result. That loop works well when the app keeps running where the agent edits it, so each change shows up in the browser within seconds. When the app must be copied out and deployed somewhere else first, every change waits for a deployment, and the review slows down to that pace.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with your choice of agent framework and foundation model (FM). AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, runs each agent session in its own isolated microVM. With Session endpoints, you can open an app running in that session from your own browser. Session Endpoints give each session an authenticated URL that forwards each request’s HTTP method, path, query string, and body, and WebSocket connections, to the ports you allow. You can watch the page update as the agent saves each file.

In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then open one local page with a chat on the left and the live website on the right. You ask the agent to switch the site to a dark color theme, follow its steps as they stream in, and watch the website change without a refresh. Finally, you look at what happens internally: a second port in the same session, and the requests the Session endpoint refuses.

The complete sample, including the notebook this post follows, is in the 14-remote-access folder of the agentcore-samples GitHub repo.

How Session endpoints work

Each session gets its own Session endpoint, and six details shape how you use it.

You choose which ports it reaches. You set allowedPorts when you call CreateAgentRuntime: 1–5 entries, each a single port or a range within 8000–12000, excluding the reserved platform ports. Allowing a port doesn’t start a server, so your application must listen on it, bound to 0.0.0.0.

The URL arrives with the session. The InvokeAgentRuntime response carries it in the X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Endpoint-Url header, which SDKs that model it expose as sessionEndpointUrl.

Every request is authenticated. For a runtime that uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), each HTTP request, HTTP/2 stream, and WebSocket handshake carries a Signature Version 4 (SigV4) signature. The caller also needs bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on the runtime and its runtime endpoint. For a runtime with an inbound JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer, each request carries a bearer token instead. Knowing the URL doesn’t grant access.

The host name selects the port. Your client connects on port 443 regardless of the target port, and a prefix on the host name chooses the port inside the session:

https://8090--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/index.html
https://8081--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/status

It carries the protocols your server speaks. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests, including server-sent events and gRPC, and WebSocket connections all pass through. This walkthrough uses HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket.

It’s scoped to one session. The URL needs credentials on every request and lasts only as long as the session, so use it to build, test, and review what your agent produces. To serve an app to your users, deploy it to a hosting service such as AWS Amplify Hosting.

A browser can’t add a SigV4 signature or a bearer token to the requests a page makes on its own, so the Session endpoint client in the bedrock-agentcore SDK can open a local endpoint on your machine. Your browser opens http://localhost:8088, and the local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and WebSocket handshake before forwarding it.

A Session endpoint is different from a runtime endpoint, which AgentCore runtime already provides. Use a runtime endpoint, such as DEFAULT, to reach your agent, which controls which version of it callers will reach. InvokeAgentRuntime calls resolve through it, so you can keep development and production on different versions and promote or roll back without changing callers. Use a Session endpoint to see what your agent runs in its session, such as a web preview. It’s an authenticated URL that reaches only the ports you allow, works with whichever version the session runs, and stops working when the session ends. For complete documentation, refer to Connect to runtime sessions through a session endpoint.

Solution overview

The sample has four parts. A coding agent runs in the session on port 8080 and edits the website’s files with four tools: list, read, write, and edit. The agent starts a Vite development server on port 8090, which serves the website and pushes each saved change to the browser over its hot-reload WebSocket. On your machine, PreviewApp serves the preview page, sends your prompts to InvokeAgentRuntime, and opens a local endpoint for the website. As Figure 1 shows, the preview page loads the website from the Vite development server on port 8090 through the local endpoint and the Session endpoint, and sends your prompts through InvokeAgentRuntime to the agent on port 8080. The numbers show the order of the steps for one request.

Figure 1: Solution architecture

Before step 1, PreviewApp has already called InvokeAgentRuntime once to start the session, which starts the agent and the Vite development server. PreviewApp read the Session endpoint URL from that response and opened a local endpoint for port 8090. The numbered steps in Figure 1 then follow one request for a change:

  • The site pane of the preview page loads the website from the local endpoint on localhost:8088. The local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and the WebSocket handshake, and forwards them to the Session endpoint. The Session endpoint checks the signature and the port against allowedPorts, then forwards them to the Vite development server on port 8090. The page keeps the Vite hot-reload WebSocket open.
  • You send a prompt from the chat pane. PreviewApp sends it to InvokeAgentRuntime as a standard AWS API call signed with your AWS credentials, and the runtime delivers it to the agent on port 8080. The agent’s steps stream back to the chat pane as it works.
  • The agent calls Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock to decide what to change.
  • The agent reads the site’s files and saves the ones it changes. The Vite development server serves those files and watches them for changes.
  • When a file is saved, Vite pushes the change over the WebSocket opened in step 1, back through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the site pane updates without a refresh.
  • From the notebook, PreviewApp reads the agent’s /status route on port 8081 through the same Session endpoint. Only the port changes.

Port 8080 isn’t in allowedPorts, because InvokeAgentRuntime reaches the agent without going through the Session endpoint.

Prerequisites

To follow the walkthrough, you need:

  • An AWS account in an AWS Region where AgentCore runtime Session endpoints are available, with credentials configured.
  • Permissions to create an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, upload to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and create a runtime, plus bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime and bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on that runtime and its DEFAULT runtime endpoint. For details, refer to IAM permissions for AgentCore runtime.
  • Python 3.10 or later, with bedrock-agentcore 1.25.2 or later and boto3 1.43.122 or later.
  • Git, to clone the sample repo, and a Jupyter environment, such as JupyterLab or Visual Studio Code with the Jupyter extension, to run the notebook.
  • Access to Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock. For model availability by Region, refer to Regional availability by models.
  • Node.js 22 or later with npm, which the deployment script uses to package the agent and the website.

The sample deploys the agent as a zip file in Amazon S3 with direct code deployment for Node.js, so you don’t need Docker or an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Session endpoints work with microVM runtimes, not with the Instances compute type, and Session endpoint URLs are reachable over public HTTPS. AWS PrivateLink isn’t supported for inbound connections.

Deploy the agent and its website

First, you deploy the runtime, and the configuration you choose here decides which ports the Session endpoint can reach. The deployment script bundles the agent into one file, adds the website and its dependencies for the runtime’s Linux on Arm64 system, uploads the zip to Amazon S3, and creates the runtime.

The following excerpt from deploy.py shows the two settings that matter for this post. protocolConfiguration says where the agent listens for InvokeAgentRuntime, and allowedPorts lists the ports the Session endpoint can reach: 8090 for the website and 8081 for the agent’s status route. Port 8080 isn’t in the list, because InvokeAgentRuntime reaches the agent without it. For the port and path settings, refer to Configure your agent’s serving port and invocation path.

agentRuntimeArtifact={"codeConfiguration": {
    "code": {"s3": {"bucket": code_bucket(), "prefix": S3_PREFIX}},
    "runtime": "NODE_22",
    "entryPoint": ["app.js"],
}},
protocolConfiguration={"serverProtocol": "HTTP", "port": 8080, "path": "/invocations"},
allowedPorts=[{"port": 8090}, {"port": 8081}],

The website’s Vite configuration makes the development server reachable from the Session endpoint. It listens on 0.0.0.0 at port 8090 and doesn’t restrict the Host header (server.allowedHosts is true), because requests arrive under a host name the runtime assigns rather than localhost. The Session endpoint authenticates every request before it reaches the server, so the server doesn’t need its own host check.

To deploy the runtime:

  1. Clone the sample repo and change to the sample folder:
git clone https://github.com/awslabs/agentcore-samples.git
cd agentcore-samples/01-features/02-host-your-agent/01-runtime/03-advanced/16-session-endpoints
  1. Open session_endpoints_preview.ipynb from the sample folder.
  1. Run the install cell, which installs the Python dependencies.
  1. Run the %run deploy.py cell. Deployment takes a few minutes, mostly waiting for the runtime to reach the READY status.

Open the preview

With the runtime ready, you start the preview. One call does three things: it starts a session (which starts the website), opens a local endpoint for port 8090, and serves the preview page on localhost:8087.

from preview_app import PreviewApp

app = PreviewApp().start()
print("Open", app.url)

Inside start(), the calls that use Session endpoints are short. The first InvokeAgentRuntime call returns the URL in a response header, session_endpoint_url reads it, and the Session endpoint client opens a local endpoint for port 8090:

answer = client.invoke_agent_runtime(
    agentRuntimeArn=runtime_arn, runtimeSessionId=session_id,
    payload=json.dumps({"prompt": ""}).encode(), contentType="application/json",
)
endpoint = client.session_endpoint_client(session_endpoint_url(answer))
local = endpoint.open_local_endpoint(port=8090, local_port=8088).start()

To open the preview:

  • Run the cell that starts PreviewApp.
  • Open the printed link, http://localhost:8087, in your browser.

The page shows the website on the right, served from port 8090 in the session, and a short guide with suggested requests on the left.

Ask the agent for a change

Now you ask for a change and watch it arrive. Each prompt goes to the agent through InvokeAgentRuntime. The agent reads the files it needs, writes the ones it changes, and reports each step as it happens. When a file is saved, the Vite development server pushes the change over its WebSocket, through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the website updates in place.

To ask for a change:

  • On the preview page, choose Switch this website to a dark coffee-house color theme.
  • Follow the agent’s steps in the chat pane as it reads and saves files.
  • Watch the site pane. It changes when the agent saves the stylesheet, and a banner names the file the change came from.

The following video shows the preview page while the agent works through several requests. Choosing a suggested request sends it to the agent, the chat pane lists each file the agent reads and saves, and the site pane on the right updates without a refresh, from the dark theme to a green Order ahead button.

Figure 2: The preview page as the agent works

The steps stream because the agent answers with server-sent events when you ask it to. You can send the same prompts from Python with app.ask, which reads the stream with iter_events from the bedrock-agentcore SDK. The open page updates in the same way:

for event in app.ask("Make the Order ahead button green"):
    if "step" in event:
        print("  ", event["step"])
    elif "done" in event:
        print(event["done"]["reply"])

The output of this Python script should resemble the following:

   Looking at the site's files
   Reading src/main.js
   Reading src/style.css
   Reading index.html
   Saved src/style.css
The Order ahead button is now green instead of brown, with white text kept for contrast. You can see it in the hero section, just below the "Small batch coffee, roasted every morning" heading at the top of the page.

Reach a second port in the same session

The website isn’t the only server you can reach. The agent serves /status on port 8081, which lists each prompt and the files it changed. The same Session endpoint reaches it, and the only difference is the port argument.

status = app.endpoint.request("GET", "/status", port=8081)
print("GET /status on port 8081: HTTP", status.status)
for edit in status.json()["edits"]:
    print("  ", edit["prompt"], "->", ", ".join(edit["files"]))

The output of this Python script should resemble the following:

GET /status on port 8081: HTTP 200
   Make the Order ahead button green -> src/style.css

What the Session endpoint refuses

When the runtime refuses a request, it answers with an HTTP status, an empty body, and an error code in a response header, so you can tell its refusals from errors your application returns. The notebook sends a request to a port outside allowedPorts and a request without credentials, and the runtime refuses both with 403 AccessDenied.

The following table lists the refusals you’re likely to meet while you build with Session endpoints.

RequestResponse from the runtime
A port that isn’t in allowedPorts403 AccessDenied
A request without valid credentials403 AccessDenied or 401 AuthenticationRequired
An allowed port with nothing listening on it502 PortNotReachable
A URL whose session no longer exists404 SessionNotFound

How access to your session is protected

The runtime removes its own authentication headers before it forwards a request, so the website doesn’t receive your signature. Requests are recorded in AWS CloudTrail as InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy events, with the event source bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com. The local endpoint acts with your credentials, so it limits who can use it. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, answers only requests addressed to its own local address, and refuses WebSocket connections opened by pages from other origins. Run the local endpoint only while you use the preview. For more information, see Log session endpoint requests in CloudTrail.

The access controls don’t separate the website from the agent. Both run in the same session, so give the execution role only the permissions the agent needs. If the runtime replaces the session’s compute, open connections close, and the agent’s edits might not survive unless the session uses persistent storage. Refer to File system configurations for AgentCore runtime if you need the files to outlast the compute.

The agent’s file tools resolve every path inside the site folder and refuse paths outside it, so a prompt can’t make the agent change other files in the session. If other people can send prompts to your coding agent, consider Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful prompts and responses, and review the agent’s changes before you publish them.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, stop the preview and delete the resources the sample created. The website the agent edited lives in the session, so it goes with the session.

To clean up:

  1. Run the stop cell, and press Enter when the notebook asks. This stops the preview page, the local endpoint, and the session.
  1. Run the %run cleanup.py cell, which deletes the runtime, the uploaded code, and the IAM role.

Conclusion

Session endpoints give you authenticated access to the applications in an AgentCore runtime session from your own tools over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and WebSocket, on the ports you allow. In this post, you deployed a coding agent with a Vite website in its session, opened the live website in your browser through a local endpoint, asked the agent for a dark theme, and watched the change arrive as the agent saved the file. You also reached a second port in the same session and confirmed what the Session endpoint refuses.

To go further, run the notebook with your own site in the site folder, or change the agent’s tools to match how your coding agent works. For the full set of options, including port ranges, OAuth, HTTP/2, and gRPC, refer to Connect to runtime sessions through a session endpoint.

To change the port or path that InvokeAgentRuntime uses in your own agent, refer to Configure your agent’s serving port and invocation path. If your agent also needs to run build or test commands in the same session, refer to Execute shell commands in AgentCore runtime sessions. To deploy your own Node.js agent from a zip file the way this sample does, refer to Direct code deployment for Node.js. For everything else the service offers, start with Host agent or tools with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, and find more examples in the agentcore-samples GitHub repo.

About the author

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amaz…
item.description: Full title: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock

Worldwide Express (part of ShipStation Global) had built something big: approximately $5 billion in systemwide revenue, over 75 less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers. But that same scale had a hidden cost. Every month, $15 million in free cash flow sat frozen, locked in billing exceptions no one had resolved yet. Each one had to be chased down by hand, carrier by carrier, with its own rules to check. Worldwide Express outsourced to a team that worked cases one at a time, calling customers and carriers for each dispute. The exceptions piled up, cash stayed stuck, and every order took longer to turn into money.

Worldwide Express worked with AWS and LTM to build a multi-agentic AI solution with Amazon Bedrock that plugs directly into their transportation management system (TMS), SpeedShip. Six months after launch, the company reported a 75 percent reduction in active exceptions, a 4-week improvement in time-to-cash, $1M annual savings, and a one-time $10M free cash flow infusion.

In this post, we describe the challenge, explain how Worldwide Express designed the multi-agent solution, and share the results.

The challenge

In LTL freight, roughly 14 percent of invoices fail the standard three-way match between the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the carrier invoice. When a match fails, the invoice enters exception handling. For Worldwide Express, exceptions fell into three categories:

  • Line-item mismatches: Quantities or service codes that didn’t align with the shipment record.
  • Pricing variances: The carrier billed a rate different from the contracted price.
  • Unexpected accessorial charges: Liftgate fees, residential surcharges, or reweigh adjustments that weren’t on the original quote.

Each exception triggered a five-step manual process:

  • Identify the exception type by cross-referencing the invoice against the purchase order, goods receipt, and pricing.
  • Research the root cause in vendor records.
  • Send email to the carrier or warehouse with dispute details.
  • Wait for a response.
  • Execute the resolution in the TMS.

With each carrier operating under its own tariff structure and dispute workflow, this process consumed most of the FinOps team’s bandwidth.

Rule-based process automation (RPA) can handle structured, predictable workflows. However, exception resolution requires contextual judgment: interpreting a carrier’s accessorial policy, comparing charges against shipment data, and deciding validity given a carrier, exception type, and dollar amount. That variability is what made the problem a fit for the agentic AI framework.

From assessment to production

In June 2025, Worldwide Express engaged the AWS Business Transformation & Value Advisory team to identify 19 automation opportunities across the Order-to-Cash lifecycle. Knowing the business value of exceptions automation, Worldwide Express moved from assessment to production in less than 6 months.

How it works

The solution runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock provides AI reasoning, and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is the engine. The design calls for fine-grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed between agents. Building the framework directly on Amazon EC2, with Amazon Bedrock providing inference, keeps that orchestration logic fully in the team’s hands and supports open source agent libraries. Production controls of business logic make each agent’s role, inputs, and decision boundaries explicit and auditable. In a billing-dispute workflow, every automated decision needs to be explainable.

Agents

When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents, each handling a specific type of billing dispute:

  • Invoice Matching Agent finds the matching shipment record and flags what doesn’t line up.
  • Pricing Variance Agent compares the carrier’s charge against the contracted rate and determines whether the difference is valid.
  • Accessorial Validation Agent checks whether unexpected fees (such as residential delivery or liftgate charges) are supported by the actual delivery events.

Each agent pulls specific carrier billing rules and policies before making a recommendation. After the exception is resolved, the system generates a plain-language note explaining what was found and what action was taken.

Each custom agent has an instruction prompt (defining its role, decision boundaries, and output format), a set of actions (integrations into SpeedShip), and access to carrier-specific knowledge bases. By using Amazon Bedrock, each agent accesses a suitable foundation model through a single API while inheriting existing AWS governance. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

Actions

The agents connect to SpeedShip through the same APIs that analysts use. That means the AI sees exactly what a human reviewer would see (contract rates, shipment details, delivery proof) and writes its resolution into the same workflow. SpeedShip has APIs on AWS, so the agents wire into the same endpoints as other existing systems.

Carrier knowledge base

Every carrier has different billing rules, fee definitions, and dispute procedures. Worldwide Express stores each carrier’s documentation: tariff rules, surcharge definitions, dispute steps, and variance thresholds. When an agent processes an exception, it retrieves that specific carrier’s policies and standard operating procedure (SOP) documents before deciding, so each decision is grounded in the carrier’s own rules. The same three agents handle all carriers without any carrier-specific code.

Human-in-the-loop

The approval step was necessary for FinOps adoption during the initial rollout. Initially, a human reviewer would use the existing SpeedShip UI to approve recommendations before they’re finalized. Eventually when accuracy exceeded 99 percent, bulk approval became the default.

Observability

Worldwide Express’s team built dashboards tracking automation rate by carrier, error rate by exception type, resolution time, and human override frequency. When a reviewer rejects a recommendation, the system logs the feedback. The team refines instruction prompts and knowledge bases based on rejection history, steadily increasing automation coverage.

End-to-end flow

The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow, from exception detection through the three specialized agents to human approval. In the diagram, exceptions from the data sources (the SpeedShip TMS, a shipping system, an electronic data interchange (EDI) server, and carrier and vendor portals) are detected and routed to one of three agents. Each agent runs on Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling, uses an agent framework with its own prompt, tools, and carrier knowledge base, and calls Amazon Bedrock for model inference. The agents produce a resolution report. Cost finalization and an AI-written note then go to a human reviewer for approval in the SpeedShip analyst UI.

Figure 1: Worldwide Express’s AI-powered exception handling architecture on AWS

Results

Six months in, Worldwide Express has deployed the solution across over 40 LTL carriers. The agents currently close 10,000 (approximately 50 percent) exceptions weekly with a less than 1 percent error rate. This shifted the FinOps team’s time from routine resolution to complex, high-value disputes.

The impact shows up most clearly in the backlog of active exceptions, which fell from $15M in June 2025 to $4M six months later, a 75 percent reduction. Worldwide Express unlocked $10M in freed-up cash flow, over $1M in annual cost savings, and 60x first-year ROI. The company reports time-to-cash improving by four weeks.

“With AWS, we’ve automated more than 40 percent of weekly billing exceptions, significantly reducing costs and accelerating billing cycles from days to minutes. Today, we release approximately $10 million more in customer billings each week at a speed that simply wasn’t possible before.”
— Nathanael Pearson, VP of FinOps, Worldwide Express

Looking forward

Worldwide Express is already expanding this approach to other parts of the Order-to-Cash cycle. For logistics companies managing high carrier volumes, the path forward is to start small. Automate the most repetitive exception type first, prove accuracy, then scale across the rest of the portfolio.

Conclusion

Worldwide Express’s exception automation shows what’s possible when agentic AI meets a well-scoped business problem. The combination of Amazon Bedrock, carrier-specific knowledge bases, and a human-in-the-loop approval design let Worldwide Express move from assessment to production in less than 6 months while maintaining financial controls. The company is now expanding automation to other Order-to-Cash processes.

To explore whether a similar approach might work for your organization, request a conversation with your account team or learn more about Amazon Bedrock. Partners like LTM can run a Proof of Value sprint with your own data.

About the authors

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS…
item.description: Full title: Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)

The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US), providing access to OpenAI’s frontier models through two components. Work completes complex, multi-step tasks and delivers review-ready results, and Codex is a coding agent for developing, testing, and reviewing software.

This walkthrough is intended for organizations whose security architecture requires model inference to use AWS GovCloud (US) identities, endpoints, and Regional controls. It configures Codex to route model requests through Amazon Bedrock Mantle in us-gov-west-1, where access can be governed using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and existing AWS GovCloud (US) network controls.

Codex is the OpenAI coding agent for AI-powered software development. With GPT models powering inference, Codex introduces a new class of intelligence optimized for complex, long-horizon developer workflows. You can use the ChatGPT desktop app, the Codex CLI, and IDE integrations with Visual Studio Code, JetBrains, and Xcode. Model inference is routed through the Responses API on Amazon Bedrock.

For customers with data residency requirements, processing stays within the Amazon Bedrock AWS Region that you select. You pay per token with no seat licenses and no per-developer commitments. Zero data retention (ZDR) is also supported. In this configurable mode, prompts and responses are processed without being written to durable storage by AWS or shared with model providers. This helps you protect sensitive information and meet stringent data-governance, privacy, and security requirements.

This post walks through a controlled local deployment of the ChatGPT desktop app that sends model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West). The configuration uses API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions. These restrictions allow access only to the approved Amazon Bedrock endpoint while disabling other external connections and network-enabled capabilities. The result is a deployment that an agency security team can test and document before approving broader use.

Using AWS GovCloud (US) and following this guide do not, by themselves, authorize your workload. Your organization remains responsible for reviewing the selected model, AWS services, Region, endpoint, workstation controls, repositories, credentials, and data flows against its system security plan and authorization process.

Solution overview

You can use the ChatGPT desktop app in two ways:

  • Work for larger tasks that need planning, research, files, and a finished result.
  • Codex for technical work such as editing code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests.

The ChatGPT desktop app runs on an organization-managed computer through the desktop app or CLI. It uses the configured AWS credentials to securely send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint in us-gov-west-1. Because this setup uses AWS directly, ChatGPT workspace rules and user roles don’t control it. The main security controls are the computer’s policies and the AWS identity and permissions being used.

Walkthrough

The configuration has three main steps: set up authentication, set up the ChatGPT desktop app configuration files, and then launch, initialize, and verify the deployment.

Prerequisites

Before setting up the ChatGPT desktop app with AWS GovCloud (US), make sure your version of the ChatGPT desktop app supports Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US). You need an approved AWS GovCloud (US) account, an IAM identity and approved credentials, access to the approved model, AWS Region, and endpoint, and permission to use them. You also need to set up the requirements.toml and config.toml files.

Step 1: Set up authentication

Select the approved AWS GovCloud (US) account and IAM identity or role with access to the approved model in us-gov-west-1. Obtain credentials through your organization’s approved mechanism. This walkthrough uses the named profile codex-il5. Keep credentials, bearer tokens, session tokens, and other secrets out of TOML files.

Protect the profile configuration, credential source, SSO token cache, and any credential helper from ChatGPT desktop app task writes, while allowing approved authentication tools to maintain and refresh credentials.

The ChatGPT desktop app supports two Amazon Bedrock authentication pathways: an Amazon Bedrock API key or the AWS SDK credential chain. AWS SSO through AWS IAM Identity Center is supported within the credential-chain pathway.

The app first checks for AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK in its environment. For desktop use, this variable can be supplied through %USERPROFILE%\.codex\.env on Windows or ~/.codex/.env on Linux and macOS. When present, the bearer token takes precedence over profile-based authentication.

If no bearer token is available, the app falls back to the standard AWS SDK credential chain. The chain can read AWS credentials from ~/.aws/credentials and related profile settings from ~/.aws/config. On Windows, the corresponding default paths are %USERPROFILE%\.aws\credentials and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\config. The chain also supports SSO profiles. For SSO, it uses the profile settings in the AWS config file and the cached SSO session to obtain temporary role credentials. These credentials don’t need to be manually stored in the AWS credentials file. See OpenAI’s Bedrock authentication documentation and the AWS IAM Identity Center credential provider documentation.

Step 2: Set up ChatGPT desktop app configuration files

You must create two ChatGPT desktop app configuration files: config.toml and requirements.toml.

Important: the configuration files need to be set up before the application is launched. The following table shows the file locations.

Operating systemUser config.tomlAdmin requirements.toml
