item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Introducing artifacts for legal work
item.content:encoded:
Today, we’re introducing ready-to-use artifacts that legal professionals can adapt to how their teams work and share with colleagues across the business. Since we launched Claude for Legal in May, the most common requests from legal teams have been for simpler setup and easier ways to work with colleagues.

Artifacts are interactive tools, such as trackers and dashboards, that teams can use and share in Claude. Our new legal gallery includes artifacts for specific tasks, such as reviewing a stack of contracts, tracking regulatory changes, and taking in legal requests from the business. Each artifact opens with an example, so legal professionals can see how the work comes together before adding their own data and connectors. Each answer or output has a link to its source.

We are also funding public interest groups building artifacts for access-to-justice work and legal education programs teaching tomorrow’s lawyers to build with Claude, and we are starting a Legal Ambassadors Program so legal professionals can learn from each other.

What’s in the gallery

With these artifacts, a legal professional brings their own documents and sources, Claude completes the first pass, and a lawyer applies their judgment to the results. They cover the work legal teams raised with us most often:

  • Cite check compares a legal document with its sources and flags quotes that don’t match, wrong page numbers, and sources that don’t support the claim.
  • Jurisdiction survey matrix compares a legal topic, such as data breach notice rules, across states or countries in one table, with links to the underlying law.
  • Matter board turns engagement letters, emails, or spreadsheets into one board of open matters, showing the owner, next step, and next deadline.
  • Playbook deviation board compares contracts with your company’s standard terms, flags each clause that differs, and sends it to the person who approves exceptions.
  • Regulatory horizon scan maps upcoming regulations on a timeline, based on your company’s business and where it operates, and ranks them by impact with links to the sources.
  • Tabular review builds a table from a set of contracts, showing the terms you ask about, such as severance or non-competes, with links to the exact language.

Tailored to how teams work and shared with guardrails

Every legal team works differently and artifacts work best when they’re connected to the systems legal teams already use. Legal professionals can ask Claude to tailor artifacts to their team and use connectors to bring in their playbooks or research sources, so nobody has to upload documents manually.

Since we launched Claude for Legal, we’ve added more than 60 legal connectors, including Bloomberg Law, Filevine, Ivo, Legora, and Patlytics. See our legal directory (opens in new tab) for the complete list.

Artifacts enable collaboration inside and outside the organization. A legal team can work on an artifact with colleagues across the business or with clients and partners, with sharing settings that ensure privacy and support ethical walls between teams.

Opening the gallery to legal tech and law firms

We partnered with legal tech companies and law firms to build artifacts for legal professionals. Each artifact is in the gallery for legal professionals to discover, test, and adapt to their work:

  • AI Governance Benchmark built by Goodwin (opens in new tab) benchmarks a company's approach to AI governance to surface potential gaps.
  • Harvey Intake built by Harvey (opens in new tab) gives business users one place in Claude to send legal questions and requests, answering routine ones from Legal’s own guidance in Harvey and routing the rest to a lawyer, whose reply comes back in Claude.
  • Obligations Checker built by Foley & Lardner (opens in new tab) reviews agreements for the obligations of both parties and helps validate expectations pre-closing and track expectations post-closing.
  • Subpoena Response Tool built by PwC (opens in new tab) turns your team's precedents, standard objections and templates into automated, audit-ready first drafts so lawyers can focus on the complex issues while responding faster.

We are excited to see legal tech companies, law firms, legal aid organizations create and share their own artifacts, and have more artifacts coming from Legora and Orrick.

“Claude continues to power us as the most widely contract review tool in the world—we're approaching 500,000 contracts per month moving through Spellbook and we wouldn't be here without Claude.”

Scott Stevenson, Co-Founder and CEO, Spellbook

“At The Access Project, we build tools that help legal teams and self-represented litigants navigate record clearance. This artifact lets anyone start the clean slate process: screen for eligibility, obtain the record, understand how state law applies to each case, and find local filing guidance.”

Nora Cregan, Executive Director, The Access Project

“There is never enough time, and every minute spent on the math is a minute not spent on who the person is beyond the charge. The Criminal Charge Reality Check tool started with one question: how do we make that part faster, so the time goes to the person instead?”

Scott Hechinger, Founder & Executive Director, Zealous

“At Accenture, Claude is helping us transform the way our legal teams work. We're excited about the opportunity to reimagine legal workflows and unlock new ways for our legal professionals to support our business.”

Mindy Lok, Legal Chief Technology Officer, Chief Intellectual Property Officer, Accenture

“Anthropic has invested heavily in building the best models for legal work. We build agents on Claude because it is best in class in our internal benchmarks and we're excited to continue pushing the frontier in legal with Anthropic.”

John Sarihan, Cofounder, Crosby

“Legal sits at the center of every agreement, but too often the work is disconnected from the rest of the business. With Anthropic, we're bringing the power of the Docusign platform directly into Claude, enabling legal teams and cross-functional stakeholders to create, review, and move agreements forward.”

Allan Thygesen, CEO, Docusign

“At Eve, we built PlaintiffBench to measure AI on the work plaintiff attorneys actually do, using real drafts, corrections and edge cases our customers have flagged. Every new model has to prove itself there before it reaches a firm, and Claude Opus 5.5 has made a real leap. For a plaintiff firm juggling hundreds of cases, those hours add up fast.”

Jay Madheswaran, CEO and Co-Founder, Eve

“Personal injury cases aren’t built in one step. They’re built over months, through hundreds of connected judgments and tasks across records, notes and emails. Claude is the frontier model we trust to orchestrate that long-running work, so EvenUp can deliver at the standard firms and their clients depend on.”

Saam Mashhad, Co-Founder & CPO, EvenUp

“Litigation demands absolute precision: retrieving case-defining facts from vast stores of evidentiary materials and deploying purpose-built agents to take follow-on action, whether preparing a witness or drafting a motion. By connecting Filevine and LOIS to Claude, our customers can take that toolkit wherever they work and act directly on their case files.”

Mike Anderson, CPO, Filevine

“We built the AI Governance Benchmark with Claude so any company can work through the same questions our AI practice uses with clients, see where its approach to AI governance has gaps, and know which areas to address first.”

Kaitlin Betancourt, Partner and Co-chair of AI practice, Goodwin

“Business teams are already bringing their questions to Claude. Harvey meets them where they work, giving Legal the ability to set the rules, see what’s being asked, and step in to manage risk. We’re proud to build with Anthropic to make that possible.”

Matt Zerweck, Head of In-House Product, Harvey

“The businesses that win act on their agreements as fast as they make decisions. Claude for Legal brings Ironclad's contracting intelligence directly into the platforms business teams already use. Ironclad's integration helps every Claude for Legal user move faster, reduce risk, and stay compliant, with trusted AI built on every agreement, approval, and obligation.”

Sunita Verma, Chief Technology Officer, Ironclad

“With Ivo and Claude, legal teams can turn the contracts they already keep in Ivo into artifacts they can share across their team—like a renewal calendar that tracks every notice date across their portfolio—with no manual uploads. Every answer is backed by the contract language it came from, and Ivo stays the system of record.”

Min-Kyu Jung, CEO and Co-Founder, Ivo

“As legal teams adopt AI across more parts of their business, they need trusted legal intelligence available in those environments. By connecting Legora to Claude, we’re making it easier for mutual customers to get answers to legal questions within their broader enterprise AI workflows, with links back to Legora for source review, citations and deeper legal work.”

Bryan Tsao, Chief Product Officer, Legora

“For those of us protecting immigrant rights, the pace of change is dizzying. Moreover, the consequences of falling behind can be devastating. Immigration Papers Reader gives overstretched teams the tools to keep up and help families in turbulent times.”

Jeffrey O'Brien, Esq., Executive Director, Mobile Pathways

“AI delivers value in Legal when it’s built into how lawyers actually work. Through our alliance with Anthropic, PwC’s engineers and our Legal Business Solutions team are building Claude-powered skills and integrations that connect directly to the systems legal teams rely on every day, with the security and governance the profession demands. This isn’t experimentation; it’s becoming part of how legal services are delivered.”

Jane Allen, Global Legal Business Solutions Leader Americas, Partner, PwC US

“For DC residents facing eviction or the burden of an old criminal record, legal assistance can change lives. Rising for Justice used Claude to develop tools that help attorneys identify rent ledger errors and assess eligibility for record sealing, streamlining case preparation and letting teams focus on clients' needs and goals.”

Chijioke Akamigbo, Esq., Executive Director, Rising for Justice

“On our chemical structure benchmark, Claude Opus 5.5 correctly identifies over 10% more structures than Opus 5 while using less than half the output tokens. In Solve, it powers patent work from drafting to litigation-grade claim charting.”

Sanj Ahilan, Chief Research Officer, Solve Intelligence

“Claude continues to power us as the most widely contract review tool in the world—we're approaching 500,000 contracts per month moving through Spellbook and we wouldn't be here without Claude.”

Scott Stevenson, Co-Founder and CEO, Spellbook

“At The Access Project, we build tools that help legal teams and self-represented litigants navigate record clearance. This artifact lets anyone start the clean slate process: screen for eligibility, obtain the record, understand how state law applies to each case, and find local filing guidance.”

Nora Cregan, Executive Director, The Access Project

“There is never enough time, and every minute spent on the math is a minute not spent on who the person is beyond the charge. The Criminal Charge Reality Check tool started with one question: how do we make that part faster, so the time goes to the person instead?”

Scott Hechinger, Founder & Executive Director, Zealous

“At Accenture, Claude is helping us transform the way our legal teams work. We're excited about the opportunity to reimagine legal workflows and unlock new ways for our legal professionals to support our business.”

Mindy Lok, Legal Chief Technology Officer, Chief Intellectual Property Officer, Accenture

“Anthropic has invested heavily in building the best models for legal work. We build agents on Claude because it is best in class in our internal benchmarks and we're excited to continue pushing the frontier in legal with Anthropic.”

John Sarihan, Cofounder, Crosby

“Legal sits at the center of every agreement, but too often the work is disconnected from the rest of the business. With Anthropic, we're bringing the power of the Docusign platform directly into Claude, enabling legal teams and cross-functional stakeholders to create, review, and move agreements forward.”

Allan Thygesen, CEO, Docusign

1/18

Access to Justice and the Legal Ambassadors Program

The gallery includes nine access-to-justice artifacts, five of which were built by nonprofit and public interest organizations we supported with Claude credits:

  • Criminal Charge Reality Check built by Zealous (opens in new tab) takes a criminal charge and shows defense teams the sentencing range, public data on how those cases usually end, and standard playbooks for release. New York only.
  • Immigration Papers Reader built by Mobile Pathways (opens in new tab) turns a client’s immigration paperwork into a plain-language first read of key dates and missing documents.
  • Rent Ledger Reviewer built by Rising for Justice (opens in new tab) helps attorneys find errors in a landlord’s rent ledger when preparing an eviction case. Based on D.C. law.
  • Record-Sealing Screener built by Rising for Justice (opens in new tab) helps attorneys assess whether a client’s criminal record is eligible for sealing. Based on D.C. law.
  • Record Clearance built by The Access Project (opens in new tab) helps legal aid teams work out whether a client’s record can be cleared under their state’s rules.

This builds on the Oxford Justice Innovators Programme, our 12-month program with the Oxford Institute of Technology and Justice and Microsoft that supports up to 10 innovators expanding access to justice.

We are also launching the Legal Ambassadors Program, a community for legal professionals who build with Claude to share their work and learn from each other. Join the waitlist (opens in new tab).

Getting started

Legal teams can browse the gallery (opens in new tab) in Claude or start from our Claude for Legal (opens in new tab) page.

To plan a rollout for your organization, talk to our sales team or work with one of our implementation partners, including Accenture, AnswerRocket, Caylent, Deloitte, KPMG, Lazer, Perficient, phData, Protiviti, Provectus, PwC, Sia Partners, and Tenex. For more information on each of these partners, see our partner directory (opens in new tab).

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] AI for Science expands to foundations and research instituti…
item.description: Full title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
item.content:encoded:
We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our AI for Science program, which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects.

We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted Team plan for scientists and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)

Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.

Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with HHMI Janelia Research Campus to develop the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the Allen Institute, a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.

AI for Science began by supporting individual scientists. By partnering with institutions and foundations, we’re now able to reach more researchers across many fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.

Science funders and societies

Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research:

  • The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics.
  • The Simons Foundation. This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute.
  • Schmidt Sciences. Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program.
  • Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy. This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science.
  • The US National Science Foundation. This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities.
  • CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society. For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS REGISTRY®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances.

Institutions

Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery:

  • Space Telescope Science Institute. STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide.
  • Wellcome Sanger Institute. One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development.
  • The Francis Crick Institute. Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease.
  • Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences. One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience.
  • EMBL. The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC.
  • Gladstone Institutes. An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.

Research projects and initiatives

As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are:

  • FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience). It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior.
  • LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system). Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land.
  • AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research). Built by a pathologist and an astrophysicist from the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging and the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, AstroPath uses calibration methods from astronomical surveys to image tumors cell by cell, with measurements consistent across slides and labs.
  • gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease). The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis.
  • Tau Ceti (mathematics). This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof.
  • Centre for Population Genomics. A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis.

What’s next

Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery. We look forward to sharing the impact of this work and showcasing new ways of working in these scientific fields.

As AI changes how science is done, our AI for Science program will continue to support and collaborate with scientists, institutions, and foundations. We hope to expand these efforts to even more partners around the world.

item.title: [Meta Llama] Meta Partners With Five US Universities to Accelerate Medica…
item.description: Full title: Meta Partners With Five US Universities to Accelerate Medical and Scientific Breakthroughs
item.content:encoded:
Back to Newsroom

Meta

October 28, 2026October 28, 2026

0.25× 0.5× 1× 1.25× 1.5× 2×

Takeaways

  • Researchers at Caltech, The Ohio State University, Louisiana State University, Indiana University, and UTHealth Houston are using Meta’s models to solve critical issues in medicine and science.
  • Their research projects aim to accelerate scientific and medical breakthroughs, improving outcomes for infants with tracheostomy tubes, identifying heart failure risk early, helping patients with dementia communicate, and more.
  • We’re supporting their work with $2 million in grants and access to our latest models.

We believe the future is for everyone, including America’s universities, professors, students, and the communities who benefit from their research. That’s why Meta is bringing Superintelligence models, research funding, and direct researcher collaboration to academia through partnerships with five US universities: California Institute of Technology, The Ohio State University College of Medicine, Louisiana State University, Indiana University, and UTHealth Houston.

We’re expanding our academic partnerships by granting $2 million across these five schools to support research that uses our models to accelerate breakthroughs in medicine, physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, and mathematics.

In medicine and healthcare, researchers will work on a diverse set of projects using Meta’s models, glasses, and mixed reality headsets to address existing gaps in medicine and healthcare. Here are a few examples of how they’re being used:

Monitoring for Infant Tracheostomies

When tracheostomy tubes become dislodged in infant patients, it’s a life-threatening emergency compounded by the fact that babies with tracheostomies can’t cry out for help. And continuous direct observation by trained staff isn’t always possible.

Dr. Michael Dunham from Louisiana State University is leading the Eyes-On project, which is developing a computer vision system to continuously detect tracheostomy tube displacement and signs of distress in infants who cannot reliably vocalize. The system is exploring usage of our open weight SAM models for tracking and is designed for integration with bedside cameras and edge computing. A proof-of-concept has been published, with more work to come.

Conversational AI for Dementia Care

People with dementia often experience communication difficulties that standard conversational AI systems handle poorly, leading to frustration rather than support. Dr. David Crandall at Indiana University is developing a project that aims to develop multimodal AI methods for analyzing conversations involving older adults living with dementia, and to use this understanding to help conversational agents — including social robots — adapt their interactions to individual users. The research tests whether AI systems can be made sensitive to the communication patterns of people with cognitive differences.

Identifying Heart Failure Risk Earlier

Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) accounts for roughly half of all heart failure cases, but it can be difficult to recognize early — its symptoms overlap with those of obesity and other common conditions, so formal evaluation often begins only after clinical suspicion has developed.

At The Ohio State University College of Medicine, AI researcher Dr. Yuan Xue is leading a project with cardiologist Dr. Yuchi Han and AI researcher Dr. Xia Ning to investigate how Meta’s open-weight models can help predict future HFpEF risk using routine abdominal CT scans, longitudinal medical records, and ECG data when available. The team is designing the model to handle missing data, since real-world clinical practice rarely provides a complete set of inputs.

You can read more on these projects on our Research Blog, and we look forward to sharing more as these projects get underway.

One open model for multilingual transcription, speaker attribution, translation, and audio Q&A, with top leaderboard results, plus the open Granary v2 data pipeline and fine-tuning recipes to adapt it.

A transcript can capture every spoken word and still leave users or applications wondering who said what, how to translate it, or how to format domain-specific jargon. Multilingual calls, fast-paced meetings, and medical dictation each need different output: a translation, speaker labels, or correctly spelled medical terms.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is an open-weight, promptable model that turns recorded speech into useful text, now available on Hugging Face and ModelScope. It brings transcription, speaker attribution (diarization), translation, and audio question answering into one checkpoint: it transcribes 40 languages, translates 31 of them to or from English, and attributes speakers in 13. It handles recordings up to an hour long and labels up to eight speakers. Developers can guide output with natural language, choose where their audio is processed, and adapt recognition to domain vocabulary and accents.

Transcribe is first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard for English and sits on Artificial Analysis’s accuracy–active-parameter frontier. For speaker attribution, it posts the lowest error rate on David AI’s 21-language diarization leaderboard and ranks first in VoiceArena’s 14-system comparison. Quantized versions are coming soon, so you can run Transcribe locally on your RTX Spark, DGX Spark, or Jetson AGX Thor—or scale up on Blackwell data-center GPUs.

Granary v2’s multilingual data (available on Hugging Face and ModelScope) and reusable curation pipeline, together with NeMo Speech fine-tuning tools, extend prompt-level control to training: developers can define the written form they need and adapt the model to the speech their applications encounter. In a medical case study, fine-tuning cut word error rate (WER) on held-out speakers by 45.8% relative to the best prompt.

Guide transcription and analysis with natural language

The same checkpoint can turn one meeting recording into different outputs, depending on the instruction:

  • “Transcribe this recording and label each speaker.”
  • “Translate this audio into English.”
  • “What decisions were made in this meeting?”

Experience the model in action in the video below, where it tackles a classic scene from the 1940 screwball comedy His Girl Friday—a film famous for its rapid-fire, heavily overlapping dialogue.

Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe captions a scene from His Girl Friday (1940) and labels speakers, including overlapping dialogue.

For unfamiliar terms, try context before training. In a healthcare setting, for example:

Transcribe this medical discussion in the original language. Possible terms: HbA1c, metformin. Use these terms only when supported by the audio. Preserve standard medical spelling and write numbers in conventional written form.

The model card has recommended presets, including reasoning for audio questions, plus the full prompt guide and a task-by-language matrix: language support differs by task, and audio question answering is trained in English. Word-level timestamps are also supported. As with any speech model, spot-check names, speaker changes, and answers against the recording.

From live classes to lasting lessons. Agora, whose real-time voice and video platform powers live conversations in apps, used word-level timestamps in a classroom demo: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe turns a recorded class into a transcript shown alongside the replay, so students can see what was said and when. Agora’s blog walks through how they built it.

Leaderboard wins from transcription to speaker attribution

Among open-weight models, Transcribe leads on what was said; on who said it, it tops two speaker-attribution benchmarks outright.

Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard. The leaderboard measures transcription accuracy as word error rate (WER) on public test sets, in three tracks:

  • English: first among open-weight models at 5.33% average WER (Figure 1).
  • Multilingual: 4.62% mean WER across seven languages, the lowest among evaluated open-weight models in the model card’s Open ASR comparison.
  • Long-form: 10.98% mean WER, also the lowest in that comparison.

Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard (English) at 5.33% average WER, with API models excluded. Lower WER means fewer transcription errors.

Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Text Leaderboard. Artificial Analysis independently ranks speech-to-text models by AA-WER, its word error rate index. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ties for first among open-weight models at 2.8% AA-WER, with about 4B active parameters versus 24B for the model it ties. On AA-AgentTalk, the held-out voice-agent speech set that makes up 50% of the AA-WER index, Transcribe scores 1.8% WER, versus 2.3% for the next-best open-weight model. Transcribe pairs its speech encoder with a hybrid Mamba–Transformer mixture-of-experts language model, so only about 4B of its 30B parameters are active per token. That puts it on Artificial Analysis’s open-weight Pareto frontier of accuracy versus active parameters. On AA’s all-model chart, it ranks ahead of several widely used proprietary speech APIs.

Figure 2. Leading AA accuracy at about one-sixth the active parameters: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe achieves 2.80% AA-WER with approximately 4B active parameters.

Speaker attribution across languages and overlap. Sortformer speaker cues reach the language model with the acoustic features, so Transcribe can tag each turn during generation instead of relying solely on a later step to attach speakers to words.

David AI DAI-ASR-I18N Leaderboard. On David AI’s DAI-ASR-I18N combined transcription-and-speaker-attribution track, Transcribe ranks first among evaluated open-weight models and second overall. On the benchmark’s diarization track, which scores who spoke when across 21 languages, it has the lowest diarization error rate of the 14 systems tested, slightly ahead of NVIDIA’s dedicated Nemotron 3 Diarization model.

Figure 3. NVIDIA models hold the top two spots on David AI’s multilingual diarization leaderboard: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe posts the lowest overall diarization error rate (DER), 18.26% across 21 languages, followed by Nemotron 3 Diarization at 18.38%. DER measures speaker-time errors; lower is better.

VoiceArena Diarization-Bench. On VoiceArena’s English full-session benchmark, Transcribe posts the lowest concatenated minimum-permutation WER (cpWER) of 14 systems and ranks first in both in-person and online settings. It also drops the fewest words: deletions are 8.32% of reference words, versus a median of about 31%.

Figure 4. NVIDIA models hold the top two spots in VoiceArena’s 14-system comparison: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe leads at 32.4% cpWER, followed by NVIDIA Multitalker Parakeet with Nemotron 3 Diarization at 34.2%. Diarization-Bench v1 covers English full sessions, overlapping speech and 2–8 speakers. cpWER counts word errors after matching speaker labels; lower is better.

More evaluations. Ocular AI’s Converse-STT evaluation ranks Transcribe the top open model. Josh Talks’ Voice of India leaderboard reports Transcribe’s results across Indian languages.

High-throughput transcription. In benchmarking, Transcribe processed 100 hours of audio in under three minutes on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, using the forthcoming NVFP4 quantized version. Results were measured on 30-second clips at high concurrency.

Serve the available checkpoint with vLLM today. Local deployment with NeMo-Speech.cpp is coming soon alongside the quantized versions. Transcribe is built for recorded audio, not live streaming.

Specialized recordings can still call for adaptation to domain vocabulary and transcript conventions. Granary v2 and NeMo Speech fine-tuning address that, starting with the data behind Transcribe.

Granary v2: The open data curation pipeline behind Transcribe

A promptable speech model requires training data with unambiguous formatting targets. Granary v2 is part of the Nemotron speech collection on Hugging Face and ModelScope. Built with NVIDIA NeMo Curator, its reusable pipeline prepared multilingual speech used in Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe’s training, producing aligned transcript variants, task labels, and inspectable quality metadata. The public manifest covers 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora, up from 25 languages in Granary v1. These figures describe the dataset release, not Transcribe’s full training mixture or its sampling weights.

Granary v2 generates three transcript forms for each recording (Table 1), the same verbatim and clean styles developers can request from Transcribe with a prompt. Beyond transcription, the pipeline produces short audio captions, code-switching restoration of loanwords, speech-grounded Q&A pairs, contextual ASR biasing terms, and translations with automatic quality scores.

Training targetIllustrative transcript
Text-normalized, verbatimI paid, uh, twenty-five euros.
Inverse text normalization, with disfluenciesI paid, uh, €25.
Inverse text normalization, without disfluenciesI paid €25.

Table 1. Granary v2 training targets for the same utterance.

The pipeline is organized into four reusable stages:

  • 1. Audio Preparation (Metadata): Segments raw or long-form audio, tracks speakers across the full recording, and tags acoustic events and language. Granary v2’s sources were already segmented, so this release skipped this stage.
  • 2. Transcription (ASR): Routes each language to primary and recovery ASR models, falling back when the primary fails a hallucination check. Human reference transcripts help preserve trusted spellings while adding spoken forms and disfluencies.
  • 3. Task Label Generation (Text): Derives transcript variants, then checks character rate, hallucination patterns, and model or human-reference agreement. Only accepted records receive contextual-ASR terms and translations.
  • 4. High Fidelity (HiFi): Filters out segments that are noisy, clipped, or contain multiple speakers, keeping a smaller set of high-quality recordings for uses beyond ASR. For the VoxPopuli dataset, it reduced 354k hours to 111k hours across 22 European languages.

Figure 6. Granary v2 data curation pipeline, following one sample from raw audio through the Metadata, ASR, and Text stages to a training example.

Developers can run the NeMo Curator pipeline with Ray and NVIDIA Dynamo backends on their own recordings or authorized public corpora, or build on the Granary v2 public manifests. The manifests include the three transcript forms as tn_raw, itn_raw, and itn_clean, the labels described above, entity hints, derived instruction pairs, provenance, and a per-record quality flag. Download source audio separately under each corpus’s original license, and follow the release’s published terms.

Adapt recognition to the vocabulary that matters

Start with a development-set prompt that specifies language, script, and transcript format. In the case study below, naming English and the Latin alphabet in the prompt cut full-benchmark WER from 30.8% to 23.8%. For domain errors that remain, the NeMo Speech fine-tuning workflow pairs representative speech with explicit written targets.

The NeMo Speech medical ASR case study shows this progression on Eka Care’s open benchmark of recordings from Indian doctors and medical students, which has 3,619 clips and no designated training split. The study builds adaptation data from generated medical text and public medicine catalogs, then combines approximately 153 hours of synthetic speech, 29 hours of accented English from Common Voice, and 63 hours of medical recordings from MultiMed.

Figure 7. On the full test set of Eka Care’s Indian medical speech benchmark, a better prompt cuts WER from 30.8% to 23.8%, and fine-tuning brings it to 11.8%, about 62% fewer transcription errors than the model out of the box. The full set includes the 855 tuning clips used to choose the prompt and checkpoints; the held-out results below are the cleaner test.

Synthetic generation separates the written target from its spoken rendering: “HbA1c” is the label, while “H B A one C” is sent to the synthesizer. Multiple TTS voices broaden the audio; real recordings add accents and recording conditions. Training text is filtered for exact matches and shared eight-word sequences with benchmark references.

As with Granary v2’s explicit targets, training examples vary digits, unit spacing, company-name expansion, and brand-name hyphens, with instructions specifying the required convention. Some prompts include term lists with near-miss distractors, so the model learns to use a spelling only when the audio supports it. The final system uses one fixed convention prompt and one model pass, without retrieval or transcript post-processing.

The recipe trains the speech encoder and projection and uses LoRA to adapt the language model. Two runs use different data mixtures; after adapter merging, selected checkpoints are uniformly averaged into one final model. Checkpoint selection uses decoded development-set results, rather than training loss alone. The full adaptation, from text generation through evaluation, took about 14 GPU-hours on one NVIDIA GB300.

Domain gains, measured on held-out speakers

The study splits the benchmark by speaker into 855 tuning clips, used to choose the prompt and checkpoints, and 2,764 held-out clips, decoded once per final system. Using Eka Care’s KARMA scoring pipeline, fine-tuning cuts held-out WER from 22.44% for the best-prompt baseline to 12.17%, a 45.8% relative reduction and the clearest evidence that the gains generalize to new speakers. Keyword WER falls from 9.2% to 6.5%, and semantic WER from 10.0% to 7.6%. On the same held-out speakers and scorer, the adapted model’s 12.17% WER beats an open medical-specialist model (13.79%) and a widely used general-purpose ASR model (14.92%).

On general English, LibriSpeech test-clean WER rises slightly, from 1.54% to 1.69%. The medical specialist still leads on exact matches for brand-name drugs and diagnostics; the study points to real recordings of clinicians saying brand names as the next step. For your own domain, keep at least 100 real, labeled clips for checkpoint selection, and evaluate the entity types your application depends on alongside general-speech retention.

The case study includes commands to reproduce each step. The fine-tuning tutorials cover recipes, resource requirements, and tools for training, export, and evaluation, including new-language and code-switching ASR. The accompanying agent skill lets a coding agent run the workflow, from baseline selection and data checks through training validation, adapter merging, and evaluation.

ModelScope also enables developers to fine-tune Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe through its ms-swift framework for specialized multimodal applications.

Get started with Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2

Try Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe in the Hugging Face demo or on ModelScope Studios, then download the checkpoint from Hugging Face or ModelScope. For self-hosted transcription, get started with vLLM or SGLang-Omni, both offering support from day one.

To skip self-hosting, use a hosted endpoint from Baseten, DeepInfra, or Simplismart.

To adapt it to your domain, start with the Granary v2 manifests on Hugging Face or ModelScope and the medical ASR case study, or let a coding agent drive the workflow with the fine-tuning agent skill.

Models & Datasets

  • Model Checkpoints: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe on Hugging Face, ModelScope | Interactive Demo on Hugging Face, ModelScope
  • Hosted Endpoints: Baseten, DeepInfra
  • Dataset Manifests: Granary v2 Manifests on Hugging Face, ModelScope
  • High Fidelity Subset: Manifests on Hugging Face, ModelScope | Space on Hugging Face

Repositories & Tutorials: NVIDIA NeMo Speech GitHub | NeMo Curator Granary v2 Pipeline | vLLM Deployment Guide | Speech Fine-Tuning Guide | Fine-Tuning Agent Skill

Partner Blogs: Agora | Inflection AI | VoiceArena | Simplismart | DeepInfra

item.title: [OpenRouter] Claude 529 Overloaded: What It Means and How to Fix It
item.content:encoded:
Claude 529 Overloaded: What It Means and How to Fix It

OpenRouter ·10/28/2026

A 529 overloaded_error from Claude means Anthropic’s API is temporarily out of capacity for the model you asked for. Your key, plan and request are fine, and the same request usually goes through a few seconds later. To keep an app working through it, retry with backoff first, then send the request to another provider that serves the same Claude model.

Most people hit this error in Claude Code, where a session stops with API Error: Repeated 529 Overloaded errors. We simulated the overload in the retry example with a local stand-in for the API, because a real one can’t be triggered on demand. Every OpenRouter request in the guide is real.

Tl;dr

  • A 529 overloaded_error means Anthropic’s API is out of capacity for that model across all users. A 429 is the error that comes from your own usage.
  • Retry with exponential backoff and some randomness first. Anthropic’s SDKs and Claude Code already do this.
  • When the overload lasts, send the same model to another provider. On OpenRouter, Claude Sonnet, Opus and Haiku 5.5 are each served by five providers, and default routing fails over for you.
  • For the rare case when every provider is busy, list a fallback model with models.
  • In Claude Code, run ori claude to start a session on OpenRouter and get the same failover.

What does 529 overloaded mean?

Anthropic’s API returns a 529 when it has more traffic for a model than it can serve. The response body looks like this:

{"type": "error", "error": {"type": "overloaded_error", "message": "Overloaded"}}

The error isn’t about you. Anthropic’s error reference says it happens when the API has high traffic across all users, so anyone calling that model at that moment can get it, whatever plan they’re on. One Max-plan user reported Claude Code retrying for more than eight minutes before it gave up.

The error that does come from your side is a 429 rate_limit_error. It means your organization has hit its own rate limit or spend cap, and you fix it by slowing down or raising the limit. A 529 isn’t your usage limit, and Claude Code’s error reference says it doesn’t count against your quota. It clears when Anthropic has capacity again, so you either wait it out or send the request somewhere that has capacity now. The next three steps do both.

Step 1: Retry with exponential backoff

Most 529s clear within seconds, so start by retrying. Wait a little longer after each attempt and add some randomness, so that many clients don’t all retry at the same moment. We pointed this loop at a small local server that returns a real-shaped 529 for the first three requests and then succeeds:

import random
import time
import requests

# The local stand-in. In production, use https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages
URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8529/v1/messages"

def call_with_backoff(body, attempts=5):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        r = requests.post(URL, json=body, timeout=60)
        if r.status_code != 529:
            return r
        if attempt == attempts - 1:
            r.raise_for_status()  # out of attempts: fail now instead of sleeping again
        wait = min(2 ** attempt, 30) + random.uniform(0, 1)
        print(f"attempt {attempt + 1}: 529 {r.json()['error']['type']}, retrying in {wait:.1f}s")
        time.sleep(wait)

r = call_with_backoff({
    "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5",
    "max_tokens": 64,
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}],
})
print(r.status_code, r.json()["content"][0]["text"])
attempt 1: 529 overloaded_error, retrying in 1.9s
attempt 2: 529 overloaded_error, retrying in 2.3s
attempt 3: 529 overloaded_error, retrying in 4.0s
200 Hello! How can I help you today?

The fourth attempt succeeded, about eight seconds after the first. If you use Anthropic’s official SDKs, you already have this. They retry 5xx errors with exponential backoff, twice by default, and you can raise that with max_retries.

Retries cover short spikes. They don’t help when a model stays overloaded for minutes, and every wait adds latency your users feel. For that, you need a second place to send the request.

Step 2: Send the same model to another provider

Anthropic’s API isn’t the only place Claude runs. On OpenRouter, Claude Sonnet 5.5 is served by five providers, and so are Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. Here’s what our endpoints API returned for Sonnet 5.5 on October 21, 2026:

ProviderSlugInput price per million tokens
Anthropicanthropic$2.00
Amazon Bedrockamazon-bedrock$2.00
Google Vertex AIgoogle-vertex$2.00 (global), $2.20 (US or Europe)
Azureazure$2.00 (global), $2.20 (US)
Claude Platform on AWSclaude-on-aws$2.00

Sending a request to a global endpoint instead of Anthropic doesn’t change what you pay for it. Latency and uptime can still differ between providers, and how to evaluate LLM provider performance shows how to compare them.

You don’t need to configure anything to use them. When you call anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5, our default routing spreads requests across the providers serving it, deprioritizes any provider that’s had significant outages in the last 30 seconds and retries a failed request at the next provider.

If you want to choose which provider goes first, set order:

import os

import requests

body = {
    "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5",
    "provider": {
        "order": ["anthropic", "amazon-bedrock", "google-vertex"],
        "allow_fallbacks": True,
    },
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the word ok."}],
    "max_tokens": 16,
}

r = requests.post(
    "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions",
    json=body,
    timeout=120,
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"},
)
data = r.json()
print(r.status_code, data["model"], data["provider"])
200 anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 Anthropic

Anthropic answered, so no failover happened. The provider field in every response names the provider that served it, so your logs show when traffic moves away from Anthropic. Setting order does turn off the default load balancing. Requests follow your list instead of our health ranking, and move on to the remaining providers only after the ones you listed fail.

Two settings stop failover, and they’re worth checking if you still see 529s:

  • "allow_fallbacks": false keeps the request on the providers you listed. If they’re all overloaded, you get the error back.
  • "only": [...] limits which providers can serve the request at all. If none of them serves the model, the request fails before it starts.

We set only to ["openai"] to see what that failure looks like:

import json
import os

import requests

body = {
    "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5",
    "provider": {"only": ["openai"]},
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the word ok."}],
    "max_tokens": 16,
}

r = requests.post(
    "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions",
    json=body,
    timeout=120,
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"},
)
print(r.status_code)
print(json.dumps(r.json(), indent=2))
404
{
  "error": {
    "message": "No allowed providers are available for the selected model. Providers serving anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5-20260928: google-vertex, amazon-bedrock, azure, claude-on-aws, anthropic, but your request's provider.only preference permits only: openai.",
    "code": 404,
    "metadata": {
      "available_providers": [
        "google-vertex",
        "amazon-bedrock",
        "azure",
        "claude-on-aws",
        "anthropic"
      ],
      "requested_providers": [
        "openai"
      ],
      "routing_funnel": [
        {
          "step": "Initial Endpoints",
          "endpoint_count": 8
        },
        {
          "step": "Filter by Regional Surcharge",
          "endpoint_count": 5
        }
      ],
      "failed_routing_step": "Filter by Allowed Providers"
    }
  }
}

The error lists every provider that could have served the request, so you can copy the slugs you need straight into your only list.

Step 3: Add a fallback model

If every provider for a model is busy at once, for example during a demand spike after a new release, a second model can answer instead. List the models in order with models and send the request the same way as in step 2:

body = {
    "models": ["anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5", "anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5"],
    "provider": {
        "order": ["anthropic", "amazon-bedrock", "google-vertex"],
        "allow_fallbacks": True,
    },
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the word ok."}],
    "max_tokens": 16,
}
200 anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 Anthropic

Sonnet was available, so it answered. If it had failed at every provider, we’d have sent the request to Haiku 5.5, and the response’s model field would name it. Model fallbacks trigger on any error from the first model, including rate limits, downtime and context-length errors. If the last model in the list fails too, you get its error back.

Pick a fallback model that’s good enough for your task. A smaller model like Haiku 5.5 suits routine work such as short summaries or classification, and our lowest-cost inference guide covers how to find the cheapest model that still does the job. For work that only the bigger model handles well, rely on a second provider and retries instead of a smaller fallback.

How do you fix 529 errors in Claude Code?

Claude Code already does step 1 for you. It retries transient failures up to 10 times with exponential backoff, and it only shows API Error: Repeated 529 Overloaded errors once those retries run out. You can change the count with CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_RETRIES, but when the model stays busy, more retries just mean a longer wait. The quickest fix without any setup is to run /model and switch models, since Anthropic tracks capacity per model.

To keep the model you chose, run Claude Code on OpenRouter, which adds step 2. The quickest way is Ori Harness, which starts the Claude Code already on your machine with OpenRouter settings in place:

curl -fsSL https://openrouter.ai/labs/ori/install.sh | bash
ori claude --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5

Ori opens a browser so you can sign in with your OpenRouter account, so there is no API key to create or paste. Only sessions you start with ori claude run on OpenRouter, and plain claude works as before.

To set it up by hand instead, set three environment variables:

export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="https://openrouter.ai/api"
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="$OPENROUTER_API_KEY"
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""  # must be empty

If you were signed in with a Claude account, run /logout once and relaunch so the variables take effect. Our Claude Code guide recommends keeping Anthropic as your top-priority provider, because that’s the one Claude Code is guaranteed to work with. When Anthropic is overloaded, requests fail over to the other providers serving the same model.

We ran Claude Code this way nine times on a small bug-fix task, with Opus, Sonnet and Haiku 5.5, and every session completed. Claude Code with OpenRouter covers the rest of the setup, including choosing a model for each role.

Frequently asked questions

Is a 529 error my fault?

No. A 529 means Anthropic’s API is at capacity for that model across all users. Your key, plan and request are fine. A 429 is the error caused by your own usage.

How long does a Claude 529 last?

Usually a few seconds, which is why retries with backoff fix most of them. During heavy demand, an overload can last minutes, and that’s when sending the request to another provider helps.

Does a paid plan or higher tier prevent 529 errors?

No. A higher tier raises your rate limits, which prevents 429s, but a 529 comes from total demand on the model. Serving the model from more than one provider is what reduces your exposure.

How do I check whether Claude is down?

Anthropic posts incidents at status.claude.com, and the old status.anthropic.com address redirects there. On OpenRouter, each model’s page shows recent uptime for every provider that serves it, for example, Claude Sonnet 5.5.

Next steps

  • Ori Harness runs Claude Code and other agent CLIs on OpenRouter with one command.
  • Provider routing covers order, allow_fallbacks, only and sorting by price or throughput.
  • Model fallbacks lists what triggers a fallback and how to order models.
  • Uptime optimization explains how we track provider health.
  • OpenRouter failover and fallbacks explained shows how provider failover and model fallbacks work together.
  • Keep your agent running when models disappear handles the longer-term version of this problem, when a model is retired.

item.title: [OpenRouter] Hit Your Claude Code Usage Limit? How to Keep Coding
item.content:encoded:
Hit Your Claude Code Usage Limit? How to Keep Coding

OpenRouter ·10/28/2026

When you hit your Claude Code usage limit, you can keep coding by running Claude Code on an OpenRouter API key. Through OpenRouter, Claude Code runs on a pay-per-token API key with the same Claude models and no five-hour window. You set three environment variables, and you switch back to your plan when it resets.

We tested this setup with Claude Code. The outputs and costs below come from those runs.

Tl;dr

  • Your Claude plan has a five-hour limit and a weekly limit. An OpenRouter API key has neither. You pay for the tokens you use instead.
  • The quickest setup is Ori Harness: ori claude starts Claude Code on OpenRouter for that session, with a browser sign-in and no key to paste.
  • To do it by hand, three environment variables point Claude Code at OpenRouter. We put them in a shell function called claude-or, so claude still uses your plan.
  • Start with Claude Sonnet 5.5. A typical short Claude Code session costs $0.16 on Sonnet 5.5, $0.31 on Opus 5.5, and less than one cent on Haiku 5.5.
  • Don’t trust the cost Claude Code prints. In our test, it showed $0.375 for a run we were billed $0.008 for. Check your key or the Activity page instead.
  • When your plan resets, type claude again. There is nothing to undo.

Why does Claude Code hit a usage limit?

Claude plans have two limits that run at the same time. The first resets five hours after your first prompt. The second resets every seven days. Anthropic does not publish an exact number of prompts for either one. Claude Code uses many more tokens than a normal chat, so you can run out in the middle of a task. When that happens, Claude Code stops and tells you when your limit resets. Anthropic’s help article on usage limits explains both limits.

An OpenRouter API key does not work this way. You pay for each token you use, and you can keep going as long as you have credit.

The quickest way: run Claude Code through Ori Harness

Ori Harness starts the Claude Code already on your machine with OpenRouter settings in place. Install it and start Claude Code through it:

curl -fsSL https://openrouter.ai/labs/ori/install.sh | bash
ori claude --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5

Ori opens a browser so you can sign in with your OpenRouter account. It uses OAuth, so there is no key to create or paste. Only sessions you start with ori claude run on OpenRouter, so plain claude keeps using your plan, and you switch back by typing claude when your plan resets. The usage goes on your OpenRouter bill. If you are in an organization, a guardrail with a budget limit on your account caps what it can spend, and OpenRouter applies it to Ori sessions too.

The steps below do the same thing by hand, with an API key and a shell function. Use them if you want a key with its own credit limit, which works on any account. The cost advice in Step 4 applies either way.

Step 1: Get an OpenRouter API key and set a limit

Create a key on the API keys page and give it a credit limit. We set ours to $4. That way, even a long session cannot spend more than $4. A credit limit is one of several ways to control spending on OpenRouter. Our guide to governing AI spend across a team covers the others.

To check the limit, ask our API about your key:

curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/key \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY"

This is the part of the response that matters:

{
  "data": {
    "limit": 4,
    "limit_remaining": 4,
    "usage": 0
  }
}

The limit_remaining number tells you how much money is left on the key. You can run this check at any time. After a request, it can take a few seconds for the new total to show.

Step 2: Add a command that switches to your key

You could add the variables to your shell profile, but then every Claude Code session would charge your key. We want your normal claude command to keep using your plan, so we put the variables in a small shell function instead. Add this to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc:

claude-or() {
  ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="https://openrouter.ai/api" \
  ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="$OPENROUTER_API_KEY" \
  ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="" \
  ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL="anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5" \
  ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL="anthropic/claude-opus-5.5" \
  ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL="anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5" \
  CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL="anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5" \
  claude "$@"
}

The first three lines are the ones that matter:

  • ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL tells Claude Code to send its requests to us.
  • ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN holds your OpenRouter key.
  • ANTHROPIC_API_KEY must be empty. If it is not, Claude Code may try to sign in to Anthropic instead.

The other four lines are optional. They tell Claude Code which Claude model to use for Sonnet, Opus, and Haiku. They also send sub-agents, the smaller helper tasks Claude Code starts on its own, to Haiku 5.5.

These variables only apply when you type claude-or. Save the file and open a new terminal so the function is ready.

Step 3: Check that Claude Code is using your key

Before you start real work, check that Claude Code is sending its requests to OpenRouter and not to your plan. The quickest way is to send one short prompt and look at which model answered. Run this in your terminal:

claude-or --model sonnet -p "Reply with exactly: ok" --output-format json

This is the part of our response that matters:

{
  "is_error": false,
  "result": "ok"
}

The reply came back with no error. The modelUsage field in the full output names the model that answered, and in our run it was anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5. We ran the same prompt with --model haiku, and modelUsage named anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5.

Then run the key check from Step 1 again. If usage has gone up, the requests were billed to your key and not to the plan. If it hasn’t, Claude Code did not pick up the variables. Open a new terminal and try again.

Step 4: Keep the cost down

On a key, you pay for every message. The table shows our prices for the three Claude 5.5 models. It also shows the median cost of a real Claude Code session of two to nine messages on OpenRouter.

ModelPrice per 1M input tokensPrice per 1M output tokensMedian session cost (2 to 9 messages)
Claude Opus 5.5$4.00$20.00$0.305
Claude Sonnet 5.5$2.00$10.00$0.155
Claude Haiku 5.5$0.10$0.50$0.007

Prices as of October 21, 2026. Session costs come from our session-cost dataset and cover the 30 days to October 18, 2026.

Start with Sonnet 5.5. It costs about half as much per session as Opus 5.5 and handles most everyday coding. When a problem is hard, type /model opus to switch, and switch back when you are done. If you build your own app on our API, you can also move a request to a stronger model automatically when the cheaper model is not confident in its answer.

Every new session starts with about 28,000 tokens of Claude Code’s own instructions and tool list (28,156 in our run on Claude Code 2.1.307, and the number changes between versions). They are written to the prompt cache on the first request, so a one-word prompt in Step 3 costs about $0.07 on Sonnet 5.5 and less than half a cent on Haiku 5.5.

Sub-agents are cheap on Haiku. When we asked Sonnet 5.5 to start a sub-agent, the main agent ran on Sonnet 5.5, and the sub-agent ran on Haiku 5.5, as the function sets.

Haiku can also handle small fixes on its own. We gave Haiku 5.5 a shopping-cart file with two bugs and three failing tests. It fixed both bugs, all three tests passed, and we were billed $0.008 for the run.

Don’t rely on the cost Claude Code prints. For that Haiku run, Claude Code reported $0.375, but we were billed $0.008. Claude Code prices the session with Anthropic’s own price table, and it guesses when it doesn’t recognize an OpenRouter model name. To see what you are really spending, check limit_remaining with the Step 1 command, or open your Activity page.

Step 5: Switch back when your plan resets

When your plan’s limit resets, type claude instead of claude-or. You do not need to change anything, because the OpenRouter settings only live inside the function. In our test, plain claude answered on the plan’s model, and the usage on our OpenRouter key did not change.

What happens if the API key runs out?

When your key reaches its credit limit, or your account runs out of credit, we stop the request before it reaches the model and return an error. The error includes a limit_source field that tells you why:

  • openrouter_key_limit means the key has used up its limit.
  • openrouter_credits means your account is out of credit.

To keep going, raise the key’s limit on the API keys page or add credit to your account. Our limits page explains every kind of limit, including ones a team admin can set.

Frequently asked questions

Does OpenRouter have usage limits for Claude Code?

There are no five-hour or weekly limits. The only limits are on spending: how much credit you have, the limit you set on your key, and any budget your team admin has set.

Are the models the same as on my Claude plan?

Yes. They are Anthropic’s Claude models. We get them from Anthropic and from cloud providers like Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex, and if one provider has a problem, we send your request to another. For Claude Code, we recommend setting Anthropic as your first choice of provider, because Claude Code is only guaranteed to work with Anthropic.

Can I use a cheaper model when I hit the limit?

Yes. Sonnet 5.5 costs about half as much per session as Opus 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 costs less than a cent per session. You can also put a different model in one of the variables in the function. Many people use other models in Claude Code through OpenRouter. This month, GLM 5.3 Flash is the second most used model in Claude Code on our apps page, after Claude Opus 5.5. Claude Code is built for Claude models, though, so try any other model on a small task first. If you call our API from your own code, you can also list fallback models so a request moves to a second model when the first one fails. For more ways to lower what you pay per request, see our guide to the lowest-cost LLM inference on OpenRouter.

When does the Claude Code usage limit reset?

The five-hour limit resets five hours after the first prompt in that window. The weekly limit resets seven days after it starts. Claude Code shows the reset time when it stops you, so you know when to type claude again.

How do I check how much usage I have left?

On your Claude plan, Claude Code tells you when your limit resets when it stops you. On OpenRouter, check limit_remaining with GET /api/v1/key, or open your Activity page.

Next steps

Our Claude Code setup guide has the full setup, including a status line that shows your cost as you work. If you want to use OpenRouter with Claude Code every day, not only when you hit a limit, our Claude Code tutorial walks you through it. To run it on OpenRouter without managing a key, Ori Harness starts Claude Code, or another agent CLI, with one command. If you are setting this up for a team, workspace budgets let you limit how much each team can spend.

item.title: [OpenRouter] How we rebuilt provider routing for better, faster inference
item.content:encoded:
How we rebuilt provider routing for better, faster inference

Scott Morse ·10/28/2026

Today we’re announcing the biggest improvement to our provider routing algorithm since the founding of OpenRouter.

Until now, our default router mostly rewarded providers for one thing: a low price. The new router rewards the inference that is actually best for you: cheap, but also fast, high-throughput, and reliable. Providers that deliver more value automatically win more traffic, so every provider has a reason to keep improving. That means the inference you get through OpenRouter keeps getting faster, more reliable, and more cost-effective, and you don’t have to change a line of code.

It’s already working. The new algorithm has unlocked significant improvements in TTFT (16.9%), throughput (16.3%) and capacity errors (a remarkable 67% reduction!), with only minor increases in cost (6.0%). That’s before providers have had any time to optimize for the new algorithm. See our full experimental results for more details.

How it works:

  • It measures what you actually get. For every model, it tracks each endpoint’s realized price, latency, throughput, and error rate, and picks the best blend of cost and performance for each request.
  • It reacts in real time. When an endpoint has trouble, traffic moves away from it until it recovers.
  • It rewards better inference. Providers that innovate are automatically rewarded with more traffic.

Routing is still cache-aware, so once we’ve sent you to a provider, your session stays put as long as the cache is warm.

Want price-only routing? You can still have it. See pinning and sorting providers in What stays the same.

Where we were: the limitations of Price-Only Routing

Most traffic (~77% of requests) on OpenRouter goes to models served by more than one provider. When a request doesn’t include an explicit sort or provider list, we need to pick a provider to send it to. Until now, we made that choice based almost entirely on input token price. The less expensive a provider was, the greater percentage of traffic it would receive, and any failed request was re-routed to the next cheapest option.

This price-only approach got users the lowest prices in the ecosystem, but it created some unintended consequences:

  • Cheap won even when it was bad. Fallbacks caught failures, but users waited through them, and speed improvements weren’t rewarded.
  • Static rankings. The algorithm was blind to real-time performance variations, so a provider had to degrade to the point of being de-ranked entirely before it was reflected in traffic distribution.
  • Vanishing margins. The only way for providers to win traffic was to cut price, putting pressure on them to reduce their investments in the very infrastructure that ensures reliability and quality.
  • Pricing games. The price we ranked by was almost all prompt input price, so a provider could keep traffic share with weird pricing cocktails like listing an artificially low input price and then making back the difference with overpriced cached or completion tokens.

We wanted to ensure a marketplace where competing providers won traffic by serving better inference, not just cheaper inference.

The New Algorithm: optimizing for what a good answer “costs”

The new routing algorithm constantly monitors the performance of each provider to calculate a real-time Routing Cost that captures what a user pays for a good answer. The Routing Cost encompasses the price in actual dollars and cents, the cost of time spent waiting for a response, and the cost of retries when a provider fails or provides an unusable response.

To put it simply: what does one try cost, and how often does it work?

What one try costs: price plus waiting

For each request, the router estimates how many input and output tokens it will use from the model’s recent traffic. That one estimate sets both parts of a try: the price you would pay and the time you would wait.

Effective price

Effective price is the price that the provider would actually charge you, calculated from recent measured traffic. It reflects the provider’s real cache hit rate and the model’s average mix of input and output tokens, so it can differ a lot from the list price. This ensures that a provider can’t win traffic by hiding expensive cached or output tokens behind a low input price.

The router prices your request at each provider’s effective price, and prioritizes the cheapest options.

Throughput

Throughput is what trades off against price: a faster provider can charge more and still win your request. It’s measured as output tokens per second end-to-end, so it includes the time to first token plus the time it takes the provider to stream the entire output response. The router adds that wait to the Routing Cost using a conversion rate set per model, based on what its providers typically charge and how fast they are.

Time to first token

Time to first token (TTFT) is how long you would wait before the response started streaming. It adds to the Routing Cost on its own, even though it already counts toward throughput, because interactive use depends on it most. In an agent session, the model may make many tool calls in a row, and each one waits for a first token.

Rate limits

A rate limit (HTTP 429) means the provider is out of capacity and turned your request away. You would have to wait for the rejection, then your full request would go to another provider. The router adds that wait plus a penalty to the provider’s Routing Cost, weighted by how often it rate limits requests, so the effect is usually small. Repeated rate limits matter more through the traffic caps and backoff described below.

How often it works: reliability and quality

A failed try still costs its price and its wait, so the Routing Cost calculates the expected cost of having to retry until one works. If 1 in 5 tries fails, you pay for 1.25 tries per good answer.

Reliability

A reliability error is a request that fails because of the provider. You would lose the attempt and have to retry, so each error carries a heavy penalty in the Routing Cost.

If a provider’s error rate climbs far above the other providers for the same model, the router stops sending it requests until it recovers.

Quality

Quality measures whether a provider’s responses are usable. Today the main check is whether tool calls come back well formed, and we’re adding more. Each bad response raises the provider’s Routing Cost, because a cheap wrong answer is expensive.

A provider flagged for broken tool calls, or for benchmark accuracy well below what the model should score, drops far behind and only gets a small amount of test traffic until the flag clears.

Close gets close: how traffic is shared

Sending every request to the single best provider would overload it, so traffic is shared. Faster providers can carry a higher Routing Cost and stay competitive. Everything inside the competitive edge shares most of the traffic, and being a little behind the best costs a little. Past the edge, traffic share drops off fast.

Three guardrails sit on top:

  • Floor: every provider keeps a trickle of traffic, so we can notice when struggling endpoints improve. New endpoints start from the model’s typical numbers, so they don’t need a traffic history.
  • Back off: a provider that starts failing or rate limiting gets less until it recovers.
  • Cap: the router learns how much load each provider can take before it returns 429s, and spills the rest to others. Add capacity and the cap rises on its own.

What stays the same

  • Requests that set provider.order bypass the new routing logic, with providers ordered as specified (default is price-based as before). Setting provider.only or provider.ignore will use the new algorithm to select from the remaining providers if there are more than one.
  • An explicit provider.sort (price, throughput, or latency) uses that sort instead of the new algorithm.
  • Only the first request in a conversation will have a provider algorithmically selected. An ongoing conversation is pinned to its original provider so that the prompt cache stays warm. If that provider becomes unavailable, the conversation will fall back to another provider automatically.
  • If a try fails, the request is retried with the next highest ranked provider.

How we measured it

In order to measure the impact of the new routing algorithm, we had to go beyond a standard A/B test, because changes in routing behavior can’t easily be isolated from the control group. For example, if the new algorithm did a better job of routing traffic away from a struggling provider, the old algorithm’s requests to that provider would find more capacity available and get faster, skewing the results. Further compounding the difficulty is the enormous variability in request shape and volume patterns. A single whale user that spins up an automated flurry of high effort requests to a single provider can artificially inflate the metrics for that provider regardless of which algorithm we used to route their requests.

So we ran a switchback experiment: We split each day into 3-hour blocks and flipped each matched pair of blocks between the new and old router, with a one-hour burn-in period of discarded data each changeover, and measured the per-model impact across a representative sample of open source models over one full week.

Results

Over the week of the experiment, we split over 24 million requests with 103 billion input tokens evenly between the old and new routing algorithms, measuring the impact on key performance metrics.

MeasureLegacyNew AlgorithmNew vs legacy95% interval
TTFT p501,007 ms837 ms16.9% lower13.9% to 19.8% lower
TTFT p954,601 ms3,733 ms18.9% lower15.7% to 21.9% lower
Throughput p5062.4 tok/s72.6 tok/s16.3% higher13.8% to 18.9% higher
Cost per K requests$1.25$1.326.0% higher5.1% to 7.0% higher
Cost per M tokens$0.301$0.3247.3% higher4.9% to 9.6% higher
Caller TTFT p501,130 ms941 ms16.7% lower13.8% to 19.7% lower
Caller TTFT p956,032 ms4,504 ms25.3% lower21.6% to 29.0% lower
Whole request p50 (time to last token)4.00 s3.24 s19.0% lower14.2% to 23.6% lower
Whole request p9541.5 s34.9 s16.0% lower12.2% to 19.7% lower
Hit at least one 4297.1%3.8%−3.4 pt 67% fewer−4.2 to −2.5 pt 62% to 72% fewer
Needed a retry10.4%6.9%−3.5 pt 47% fewer−4.4 to −2.6 pt 41% to 52% fewer
Time spent in failed attempts, per req349 ms242 ms−106 ms 55% less−181 to −35 ms 48% to 60% less

Get started

If you use default routing, you’re done. The provider that served each request is in the response and on your activity page.

To keep the old price-only routing, set provider.sort to "price", append :floor to the model slug, or set your default sort to price in account settings. To pick providers yourself, use provider.order or provider.only. See the provider routing guide.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to change my code to use the new routing?

No. Requests with no explicit provider sort and no provider order, only, or ignore list use the new router automatically on the models where it's enabled. Your API key, request body, and model IDs stay the same.

How do I keep price-only routing?

Set provider.sort to price in the request body, append :floor to the model slug, or set your default provider sort to price in account settings. Any explicit sort bypasses the new router.

Does the new routing override my provider order or only list?

provider.order bypasses the new router and routes in the order you specify. provider.only and provider.ignore still filter the candidate set, but the new algorithm picks among the providers that remain.

Will the new routing cost more than price-only routing?

It can, since it will sometimes pick a faster or more reliable provider over the cheapest one. In our live experiment, cost per request increased by 6.0%, while realizing a 16.9% improvement in TTFT, a 16.3% improvement in throughput, and a 67% decrease in 429 error rate.

How does a provider get more traffic under the new routing?

Improve the signals the router scores: effective price, time to first token, throughput, error and rate-limit rates, and output quality.

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Building an Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence
